[c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}}{Y^{{{\zeta}}}_{{\mathchoice{\makebox[5.25pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[5.25pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[3.67499pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[2.625pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}}{Y^{{{\zeta}}}_{{\mathchoice{\makebox[5.25pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[5.25pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[3.67499pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[2.625pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}}+\mathchoice{\Gamma^{{{\zeta}\mathchoice{\makebox[5.25pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[5.25pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[3.67499pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[2.625pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}\mathchoice{\makebox[5.25pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[5.25pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[3.67499pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[2.625pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}_{{\mathchoice{\makebox[5.25pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[5.25pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[3.67499pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[2.625pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}{\zeta}{\zeta}}}}{\Gamma^{{{\zeta}\mathchoice{\makebox[5.25pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[5.25pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[3.67499pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[2.625pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}\mathchoice{\makebox[5.25pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[5.25pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[3.67499pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[2.625pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}_{{\mathchoice{\makebox[5.25pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[5.25pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[3.67499pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[2.625pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}{\zeta}{\zeta}}}}{\Gamma^{{{\zeta}\mathchoice{\makebox[5.25pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[5.25pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[3.67499pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[2.625pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}\mathchoice{\makebox[5.25pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[5.25pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[3.67499pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[2.625pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}_{{\mathchoice{\makebox[5.25pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[5.25pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[3.67499pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[2.625pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}{\zeta}{\zeta}}}}{\Gamma^{{{\zeta}\mathchoice{\makebox[5.25pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[5.25pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[3.67499pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[2.625pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}\mathchoice{\makebox[5.25pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[5.25pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[3.67499pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[2.625pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}_{{\mathchoice{\makebox[5.25pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[5.25pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[3.67499pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[2.625pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}{\zeta}{\zeta}}}}\mathchoice{Y^{{{\zeta}}}_{{\mathchoice{\makebox[5.25pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[5.25pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[3.67499pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[2.625pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}}{Y^{{{\zeta}}}_{{\mathchoice{\makebox[5.25pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[5.25pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[3.67499pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[2.625pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}}{Y^{{{\zeta}}}_{{\mathchoice{\makebox[5.25pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[5.25pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[3.67499pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[2.625pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}}{Y^{{{\zeta}}}_{{\mathchoice{\makebox[5.25pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[5.25pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[3.67499pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[2.625pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}}

\displaystyle=\mathchoice{\nabla^{{\mathchoice{\makebox[3.57375pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[3.57375pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.1205pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.51463pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}_{{{c}}}}{\nabla^{{\mathchoice{\makebox[3.57375pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[3.57375pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.1205pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.51463pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}_{{{c}}}}{\nabla^{{\mathchoice{\makebox[3.57375pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[3.57375pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.1205pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.51463pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}_{{{c}}}}{\nabla^{{\mathchoice{\makebox[3.57375pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[3.57375pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.1205pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.51463pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}_{{{c}}}}\mathchoice{Y^{{{c}}}_{{\mathchoice{\makebox[3.57375pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[3.57375pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.1205pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.51463pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}}{Y^{{{c}}}_{{\mathchoice{\makebox[3.57375pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[3.57375pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.1205pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.51463pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}}{Y^{{{c}}}_{{\mathchoice{\makebox[3.57375pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[3.57375pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.1205pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.51463pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}}{Y^{{{c}}}_{{\mathchoice{\makebox[3.57375pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[3.57375pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.1205pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.51463pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}}.

(71c)

Eq.

71c
is trivial. The derivatives in
Eqs.

71a
and
71b
should be understood as Wirtinger derivatives, which are defined and discussed on Appendix
A
. In summary, for
\zeta=x+iy
they are the linear operators

\partialderivative{\zeta}=\frac{1}{2}\quantity(\pdv{x} - i \pdv{y})\quad\mbox{and}\quad\partialderivative{\bar{\zeta}}=\frac{1}{2}\quantity(\pdv{x} + i \pdv{y})

(72)

and, as a consequence, the equation

\partialderivative{f}{\bar{\zeta}}=0

(73)

is equivalent to the Cauchy–Riemann equations. It follows that
f
is a holomorphic function of
\zeta
if, and only if, it is real-differentiable on the plane and
\partialderivative*{f}{\bar{\zeta}}=0
. Hence,
Eqs.

71a
and
71b
imply that
\mathchoice{Y^{{{\zeta}}}_{{\mathchoice{\makebox[5.25pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[5.25pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[3.67499pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[2.625pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}}{Y^{{{\zeta}}}_{{\mathchoice{\makebox[5.25pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[5.25pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[3.67499pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[2.625pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}}{Y^{{{\zeta}}}_{{\mathchoice{\makebox[5.25pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[5.25pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[3.67499pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[2.625pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}}{Y^{{{\zeta}}}_{{\mathchoice{\makebox[5.25pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[5.25pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[3.67499pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[2.625pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}}
(resp.
\mathchoice{Y^{{{\bar{\zeta}}}}_{{\mathchoice{\makebox[5.00002pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[5.00002pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[5.00002pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[5.00002pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}}{Y^{{{\bar{\zeta}}}}_{{\mathchoice{\makebox[5.00002pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[5.00002pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[5.00002pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[5.00002pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}}{Y^{{{\bar{\zeta}}}}_{{\mathchoice{\makebox[5.00002pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[5.00002pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[5.00002pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[5.00002pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}}{Y^{{{\bar{\zeta}}}}_{{\mathchoice{\makebox[5.00002pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[5.00002pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[5.00002pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[5.00002pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}}
) is a holomorphic function of
\zeta
(
\bar{\zeta}
).

It follows that the local Killing vector fields are characterized by linear combinations of fields with the form
\mathchoice{Y^{{{\zeta}}}_{{\mathchoice{\makebox[5.25pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[5.25pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[3.67499pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[2.625pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}}{Y^{{{\zeta}}}_{{\mathchoice{\makebox[5.25pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[5.25pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[3.67499pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[2.625pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}}{Y^{{{\zeta}}}_{{\mathchoice{\makebox[5.25pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[5.25pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[3.67499pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[2.625pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}}{Y^{{{\zeta}}}_{{\mathchoice{\makebox[5.25pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[5.25pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[3.67499pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[2.625pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}}=\alpha\zeta^{n}
for
\alpha\in\mdmathbb{C}
and
n\geq 0
an integer. There is, however, a caveat: some of these fields may not be global Killing vector fields (as we would need for a complete Killing vector field). This is because the stereographic coordinate we are working with is only defined away from the north pole, since
\zeta=\infty

at
the north pole. To avoid this, we define a new stereographic coordinate
\xi
through

\xi=-e^{i\phi}\tan(\frac{\theta}{2})=\frac{z-r}{x-iy}.

(74)

\xi
is then the coordinate antipodally related to
\zeta
. These two coordinate systems are related by

\xi=-\frac{1}{\bar{\zeta}},

(75)

with an analogous expression for the conjugates. The line element in the
\xi
coordinate is identical to the expression in terms of the
\zeta
coordinate, and hence so are the results of the Killing equation:
\mathchoice{Y^{{{\xi}}}_{{\mathchoice{\makebox[5.25pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[5.25pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[3.67499pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[2.625pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}}{Y^{{{\xi}}}_{{\mathchoice{\makebox[5.25pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[5.25pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[3.67499pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[2.625pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}}{Y^{{{\xi}}}_{{\mathchoice{\makebox[5.25pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[5.25pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[3.67499pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[2.625pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}}{Y^{{{\xi}}}_{{\mathchoice{\makebox[5.25pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[5.25pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[3.67499pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[2.625pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}}
must be a holomorphic function of
\xi
.

Consider now the vector field defined by
\mathchoice{Y^{{{\zeta}}}_{{\mathchoice{\makebox[5.25pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[5.25pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[3.67499pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[2.625pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}}{Y^{{{\zeta}}}_{{\mathchoice{\makebox[5.25pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[5.25pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[3.67499pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[2.625pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}}{Y^{{{\zeta}}}_{{\mathchoice{\makebox[5.25pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[5.25pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[3.67499pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[2.625pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}}{Y^{{{\zeta}}}_{{\mathchoice{\makebox[5.25pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[5.25pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[3.67499pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[2.625pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}}=\alpha\zeta^{n}
. When we change coordinates from
\zeta
to
\xi
, we find that the same vector field has the component

\mathchoice{Y^{{{\xi}}}_{{\mathchoice{\makebox[5.25pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[5.25pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[3.67499pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[2.625pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}}{Y^{{{\xi}}}_{{\mathchoice{\makebox[5.25pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[5.25pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[3.67499pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[2.625pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}}{Y^{{{\xi}}}_{{\mathchoice{\makebox[5.25pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[5.25pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[3.67499pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[2.625pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}}{Y^{{{\xi}}}_{{\mathchoice{\makebox[5.25pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[5.25pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[3.67499pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[2.625pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}}=\frac{(-1)^{n}\bar{\alpha}}{\xi^{n-2}}.

(76)

This is only a holomorphic function of
\xi
for
n\leq 2
.

Therefore, we find that there is a six-dimensional real space of possible conformal Killing vector fields, which is spanned by
\mathchoice{Y^{{{\zeta}}}_{{\mathchoice{\makebox[5.25pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[5.25pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[3.67499pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[2.625pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}}{Y^{{{\zeta}}}_{{\mathchoice{\makebox[5.25pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[5.25pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[3.67499pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[2.625pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}}{Y^{{{\zeta}}}_{{\mathchoice{\makebox[5.25pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[5.25pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[3.67499pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[2.625pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}}{Y^{{{\zeta}}}_{{\mathchoice{\makebox[5.25pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[5.25pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[3.67499pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[2.625pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}}=1,\zeta,\zeta^{2},i,i\zeta,i\zeta^{2}
. Are these vector fields complete?

Let us consider some curve that is everywhere parallel to the most general vector field with

\mathchoice{Y^{{{\zeta}}}_{{\mathchoice{\makebox[5.25pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[5.25pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[3.67499pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[2.625pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}}{Y^{{{\zeta}}}_{{\mathchoice{\makebox[5.25pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[5.25pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[3.67499pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[2.625pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}}{Y^{{{\zeta}}}_{{\mathchoice{\makebox[5.25pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[5.25pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[3.67499pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[2.625pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}}{Y^{{{\zeta}}}_{{\mathchoice{\makebox[5.25pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[5.25pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[3.67499pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[2.625pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}}=\alpha+\beta\zeta+\gamma\zeta^{2}

(77)

for
\alpha,\beta,\gamma\in\mdmathbb{C}
. This curve is characterized by the differential equation

\derivative{\zeta}{t}=\alpha+\beta\zeta+\gamma\zeta^{2}.

(78)

The full solution has the form

\zeta(t)=\frac{a(t)\zeta(0)+b(t)}{c(t)\zeta(0)+d(t)},

(79)

where the specific functional form of
a(t)
,
b(t)
,
c(t)
, and
d(t)
depends on the values of
\alpha,\beta,\gamma
, and the general case is particularly complicated. One can choose their normalization such that
ad-bc=1
. Such a transformation
\zeta(0)\to\zeta(t)
is known as a Möbius transformation, and these transformations correspond precisely to the conformal transformations on the Riemann sphere.

Notice that a Möbius transformation

\zeta\to\frac{a\zeta+b}{c\zeta+d}

(80)

with
ad-bc=1
has precisely one pole at
\zeta=-d/c
and one zero at
\zeta=-b/a
. They are meromorphic in the complex plane and are a diffeomorphism of the Riemann sphere onto itself.

The (non-conformal) Killing vector fields on the sphere are the conformal Killing vector fields which satisfy the extra condition
\mathchoice{\nabla^{{\mathchoice{\makebox[4.33765pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[4.33765pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.59009pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.85005pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}_{{{a}}}}{\nabla^{{\mathchoice{\makebox[4.33765pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[4.33765pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.59009pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.85005pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}_{{{a}}}}{\nabla^{{\mathchoice{\makebox[4.33765pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[4.33765pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.59009pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.85005pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}_{{{a}}}}{\nabla^{{\mathchoice{\makebox[4.33765pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[4.33765pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.59009pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.85005pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}_{{{a}}}}\mathchoice{Y^{{{a}}}_{{\mathchoice{\makebox[4.33765pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[4.33765pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.59009pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.85005pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}}{Y^{{{a}}}_{{\mathchoice{\makebox[4.33765pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[4.33765pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.59009pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.85005pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}}{Y^{{{a}}}_{{\mathchoice{\makebox[4.33765pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[4.33765pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.59009pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.85005pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}}{Y^{{{a}}}_{{\mathchoice{\makebox[4.33765pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[4.33765pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.59009pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.85005pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}}=0
. Imposing this condition on a vector field with the form (
77
) we conclude that a (non-conformal) Killing vector field has the form (
77
) with the extra conditions that
\beta+\bar{\beta}=0
and
\gamma=\bar{\alpha}
. These are three real constraints, so we get a three-dimensional real space of Killing vector fields.

What is the group of confomorphisms on the sphere? To answer this question, we must study how two Möbius transformations compose. Consider two consecutive Möbius transformations

\zeta\to\zeta^{\prime}=\frac{a\zeta+b}{c\zeta+d}\quad\mbox{and}\quad\zeta^{\prime}\to\zeta^{\prime\prime}=\frac{a^{\prime}\zeta^{\prime}+b^{\prime}}{c^{\prime}\zeta^{\prime}+d^{\prime}}.

(81)

We want to express the coefficients of the resulting transformation

\zeta\to\zeta^{\prime\prime}=\frac{a^{\prime\prime}\zeta+b^{\prime\prime}}{c^{\prime\prime}\zeta+d^{\prime\prime}}

(82)

in terms of the original coefficients. We assume that

ad-bc=a^{\prime}d^{\prime}-b^{\prime}c^{\prime}=1.

(83)

One can show that

\matrixquantity(\lx@physics@matrix a'' & b'' \\ c'' & d''\endlx@physics@matrix)=\matrixquantity(\lx@physics@matrix a' & b' \\ c' & d'\endlx@physics@matrix)\matrixquantity(\lx@physics@matrix a & b \\ c & d\endlx@physics@matrix),

(84)

with

a^{\prime\prime}d^{\prime\prime}-b^{\prime\prime}c^{\prime\prime}=1.

(85)

This is the product of two
2\times 2
complex matrices with unit determinant. Furthermore, notice that the Möbius transformation corresponding to the matrix
L
is the same Möbius transformation corresponding to the matrix
-L
. Hence, the group is the group
\mathrm{SL}(2,\mdmathbb{C})/\mdmathbb{Z}_{2}
: the group of
2\times 2
complex matrices with unit determinant up to sign. This may seem complicated, but it turns out that there is an isomorphism

\mathrm{SL}(2,\mdmathbb{C})/\mdmathbb{Z}_{2}\cong\mathrm{SO}^{+}(3,1),

(86)

which is proven on Appendix
B
. Hence, the group of confomorphisms on the two-sphere is just the restricted Lorentz group!

It can also be shown that the group of isometries on the two-sphere is
\mathrm{SO}(3)
, as one would expect. This is done by proving the matrices representing the Möbius transformations are now unitary,
L^{\dagger}L=\text{1}
. As a consequence, they now live in the group
\mathrm{SU}(2)
of
2\times 2
unitary matrices. Up to sign, we get
\mathrm{SU}(2)/\mdmathbb{Z}_{2}\cong\mathrm{SO}(3)
through arguments analogous to those of Appendix
B
.

3.5
Case Study: Isometries on Minkowski Spacetime

It is instructive to consider as a second case study the isometries in Minkowski spacetime. We should, of course, recover the Poincaré transformations. We work in
n
-dimensional Minkowski spacetime, for generality.

The Killing equation is

\mathchoice{\partial^{{\mathchoice{\makebox[5.25pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[5.25pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[3.67499pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[2.625pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}_{{{\rho}}}}{\partial^{{\mathchoice{\makebox[5.25pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[5.25pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[3.67499pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[2.625pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}_{{{\rho}}}}{\partial^{{\mathchoice{\makebox[5.25pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[5.25pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[3.67499pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[2.625pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}_{{{\rho}}}}{\partial^{{\mathchoice{\makebox[5.25pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[5.25pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[3.67499pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[2.625pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}_{{{\rho}}}}\mathchoice{\partial^{{\mathchoice{\makebox[5.25pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[5.25pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[3.67499pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[2.625pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}_{{{\mu}}}}{\partial^{{\mathchoice{\makebox[5.25pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[5.25pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[3.67499pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[2.625pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}_{{{\mu}}}}{\partial^{{\mathchoice{\makebox[5.25pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[5.25pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[3.67499pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[2.625pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}_{{{\mu}}}}{\partial^{{\mathchoice{\makebox[5.25pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[5.25pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[3.67499pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[2.625pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}_{{{\mu}}}}\mathchoice{\xi^{{\mathchoice{\makebox[5.25pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[5.25pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[3.67499pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[2.625pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}_{{{\nu}}}}{\xi^{{\mathchoice{\makebox[5.25pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[5.25pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[3.67499pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[2.625pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}_{{{\nu}}}}{\xi^{{\mathchoice{\makebox[5.25pt][c]{$\di (90)

meaning
\mathchoice{\xi^{{\mathchoice{\makebox[5.25pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[5.25pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[3.67499pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[2.625pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}_{{{\mu}}}}{\xi^{{\mathchoice{\makebox[5.25pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[5.25pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[3.67499pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[2.625pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}_{{{\mu}}}}{\xi^{{\mathchoice{\makebox[5.25pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[5.25pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[3.67499pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[2.625pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}_{{{\mu}}}}{\xi^{{\mathchoice{\makebox[5.25pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[5.25pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[3.67499pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[2.625pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}_{{{\mu}}}}
is at most linear in the coordinates.

The most general expression for
\mathchoice{\xi^{{{a}}}_{{\mathchoice{\makebox[4.33765pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[4.33765pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.59009pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.85005pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}}{\xi^{{{a}}}_{{\mathchoice{\makebox[4.33765pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[4.33765pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.59009pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.85005pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}}{\xi^{{{a}}}_{{\mathchoice{\makebox[4.33765pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[4.33765pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.59009pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.85005pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}}{\xi^{{{a}}}_{{\mathchoice{\makebox[4.33765pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[4.33765pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.59009pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.85005pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}}

(91)

Eq.

88
now yields

\mathchoice{\beta^{{\mathchoice{\makebox[5.25pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[5.25pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[3.67499pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[2.625pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}\mathchoice{\makebox[5.25pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[5.25pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[3.67499pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[2.625pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}_{{{\nu}{\mu}}}}{\beta^{{\mathchoice{\makebox[5.25pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[5.25pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[3.67499pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[2.625pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}\mathchoice{\makebox[5.25pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[5.25pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[3.67499pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[2.625pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}_{{{\nu}{\mu}}}}{\beta^{{\mathchoice{\makebox[5.25pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[5.25pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[3.67499pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[2.625pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}\mathchoice{\makebox[5.25pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[5.25pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[3.67499pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[2.625pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}_{{{\nu}{\mu}}}}{\beta^{{\mathchoice{\makebox[5.25pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[5.25pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[3.67499pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[2.625pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}\mathchoice{\makebox[5.25pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[5.25pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[3.67499pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[2.625pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}_{{{\nu}{\mu}}}}+\mathchoice{\beta^{{\mathchoice{\makebox[5.25pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[5.25pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[3.67499pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[2.625pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}\mathchoice{\makebox[5.25pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[5.25pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[3.67499pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[2.625pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}_{{{\mu}{\nu}}}}{\beta^{{\mathchoice{\makebox[5.25pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[5.25pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[3.67499pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[2.625pt][c]{$\scrip (92)

establishing that
\mathchoice{\beta^{{\mathchoice{\makebox[5.25pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[5.25pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[3.67499pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[2.625pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}\mathchoice{\makebox[5.25pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[5.25pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[3.67499pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[2.625pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}_{{{\mu}{\nu}}}}{\beta^{{\mathchoice{\makebox[5.25pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[5.25pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[3.67499pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[2.625pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}\mathchoice{\makebox[5.25pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[5.25pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[3.67499pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[2.625pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}_{{{\mu}{\nu}}}}{\beta^{{\mathchoice{\makebox[5.25pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[5.25pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[3.67499pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[2.625pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}\mathchoice{\makebox[5.25pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[5.25pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[3.67499pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[2.625pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}_{{{\mu}{\nu}}}}{\beta^{{\mathchoice{\makebox[5.25pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[5.25pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[3.67499pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[2.625pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}\mathchoice{\makebox[5.25pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[5.25pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[3.67499pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[2.625pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}_{{{\mu}{\nu}}}}
is antisymmetric.

We thus see that the most general Killing vector field for Minkowski spacetime is

\mathchoice{\xi^{{{a}}}_{{\mathchoice{\makebox[4.33765pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[4.33765pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.59009pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.85005pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}}{\xi^{{{a}}}_{{\mathchoice{\makebox[4.33765pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[4.33765pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.59009pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.85005pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}}{\xi^{{{a}}}_{{\mathchoice{\makebox[4.33765pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[4.33765pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.59009pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.85005pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}}{\xi^{{{a}}}_{{\mathchoice{\makebox[4.33765pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[4.33765pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.59009pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.85005pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}}=(\mathchoice{\alpha^{{{\mu}}}_{{\mathchoice{\makebox[5.25pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[5.25pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[3.67499pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[2.625pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}}{\alpha^{{{\mu}}}_{{\mathchoice{\makebox[5.25pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[5.25pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[3.67499pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[2.625pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}}{\alpha^{{{\mu}}}_{{\mathchoice{\makebox[5.25pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[5.25pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[3.67499pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[2.625pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}}{\alpha^{{{\mu}}}_{{\mathchoice{\makebox[5.25pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[5.25pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[3.67499pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[2.625pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}}+\mathchoice{\beta^{{{\mu}\mathchoice{\makebox[5.25pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[5.25pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[3.67499pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[2.625pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}_{{\mathchoice{\makebox[5.25pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[5.25pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[3.67499pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[2.625pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}{\nu}}}}{\beta^{{{\mu}\mathchoice{\makebox[5.25pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[5.25pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[3.67499pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[2.625pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}_{{\mathchoice{\makebox[5.25pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[5.25pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[3.67499pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[2.625pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}{\nu}}}}{\beta^{{{\mu}\mathchoice{\makebox[5.25pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[5.25pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[3.67499pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[2.625pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}_{{\mathchoice{\makebox[5.25pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[5.25pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[3.67499pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[2.625pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}{\nu}}}}{\beta^{{{\mu}\mathchoice{\makebox[5.25pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[5.25pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[3.67499pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[2.625pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}_{{\mathchoice{\makebox[5.25pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[5.25pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[3.67499pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[2.625pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}{\nu}}}}\mathchoice{x^{{{\nu}}}_{{\mathchoice{\makebox[5.25pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[5.25pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[3.67499pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[2.625pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}}{x^{{{\nu}}}_{{\mathchoice{\makebox[5.25pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[5.25pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[3.67499pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[2.625pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}}{x^{{{\nu}}}_{{\mathchoice{\makebox[5.25pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[5.25pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[3.67499pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[2.625pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}}{x^{{{\nu}}}_{{\mathchoice{\makebox[5.25pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[5.25pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[3.67499pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[2.625pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}})\mathchoice{\quantity(\pdv{\tensor{x}{^\mu}})^{{{a}}}_{{\mathchoice{\makebox[4.33765pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[4.33765pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.59009pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.85005pt][c]{$\scri (93)

This field is defined everywhere.

Let us compute the flow of this Killing vector field. In Cartesian coordinates, it is given by the system of differential equations

\derivative{\tensor{x}{^\mu}}{\lambda}=\mathchoice{\alpha^{{{\mu}}}_{{\mathchoice{\makebox[5.25pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[5.25pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[3.67499pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[2.625pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}}{\alpha^{{{\mu}}}_{{\mathchoice{\makebox[5.25pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[5.25pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[3.67499pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[2.625pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}}{\alpha^{{{\mu}}}_{{\mathchoice{\makebox[5.25pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[5.25pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[3.67499pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[2.625pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}}{\alpha^{{{\mu}}}_{{\mathchoice{\makebox[5.25pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[5.25pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[3.67499pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[2.625pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}}+\mathchoice{\beta^{{{\mu}\mathchoice{\makebox[5.25pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[5.25pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[3.67499pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[2.625pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}_{{\mathchoice{\makebox[5.25pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[5.25pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[3.67499pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[2.625pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}{\nu}}}}{\beta^{{{\mu}\mathchoice{\makebox[5.25pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[5.25pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[3.67499pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[2.625pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}_{{\mathchoice{\makebox[5.25pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[5.25pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[3.67499pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[2.625pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}{\nu}}}}{\beta^{{{\mu}\mathchoice{\makebox[5.25pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[5.25pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[3.67499pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[2.625pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}_{{\mathchoice{\makebox[5.25pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[5.25pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[3.67499pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[2.625pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}{\nu}}}}{\beta^{{{\mu}\mathchoice{\makebox[5.25pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[5.25pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[3.67499pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[2.625pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}_{{\mathchoice{\makebox[5.25pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[5.25pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[3.67499pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[2.625pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}{\nu}}}}\mathchoice{x^{{{\nu}}}_{{\mathchoice{\makebox[5.25pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[5.25pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[3.67499pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[2.625pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}}{x^{{{\nu}}}_{{\mathchoice{\makebox[5.25pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[5.25pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[3.67499pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[2.625pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}}{x^{{{\nu}}}_{{\mathchoice{\makebox[5.25pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[5.25pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[3.67499pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[2.625pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}}{x^{{{\nu}}}_{{\mathchoice{\makebox[5.25pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[5.25pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[3.67499pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[2.625pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}}.

(94)

This can be written in matrix form as

\derivative{x}{\lambda}=\alpha+\beta x,

(95)

and one can then promptly integrate the system to get, in terms of matrix exponentials,

x(\lambda)=e^{\lambda\beta}x(0)+e^{\lambda\beta}\int_{0}^{\lambda}e^{-\lambda^{\prime}\beta}\differential{\lambda'}\alpha.

(96)

The second term on the
\gls
RHS is an element of
\mdmathbb{R}^{n}
, and hence this transformation is quite similar to the general transformation rule for the Poincaré group,
Eq.

19
. There is, however, an important question: is the matrix
e^{\lambda\beta}
an element of the Lorentz group
\mathrm{SO}^{+}(n-1,1)
?

To prove it is, first notice that

\displaystyle=0,

(97b)

\displaystyle\beta^{\intercal}\eta+\eta\beta

\displaystyle=0,

(97c)

which translates the antisymmetry properties of

to the matrix

\mathchoice{\beta^{{{\mu}\mathchoice{\makebox[5.25pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[5.25pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[3.67499pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[2.625pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}_{{\mathchoice{\makebox[5.25pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[5.25pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[3.67499pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[2.625pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}{\nu}}}}{\beta^{{{\mu}\mathchoice{\makebox[5.25pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[5.25pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[3.67499pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[2.625pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}_{{\mathchoice{\makebox[5.25pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[5.25pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[3.67499pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[2.625pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}{\nu}}}}{\beta^{{{\mu}\mathchoice{\makebox[5.25pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[5.25pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[3.67499pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[2.625pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}_{{\mathchoice{\makebox[5.25pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[5.25pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[3.67499pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[2.625pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}{\nu}}}}{\beta^{{{\mu}\mathchoice{\makebox[5.25pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[5.25pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[3.67499pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[2.625pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}_{{\mathchoice{\makebox[5.25pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[5.25pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[3.67499pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[2.625pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}{\nu}}}}
). With this expression in mind, we notice that

\displaystyle\quantity(e^{\lambda\beta})^{\intercal}\eta\quantity(e^{\lambda\beta})

\displaystyle=\sum_{n=0}^{+\infty}\frac{\lambda^{n}}{n!}(\beta^{\intercal})^{n}\eta\quantity(e^{\lambda\beta}),

(98a)

\displaystyle=\sum_{n=0}^{+\infty}\frac{(-1)^{n}\lambda^{n}}{n!}\eta\beta^{n}\quantity(e^{\lambda\beta}),

(98b)

\displaystyle=\eta e^{-\lambda\beta}e^{\lambda\beta},

(98c)

\displaystyle=\eta.

(98d)

Therefore,

. Since

and

is continuous in

Hence, we conclude (

) represents a Poincaré transformation. By carefully selecting

and

one can show that all Poincaré transformations are of the form (

One may notice that we have

parameters in between

as a Lie group (

The vectors

generate translations, the

4
Asymptotically Flat Spacetimes

Our goal in these lectures is to understand the asymptotic symmetries of asymptotically flat spacetimes. For that end, we must have a good understanding of what we mean by “asymptotic” and what we mean by “asymptotically flat”. The goal of this section is to give attention to these terms and discuss how they are currently understood in
\gls
GR.

Asymptotic flatness and the
\gls
BMS group depend crucially on the spacetime dimension
[
8
,
135
,
136
]
. As a consequence, from this point onward I will focus on the four-dimensional case.

4.1
Infinity in Minkowski Spacetime

We shall begin by giving meaning to “infinity” in Minkowski spacetime. Our approach is similar in nature to the discussion in Chap. 11 of Ref.
\citeonline
wald1984GeneralRelativity.

To begin our discussion, let us choose a system of coordinates to better visualize what we are doing. Spherical coordinates turn out to be convenient, so we write the Minkowski line element as

\differential{s}^{2}=-\differential{t}^{2}+\differential{r}^{2}+r^{2}\differential{\Sph}^{2},

(100)

where
\differential{\Sph}^{2}
stands for the line element of the round metric on the sphere.

When we talk about what happens “at infinity” in Minkowski spacetime, there are three possibilities we could be considering. Namely, we could be thinking about taking the limit
t\to\pm\infty
or taking the limit
r\to+\infty
. This, however, is not a clear enough picture of what infinity is. For instance, we do not know if taking
r\to+\infty
toward different angular directions will lead to the same result. Furthermore, we could take
r\to+\infty
while holding
t
constant or while holding
u=t-r
constant, for example, and these options turn out to lead to very different results. Therefore, we must be more careful.

For concreteness, let us assume we want to take the limit
r\to+\infty
at constant
u=t-r
. In this case, it makes sense to change coordinates so we use
u
rather than
t
when writing the line element. Doing so leads us to the line element

\differential{s}^{2}=-\differential{u}^{2}-2\differential{u}\differential{r}+r^{2}\differential{\Sph}^{2}.

(101)

At this point we could attempt to take the limit
r\to+\infty
in order to understand what is the geometry of infinity in Minkowski spacetime. Nevertheless, there is a difficulty in doing so: this limit leads to a divergence in the metric. This divergence is not due to a bad choice of coordinates, because it has geometrical (and hence physical) implications. Namely, the area of a sphere with radius
r
diverges as we take
r\to+\infty
. Hence, it is not possible to take this limit for this metric.

Despite this difficulty, we would still like to understand the structure of infinity. To do so, we will make a new change of coordinates. We define a new coordinate
l=1/r
, which turns the line element into

\differential{s}^{2}=-\differential{u}^{2}+2l^{-2}\differential{u}\differential{l}+l^{-2}\differential{\Sph}^{2}.

(102)

A few comments are in order. Firstly, notice that the physical region of Minkowski spacetime corresponds to
l>0
—the limiting case
l=0
would in principle be infinity (in the sense that
r\to+\infty
as
l\to 0^{+}
) and
l<0
is non-physical. Secondly, this coordinate patch does not cover the points with
r=0
, since
l
diverges there. Thirdly, notice that this was merely a coordinate change, and taking the limit
l\to 0^{+}
is not any more possible than taking the limit
r\to+\infty
was before.

Nevertheless, this new coordinate system seems to be “better behaved” at infinity. Namely, we know infinity sits at
l=0
, which we can barely grasp. The only problem we face now is the presence of the
l^{-2}
factors in
Eq.

102
. To deal with them, we will take an apparently
ad hoc
approach. We will define a new, unphysical metric
\mathchoice{\tilde{g}^{{\mathchoice{\makebox[4.33765pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[4.33765pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.59009pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.85005pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}\mathchoice{\makebox[3.51666pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[3.51666pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.1029pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.50208pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}_{{{a}{b}}}}{\tilde{g}^{{\mathchoice{\makebox[4.33765pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[4.33765pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.59009pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.85005pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}\mathchoice{\makebox[3.51666pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[3.51666pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.1029pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.50208pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}_{{{a}{b}}}}{\tilde{g}^{{\mathchoice{\makebox[4.33765pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[4.33765pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.59009pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.85005pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}\mathchoice{\makebox[3.51666pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[3.51666pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.1029pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.50208pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}_{{{a}{b}}}}{\tilde{g}^{{\mathchoice{\makebox[4.33765pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[4.33765pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.59009pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.85005pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}\mathchoice{\makebox[3.51666pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[3.51666pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.1029pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.50208pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}_{{{a}{b}}}}
through

is the Minkowski metric. The line element for this new unphysical metric is

\differential{\tilde{s}}^{2}=-l^{2}\differential{u}^{2}+2\differential{u}\differential{l}+\differential{\Sph}^{2}.

(104)

This new unphysical metric has an advantage: it is well-behaved in the
l\to 0^{+}
limit. We can thus describe the geometry of infinity by plugging in
l=0
and getting the induced metric

\differential{\tilde{\sigma}}^{2}=0\differential{u}^{2}+\differential{\Sph}^{2},

(105)

where we write
0\differential{u}^{2}
explicitly as a reminder that this is a metric in a three-dimensional manifold. I wrote
\differential{\tilde{\sigma}}^{2}
instead of
\differential{\tilde{s}}^{2}
because this is the induced metric. We can now consider the behavior of tensor fields at infinity by mapping them from the original spacetime with metric

is finite in the region we wanted to study. Hence, we decided to let go of
\mathchoice{\eta^{{\mathchoice{\makebox[4.33765pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[4.33765pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.59009pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.85005pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}\mathchoice{\makebox[3.51666pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[3.51666pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.1029pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.50208pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}_{{{a}{b}}}}{\eta^{{\mathchoice{\makebox[4.33765pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[4.33765pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.59009pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.85005pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}\mathchoice{\makebox[3.51666pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[3.51666pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.1029pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.50208pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}_{{{a}{b}}}}{\eta^{{\mathchoice{\makebox[4.33765pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[4.33765pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.59009pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.85005pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}\mathchoice{\makebox[3.51666pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[3.51666pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.1029pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.50208pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}_{{{a}{b}}}}{\eta^{{\mathchoice{\makebox[4.33765pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[4.33765pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.59009pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.85005pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}\mathchoice{\makebox[3.51666pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[3.51666pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.1029pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.50208pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}_{{{a}{b}}}}

instead, at least while we are considering the behavior at infinity. By making appropriate transformations of tensor fields so they can be understood as being defined in the spacetime given by
\mathchoice{\tilde{g}^{{\mathchoice{\makebox[4.33765pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[4.33765pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.59009pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.85005pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}\mathchoice{\makebox[3.51666pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[3.51666pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.1029pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.50208pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}_{{{a}{b}}}}{\tilde{g}^{{\mathchoice{\makebox[4.33765pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[4.33765pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.59009pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.85005pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}\mathchoice{\makebox[3.51666pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[3.51666pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.1029pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.50208pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}_{{{a}{b}}}}{\tilde{g}^{{\mathchoice{\makebox[4.33765pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[4.33765pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.59009pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.85005pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}\mathchoice{\makebox[3.51666pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[3.51666pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.1029pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.50208pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}_{{{a}{b}}}}{\tilde{g}^{{\mathchoice{\makebox[4.33765pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[4.33765pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.59009pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.85005pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}\mathchoice{\makebox[3.51666pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[3.51666pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.1029pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.50208pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}_{{{a}{b}}}}
, we can analyze their behavior at infinity by simply evaluating them at infinity, which became a set of regular points in the new unphysical spacetime.

It is important to emphasize that
\mathchoice{\tilde{g}^{{\mathchoice{\makebox[4.33765pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[4.33765pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.59009pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.85005pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}\mathchoice{\makebox[3.51666pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[3.51666pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.1029pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.50208pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}_{{{a}{b}}}}{\tilde{g}^{{\mathchoice{\makebox[4.33765pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[4.33765pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.59009pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.85005pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}\mathchoice{\makebox[3.51666pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[3.51666pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.1029pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.50208pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}_{{{a}{b}}}}{\tilde{g}^{{\mathchoice{\makebox[4.33765pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[4.33765pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.59009pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.85005pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}\mathchoice{\makebox[3.51666pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[3.51666pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.1029pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.50208pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}_{{{a}{b}}}}{\tilde{g}^{{\mathchoice{\makebox[4.33765pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[4.33765pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.59009pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.85005pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}\mathchoice{\makebox[3.51666pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[3.51666pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.1029pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.50208pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}_{{{a}{b}}}}
is an unphysical metric. It is not the metric that describes the spacetime geometry as measured in experiments. It is defined as a mathematical construction that allows us to “bring in infinity” and consider it as a regular point. In general,
\mathchoice{\tilde{g}^{{\mathchoice{\makebox[4.33765pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[4.33765pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.59009pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.85005pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}\mathchoice{\makebox[3.51666pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[3.51666pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.1029pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.50208pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}_{{{a}{b}}}}{\tilde{g}^{{\mathchoice{\makebox[4.33765pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[4.33765pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.59009pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.85005pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}\mathchoice{\makebox[3.51666pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[3.51666pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.1029pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.50208pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}_{{{a}{b}}}}{\tilde{g}^{{\mathchoice{\makebox[4.33765pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[4.33765pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.59009pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.85005pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}\mathchoice{\makebox[3.51666pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[3.51666pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.1029pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.50208pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}_{{{a}{b}}}}{\tilde{g}^{{\mathchoice{\makebox[4.33765pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[4.33765pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.59009pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.85005pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}\mathchoice{\makebox[3.51666pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[3.51666pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.1029pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.50208pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}_{{{a}{b}}}}
will not even satisfy the Einstein field equations, so it is not an accurate model of the bulk spacetime
9
9

9

By “bulk” I mean the interior of the spacetime, or the set of all “finite” points. This contrasts with infinity, which would be the “boundary” of spacetime.
we are trying to describe. Nevertheless, the price we pay to study infinity is that we are forced to work with
\mathchoice{\tilde{g}^{{\mathchoice{\makebox[4.33765pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[4.33765pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.59009pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.85005pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}\mathchoice{\makebox[3.51666pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[3.51666pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.1029pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.50208pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}_{{{a}{b}}}}{\tilde{g}^{{\mathchoice{\makebox[4.33765pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[4.33765pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.59009pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.85005pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}\mathchoice{\makebox[3.51666pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[3.51666pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.1029pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.50208pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}_{{{a}{b}}}}{\tilde{g}^{{\mathchoice{\makebox[4.33765pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[4.33765pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.59009pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.85005pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}\mathchoice{\makebox[3.51666pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[3.51666pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.1029pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.50208pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}_{{{a}{b}}}}{\tilde{g}^{{\mathchoice{\makebox[4.33765pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[4.33765pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.59009pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.85005pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}\mathchoice{\makebox[3.51666pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[3.51666pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.1029pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.50208pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}_{{{a}{b}}}}
rather than with the physical metric
\mathchoice{\eta^{{\mathchoice{\makebox[4.33765pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[4.33765pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.59009pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.85005pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}\mathchoice{\makebox[3.51666pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[3.51666pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.1029pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.50208pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}_{{{a}{b}}}}{\eta^{{\mathchoice{\makebox[4.33765pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[4.33765pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.59009pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.85005pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}\mathchoice{\makebox[3.51666pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[3.51666pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.1029pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.50208pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}_{{{a}{b}}}}{\eta^{{\mathchoice{\makebox[4.33765pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[4.33765pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.59009pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.85005pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}\mathchoice{\makebox[3.51666pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[3.51666pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.1029pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.50208pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}_{{{a}{b}}}}{\eta^{{\mathchoice{\makebox[4.33765pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[4.33765pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.59009pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.85005pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}\mathchoice{\makebox[3.51666pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[3.51666pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.1029pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.50208pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}_{{{a}{b}}}}
.

This procedure is called a conformal compactification. It is conformal because we have a transformation of the form
\mathchoice{\eta^{{\mathchoice{\makebox[4.33765pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[4.33765pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.59009pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.85005pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}\mathchoice{\makebox[3.51666pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[3.51666pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.1029pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.50208pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}_{{{a}{b}}}}{\eta^{{\mathchoice{\makebox[4.33765pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[4.33765pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.59009pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.85005pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}\mathchoice{\makebox[3.51666pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[3.51666pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.1029pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.50208pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}_{{{a}{b}}}}{\eta^{{\mathchoice{\makebox[4.33765pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[4.33765pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.59009pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.85005pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}\mathchoice{\makebox[3.51666pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[3.51666pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.1029pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.50208pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}_{{{a}{b}}}}{\eta^{{\mathchoice{\makebox[4.33765pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[4.33765pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.59009pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.85005pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}\mathchoice{\makebox[3.51666pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[3.51666pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.1029pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.50208pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}_{{{a}{b}}}}\to{}^{2}\mathchoice{\eta^{{\mathchoice{\makebox[4.33765pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[4.33765pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.59009pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.85005pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}\mathchoice{\makebox[3.51666pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[3.51666pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.1029pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.50208pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}_{{{a}{b}}}}{\eta^{{\mathchoice{\makebox[4.33765pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[4.33765pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.59009pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.85005pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}\mathchoice{\makebox[3.51666pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[3.51666pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.1029pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.50208pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}_{{{a}{b}}}}{\eta^{{\mathchoice{\makebox[4.33765pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[4.33765pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.59009pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.85005pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}\mathchoice{\makebox[3.51666pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[3.51666pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.1029pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.50208pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}_{{{a}{b}}}}{\eta^{{\mathchoice{\makebox[4.33765pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[4.33765pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.59009pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.85005pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}\mathchoice{\makebox[3.51666pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[3.51666pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.1029pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.50208pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}_{{{a}{b}}}}
for some function
\Omega
which is positive in the bulk spacetime. It is a compactification because it transforms a spacetime that is not compact into a spacetime that is compact by adding the points at infinity. There are, however, better choices of compactification. In our construction, we defined a function
\Omega=l
which was not defined at some points of spacetime—namely those with
r=0
. We can, however, define a conformal compactification that takes proper account of all points in Minkowski spacetime.

To that end, we will make some more changes of coordinates. We begin by defining the advanced time coordinate
v=t+r
. This is in contrast to the retarded time coordinate
u=t-r
. Both of these coordinates are depicted on
Fig.

2
. In terms of retarded and advanced times and angular coordinates the Minkowski line element is written as

\differential{s}^{2}=-\differential{u}\differential{v}+\frac{1}{4}(v-u)^{2}\differential{\Sph^2}.

(106)

It is convenient to work with null coordinates—
i.e.
, coordinates that are constant on a hypersurface normal to a null vector—because we can compactify each of these coordinates separately and still get null coordinates. This will allow us at the end to draw a diagram in which all (radial) null geodesics are at
[formula]
angles, which is convenient for reading the causal structure of spacetime.

Figure 2:
Illustration, with one dimension suppressed, of the physical meaning of the null coordinates
u
and
v
. Surfaces of constant
u
are outgoing spherical “waves”, while surfaces of constant
v
are their incoming analogues. This figure is based on Fig. 12.i of Ref.
\citeonline
hawking1973LargeScaleStructure.

We will now compactify the coordinates of
Eq.

106
. Our goal is to take the coordinates
u
and
v
which obey

-\infty<u\leq v<+\infty

(107)

and map them to coordinates with range in a finite interval. This can be done by means of a function
f\colon(a,b)\to\mdmathbb{R}
where
-\infty<a<b<+\infty
and such that
f
is injective. Two examples are the functions

\displaystyle\trigbraces{\arhyptangent}\colon(-1,1)\to\mdmathbb{R}

(108)

and

\displaystyle\tan\colon\quantity(-\frac{\pi}{2},+\frac{\pi}{2})\to\mdmathbb{R},

(109)

but one could also work with other options. We will use the tangent function. We define new compactified null coordinates
U
and
V
through

u=\tan U\quad\mbox{and}\quad v=\tan V.

(110)

Notice that this maps the infinite range of
u
and
v
to a finite range of
U
and
V
. Namely,
U
and
V
satisfy

-\frac{\pi}{2}<U\leq V<+\frac{\pi}{2}.

(111)

The middle inequality holds because
\tan
is crescent and
u\leq v
.

In our new choice of coordinates, we have the line element

\differential{s}^{2}=\sec^{2}U\sec^{2}V\quantity[- \dd{U}\dd{V} + \frac{1}{4}\sin[2](V-U)\dd{\Sph}^2].

(112)

At this stage, our coordinates are already compactified. We just need to get rid of the divergences of the metric at infinity. To do so, we perform a conformal transformation. As
Eq.

112
suggests, we take

\Omega=2\cos U\cos V

(113)

so that we define
\mathchoice{\tilde{g}^{{\mathchoice{\makebox[4.33765pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[4.33765pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.59009pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.85005pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}\mathchoice{\makebox[3.51666pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[3.51666pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.1029pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.50208pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}_{{{a}{b}}}}{\tilde{g}^{{\mathchoice{\makebox[4.33765pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[4.33765pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.59009pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.85005pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}\mathchoice{\makebox[3.51666pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[3.51666pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.1029pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.50208pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}_{{{a}{b}}}}{\tilde{g}^{{\mathchoice{\makebox[4.33765pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[4.33765pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.59009pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.85005pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}\mathchoice{\makebox[3.51666pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[3.51666pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.1029pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.50208pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}_{{{a}{b}}}}{\tilde{g}^{{\mathchoice{\makebox[4.33765pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[4.33765pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.59009pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.85005pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}\mathchoice{\makebox[3.51666pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[3.51666pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.1029pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.50208pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}_{{{a}{b}}}}={}^{2}\mathchoice{\eta^{{\mathchoice{\makebox[4.33765pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[4.33765pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.59009pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.85005pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}\mathchoice{\makebox[3.51666pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[3.51666pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.1029pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.50208pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}_{{{a}{b}}}}{\eta^{{\mathchoice{\makebox[4.33765pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[4.33765pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.59009pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.85005pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}\mathchoice{\makebox[3.51666pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[3.51666pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.1029pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.50208pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}_{{{a}{b}}}}{\eta^{{\mathchoice{\makebox[4.33765pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[4.33765pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.59009pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.85005pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}\mathchoice{\makebox[3.51666pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[3.51666pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.1029pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.50208pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}_{{{a}{b}}}}{\eta^{{\mathchoice{\makebox[4.33765pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[4.33765pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.59009pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.85005pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}\mathchoice{\makebox[3.51666pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[3.51666pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.1029pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.50208pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}_{{{a}{b}}}}
and get

\differential{\tilde{s}}^{2}=-4\differential{U}\differential{V}+\sin[2](V-U)\differential{\Sph}^{2}.

(114)

For convenience, we finally introduce coordinates
T
and
R
through

T=U+V\quad\mbox{and}\quad R=V-U

(115)

which mimic (up to normalization)
u=t-r
and
v=t+r
. This finally leads to the unphysical metric

\differential{\tilde{s}}^{2}=-\differential{T}^{2}+\differential{R}^{2}+\sin^{2}R\differential{\Sph}^{2}.

(116)

The physical region corresponds to the limits

-\pi<T-R\leq T+R<+\pi,

(117)

which in particular imply
R\geq 0
.

Eq.

116
is the line element for the Einstein static universe (see,
e.g.
, Sec. VII.2.1 of Ref.
\citeonline
choquet-bruhat2015IntroductionGeneralRelativity). This spacetime has topology
\mdmathbb{R}\times\mdmathbb{S}^{3}
and it is a solution to the Einstein field equations, but for a perfect fluid stress tensor with a cosmological constant component. This is, of course, a very different scenario from the Minkowski metric, which is a vacuum solution. This greatly exemplifies that the unphysical metric is really unphysical.

We can make a plot of the region given on
Eq.

117
. Plotting
R
on the horizontal axis and
T
on the vertical axis, we get the diagram shown in
Fig.

3
. This is known as the Carter–Penrose diagram for Minkowski spacetime. It is a finite drawing of all of Minkowski spacetime, with each point representing a sphere
\mdmathbb{S}^{2}
(except for the points on the
R=0
line and the vertices of the diagram, which represent a single point each). We can “double” the diagram by letting each point be a hemisphere, and this version of the diagram is interesting because it can be “wrapped around the Einstein static universe”, as shown in
Fig.

4
.

Figure 3:
Carter–Penrose diagram of Minkowski spacetime.

Figure 4:
Minkowski spacetime embedded in the Einstein static universe (two spatial dimensions are suppressed). Since the Einstein static universe has the topology
\mdmathbb{R}\times\mdmathbb{S}^{3}
, it is often depicted as a cylinder. The Carter–Penrose diagram for Minkowski spacetime is wrapped around the Einstein cylinder.

The region
T+R=+\pi
of the Carter–Penrose diagram corresponds to the limits
r\to+\infty
at constant
u
. Each angular direction leads to a different point and each different value of
u
leads to a different point as well. In total, we get a three-dimensional manifold
\mathscr{I}^{+}
with topology
\mdmathbb{R}\times\mdmathbb{S}^{2}
:
\mdmathbb{R}
corresponds to the values of
u
and
\mdmathbb{S}^{2}
to the possible angular directions. Similarly,
T-R=-\pi
is the region
\mathscr{I}^{-}
of limits
r\to+\infty
under constant
v
and it also has topology
\mdmathbb{R}\times\mdmathbb{S}^{2}
for analogous reasons.
\mathscr{I}^{+}
is known as the future null infinity and the symbol
\mathscr{I}^{+}
is pronounced “scri-plus”.
\mathscr{I}^{-}
(“scri-minus”) is the past null infinity.

The point
T=0
with
R=\pi
is at the boundary between
\mathscr{I}^{+}
and
\mathscr{I}^{-}
. Notice this is indeed a point—
R=\pi
is one of the poles of the Einstein universe’s three-sphere, which is thus a single point. This point, denoted
i^{0}
, is known as spatial infinity and it corresponds to the limits
r\to+\infty
at constant
t
. Notice that, since this is a single point, limits in different angular directions all coincide.

We still have two interesting points.
T=\pi
with
R=0
is at the future of
\mathscr{I}^{+}
. This is located at the other pole of the three-sphere and thus it also corresponds to a single point, denoted
i^{+}
and known as future timelike infinity. This is the limit
t\to+\infty
at constant
r
, and there is no angular direction-dependence either. Similar comments are in order for the past timelike infinity
i^{-}
, located at
T=-\pi
with
R=0
.

All timelike curves start at
i^{-}
and end at
i^{+}
. All null curves start at
\mathscr{I}^{-}
and end at
\mathscr{I}^{+}
. All spacelike curves start and end at
i^{0}
.
Fig.

5
illustrates some curves of interest on the Carter–Penrose diagram for Minkowski spacetime.

Figure 5:
Different curves represented in the Carter–Penrose diagram for Minkowski spacetime. Vertical curves (far-left) are curves with constant
r
. Horizontal curves (center-left) are curves with constant
t
. Diagonal lines have constant
u
(outgoing, center-right) or
v
(incoming, far-right).

Conformal compactifications were introduced in
\gls
GR by
[
189
,
190
,
191
]
, who also presented the first versions of conformal diagrams, which were similar to
Fig.

4
.
[
52
]
later adapted them to the modern two-dimensional version. We shall extensively use these techniques in the rest of these notes.

I should mention an important property of the conformal transformations we are employing to find an unphysical spacetime. While it is true that

\mathchoice{\tilde{g}^{{\mathchoice{\makebox[4.33765pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[4.33765pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.59009pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.85005pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}\mathchoice{\makebox[3.51666pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[3.51666pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.1029pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.50208pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}_{{{a}{b}}}}{\tilde{g}^{{\mathchoice{\makebox[4.33765pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[4.33765pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.59009pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.85005pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}\mathchoice{\makebox[3.51666pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[3.51666pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.1029pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.50208pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}_{{{a}{b}}}}{\tilde{g}^{{\mathchoice{\makebox[4.33765pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[4.33765pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.59009pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.85005pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}\mathchoice{\makebox[3.51666pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[3.51666pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.1029pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.50208pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}_{{{a}{b}}}}{\tilde{g}^{{\mathchoice{\makebox[4.33765pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[4.33765pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.59009pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.85005pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}\mathchoice{\makebox[3.51666pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[3.51666pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.1029pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.50208pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}_{{{a}{b}}}}\mathchoice{k^{{{a}}}_{{\mathchoice{\makebox[4.33765pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[4.33765pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.59009pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.85005pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}}{k^{{{a}}}_{{\mathchoice{\makebox[4.33765pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[4.33765pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.59009pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.85005pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}}{k^{{{a}}}_{{\mathchoice{\makebox[4.33765pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[4.33765 . As a consequence, conformal transformations preserve lightcones, and thus they preserve the causal structure of spacetime. This means that Carter–Penrose diagrams are useful tools for analyzing the causal structure of spacetime.

Notice also that in the Carter–Penrose diagram for Minkowski spacetime all radial light rays move at
[formula]
angles. This allows us to read the causal structure of Minkowski spacetime directly from its Carter–Penrose diagram. This is the reason why these sorts of diagrams are popular in
\gls
GR.

4.2
Asymptotically Flat Spacetimes

At this point we would like to adapt our discussion of infinity to more general spacetimes. This is related to defining what is an asymptotically flat spacetime.

In a general spacetime, the structure of infinity could be much different from that of Minkowski spacetime. Some spacetimes might not even get to infinity. Consider a dust-filled and spatially closed
\gls
FLRW universe, for example. Such a universe begins at a Big Bang, ends at a Big Crunch, and has compact spatial sections (it is spatially a sphere). Therefore, we never really get to infinity. We either reach the north or south pole of the spatial spheres or we reach the singularities at the beginning or end of spacetime.

We want to consider spacetimes that asymptotically look like Minkowski spacetime. Hence, their behavior at infinity should somehow resemble that of Minkowski spacetime. We know Minkowski spacetime has five different infinities, so there are five different meanings we can give to “asymptotically flat”, plus combinations of them.

What are reasonable conditions we can impose? It makes sense to consider spacetimes in which the gravitational field falls off away from a central distribution of matter, so we have an asymptotically flat spacetime at null and spatial infinities. There is less interest in spacetimes which are asymptotically flat at timelike infinities, though, because this means the spacetime becomes flat at late or early times, so the matter content has dispersed. While there are situations in which this can be interesting, they are not what we are looking for at this stage. Hence, one often defines asymptotic flatness at spatial and null infinities.

Our definition will actually be even simpler than that. For our purposes, a single null infinity will typically be enough. Hence, we will discuss asymptotically flat spacetimes at future null infinity (the past case is analogous). We follow Chap. 2 of Ref.
\citeonline
dappiaggi2017HadamardStatesLightlike, which also discusses the timelike case. For the more complete case involving null and spatial infinity, see the Chap. 11 of Ref.
\citeonline
wald1984GeneralRelativity.

I will first discuss in a handwaving way each of the axioms that we will employ and then state the final definition. The goal is to motivate the definition. We will find a definition by mimicking and generalizing the construction of conformal infinity we performed for Minkowski spacetime.

We start with a spacetime
(M,\mathchoice{g^{{\mathchoice{\makebox[4.33765pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[4.33765pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.59009pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.85005pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}\mathchoice{\makebox[3.51666pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[3.51666pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.1029pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.50208pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}_{{{a}{b}}}}{g^{{\mathchoice{\makebox[4.33765pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[4.33765pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.59009pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.85005pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}\mathchoice{\makebox[3.51666pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[3.51666pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.1029pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.50208pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}_{{{a}{b}}}}{g^{{\mathchoice{\makebox[4.33765pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[4.33765pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.59009pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.85005pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}\mathchoice{\makebox[3.51666pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[3.51666pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.1029pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.50208pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}_{{{a}{b}}}}{g^{{\mathchoice{\makebox[4.33765pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[4.33765pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.59009pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.85005pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}\mathchoice{\makebox[3.51666pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[3.51666pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.1029pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.50208pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}_{{{a}{b}}}})

We need a way of injecting
M
into
\tilde{M}
. Before, we had a natural way of viewing Minkowski spacetime as a submanifold of the Einstein static universe, which was given by the coordinate restrictions on the Einstein universe. In our more general case, this role is played by a function
\psi\colon M\to\tilde{M}
that should satisfy some convenient properties. In practice, it is convenient to choose
\psi
to be an embedding. Let us define this by following
[
230
]
.

Definition 9

(Immersion)
.

Let
\psi\colon M\to\tilde{M}
be a smooth map between the manifolds
M
and
\tilde{M}
. We say
\psi
is an immersion if, and only if, the pushforward
{}^{*}\colon T_{p}M\to T_{\psi(p)}\tilde{M}
is injective for all
p\in M
.

Definition 10

(Embedding)
.

Let
M
and
\tilde{M}
be smooth manifolds. An immersion
\psi\colon M\to\tilde{M}
is called an embedding if, and only if, it is injective and
\psi\colon M\to\psi(M)
is continuous with a continuous inverse.

Definition 11

(Embedded Submanifold)
.

Let
M
and
\tilde{M}
be smooth manifolds. If
\psi\colon M\to\tilde{M}
is an embedding, we say that
\psi(M)
is an embedded submanifold of
\tilde{M}
.

Embeddings are diffeomorphisms onto their ranges. Hence, we can think of an embedding as being a generalization of diffeomorphism that does not need to be surjective. It makes a copy of
M
in
\tilde{M}
.
