(118)

This ensures that
\psi
represents a conformal transformation between the spacetimes
(M,\mathchoice{g^{{\mathchoice{\makebox[4.33765pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[4.33765pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.59009pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.85005pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}\mathchoice{\makebox[3.51666pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[3.51666pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.1029pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.50208pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}_{{{a}{b}}}}{g^{{\mathchoice{\makebox[4.33765pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[4.33765pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.59009pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.85005pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}\mathchoice{\makebox[3.51666pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[3.51666pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.1029pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.50208pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}_{{{a}{b}}}}{g^{{\mathchoice{\makebox[4.33765pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[4.33765pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.59009pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.85005pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}\mathchoice{\makebox[3.51666pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[3.51666pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.1029pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.50208pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}_{{{a}{b}}}}{g^{{\mathchoice{\makebox[4.33765pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[4.33765pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.59009pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.85005pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}\mathchoice{\makebox[3.51666pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[3.51666pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.1029pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.50208pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}_{{{a}{b}}}})
and
(\tilde{M},\mathchoice{\tilde{g}^{{\mathchoice{\makebox[4.33765pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[4.33765pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.59009pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.85005pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}\mathchoice{\makebox[3.51666pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[3.51666pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.1029pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.50208pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}_{{{a}{b}}}}{\tilde{g}^{{\mathchoice{\makebox[4.33765pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[4.33765pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.59009pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.85005pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}\mathchoice{\makebox[3.51666pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[3.51666pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.1029pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.50208pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}_{{{a}{b}}}}{\tilde{g}^{{\mathchoice{\makebox[4.33765pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[4.33765pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.59009pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.85005pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}\mathchoice{\makebox[3.51666pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[3.51666pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.1029pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.50208pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}_{{{a}{b}}}}{\tilde{g}^{{\mathchoice{\makebox[4.33765pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[4.33765pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.59009pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.85005pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}\mathchoice{\makebox[3.51666pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[3.51666pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.1029pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.50208pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}_{{{a}{b}}}})
.

Given these objects, we define future null infinity as the boundary
\mathscr{I}^{+}=\partial\psi(M)
.
\mathscr{I}^{+}
is an embedded submanifold of
\tilde{M}
and it is not to the past of any points of
\psi(M)
. In symbols, we write

\mathscr{I}^{+}\cap J^{-}\pqty{\psi(M);\tilde{M}}=\varnothing.

(119)

The causal past of a set
S
,
J^{-}\pqty{S}
, is defined as follows.

Definition 12

(Causal Past)
.

Let
(M,\mathchoice{g^{{\mathchoice{\makebox[4.33765pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[4.33765pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.59009pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.85005pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}\mathchoice{\makebox[3.51666pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[3.51666pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.1029pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.50208pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}_{{{a}{b}}}}{g^{{\mathchoice{\makebox[4.33765pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[4.33765pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.59009pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.85005pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}\mathchoice{\makebox[3.51666pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[3.51666pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.1029pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.50208pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}_{{{a}{b}}}}{g^{{\mathchoice{\makebox[4.33765pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[4.33765pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.59009pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.85005pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}\mathchoice{\makebox[3.51666pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[3.51666pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.1029pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.50208pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}_{{{a}{b}}}}{g^{{\mathchoice{\makebox[4.33765pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[4.33765pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.59009pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.85005pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}\mathchoice{\makebox[3.51666pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[3.51666pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.1029pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.50208pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}_{{{a}{b}}}})
be a spacetime. Consider a set
S\subseteq M
. The causal past of
S
in
M
, denoted
J^{-}\pqty{S;M}
or simply
J^{-}\pqty{S}
when
M
is understood, is defined as the set of all points in
M
from which one can reach
S
by means of a future-directed causal curve. See Chap. 8 of Ref.
\citeonline
wald1984GeneralRelativity for further details.

Hence,
\mathscr{I}^{+}
is defined in this general construction as a submanifold of
\tilde{M}
satisfying a couple of special properties. In particular, it is a future boundary in the sense that is is not in the past of any points in the physical spacetime.

Near infinity we expect the spacetime to be reasonably well-behaved, so that it actually looks like Minkowski spacetime. Thus, we demand it enjoys reasonably good causal properties. We cannot allow for closed timelike curves near infinity, for example. We enforce this behavior by demanding that strong causality holds in a neighborhood of infinity.

Definition 13

(Strong Causality)
.

Consider a spacetime
(M,\mathchoice{g^{{\mathchoice{\makebox[4.33765pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[4.33765pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.59009pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.85005pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}\mathchoice{\makebox[3.51666pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[3.51666pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.1029pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.50208pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}_{{{a}{b}}}}{g^{{\mathchoice{\makebox[4.33765pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[4.33765pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.59009pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.85005pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}\mathchoice{\makebox[3.51666pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[3.51666pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.1029pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.50208pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}_{{{a}{b}}}}{g^{{\mathchoice{\makebox[4.33765pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[4.33765pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.59009pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.85005pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}\mathchoice{\makebox[3.51666pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[3.51666pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.1029pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.50208pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}_{{{a}{b}}}}{g^{{\mathchoice{\makebox[4.33765pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[4.33765pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.59009pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.85005pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}\mathchoice{\makebox[3.51666pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[3.51666pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.1029pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.50208pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}_{{{a}{b}}}})
. We say
(M,\mathchoice{g^{{\mathchoice{\makebox[4.33765pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[4.33765pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.59009pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.85005pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}\mathchoice{\makebox[3.51666pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[3.51666pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.1029pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.50208pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}_{{{a}{b}}}}{g^{{\mathchoice{\makebox[4.33765pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[4.33765pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.59009pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.85005pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}\mathchoice{\makebox[3.51666pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[3.51666pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.1029pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.50208pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}_{{{a}{b}}}}{g^{{\mathchoice{\makebox[4.33765pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[4.33765pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.59009pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.85005pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}\mathchoice{\makebox[3.51666pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[3.51666pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.1029pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.50208pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}_{{{a}{b}}}}{g^{{\mathchoice{\makebox[4.33765pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[4.33765pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.59009pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.85005pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}\mathchoice{\makebox[3.51666pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[3.51666pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.1029pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.50208pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}_{{{a}{b}}}})
is strongly causal if for any point
p\in M
and every neighborhood
U
of
p
there is a neighborhood
V
of
p
with
p\in V\subseteq U
such that no causal curve intersects
V
more than once.

As discussed in Chap. 8 of Ref.
\citeonline
wald1984GeneralRelativity, strong causality essentially means that no causal curve comes arbitrarily close to intersecting itself. This prevents causality violations upon small perturbations of the metric. There are stronger causality impositions one could consider, but we shall assume only strong causality.

We need to impose that
\Omega
brings infinity in. This is done by imposing that
\Omega
vanishes on
\mathscr{I}^{+}
. However, we defined
\Omega
only on
\psi(M)
. Hence, we ask that
\Omega
extends to a function
\Omega\in\mathcal{C}^{\infty}(\tilde{M})
such that

\Omega|_{\mathscr{I}^{+}}=0.

(120)

Furthermore, we want
\mathscr{I}^{+}
to be precisely the submanifold with
\Omega=0
, so we must also require that

\mathchoice{\tilde{\nabla}^{{\mathchoice{\makebox[4.33765pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[4.33765pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.59009pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.85005pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}_{{{a}}}}{\tilde{\nabla}^{{\mathchoice{\makebox[4.33765pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[4.33765pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.59009pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.85005pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}_{{{a}}}}{\tilde{\nabla}^{{\mathchoice{\makebox[4.33765pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[4.33765pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.59009pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.85005pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}_{{{a}}}}{\tilde{\nabla}^{{\mathchoice{\makebox[4.33765pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[4.33765pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.59009pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.85005pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}_{{{a}}}}\Omega|_{\mathscr{I}^{+}}\neq 0.

(121)

This ensures
\Omega=0
is indeed a hypersurface and ensures there is a non-vanishing vector normal to the surface. Hence, we get a single “sheet” with
\Omega=0
, as opposed to a plateau.

We want to obtain the full range of limits
r\to+\infty
at constant
u
’s. To ensure we get all points at infinity, we define the vector field
\mathchoice{n^{{{a}}}_{{\mathchoice{\makebox[4.33765pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[4.33765pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.59009pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.85005pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}}{n^{{{a}}}_{{\mathchoice{\makebox[4.33765pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[4.33765pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.59009pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.85005pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}}{n^{{{a}}}_{{\mathchoice{\makebox[4.33765pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[4.33765pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.59009pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.85005pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}}{n^{{{a}}}_{{\mathchoice{\makebox[4.33765pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[4.33765pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.59009pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.85005pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}}=\mathchoice{\tilde{g}^{{{a}{b}}}_{{\mathchoice{\makebox[4.33765pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[4.33765pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.59009pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.85005pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}\mathchoice{\makebox[3.51666pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[3.51666pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.1029pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.50208pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}}{\tilde{g}^{{{a}{b}}}_{{\mathchoice{\makebox[4.33765pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[4.33765pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.59009pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.85005pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}\mathchoice{\makebox[3.51666pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[3.51666pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.1029pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.50208pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}}{\tilde{g}^{{{a}{b}}}_{{\mathchoice{\makebox[4.33765pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[4.33765pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.59009pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.85005pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}\mathchoice{\makebox[3.51666pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[3.51666pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.1029pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.50208pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}}{\tilde{g}^{{{a}{b}}}_{{\mathchoice{\makebox[4.33765pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[4.33765pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.59009pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.85005pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}\mathchoice{\makebox[3.51666pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[3.51666pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.1029pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.50208pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}}\mathchoice{\tilde{\nabla}^{{\mathchoice{\makebox[3.51666pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[3.51666pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.1029pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.50208pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}_{{{b}}}}{\tilde{\nabla}^{{\mathchoice{\makebox[3.51666pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[3.51666pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.1029pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.50208pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}_{{{b}}}}{\tilde{\nabla}^{{\mathchoice{\makebox[3.51666pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[3.51666pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.1029pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.50208pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}_{{{b}}}}{\tilde{\nabla}^{{\mathchoice{\makebox[3.51666pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[3.51666pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.1029pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.50208pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}_{{{b}}}}\Omega
. We then demand the existence of a function
\omega\in\mathcal{C}^{\infty}(\tilde{M})
with
\omega>0
on
\psi(M)\cup\mathscr{I}^{+}
such that

\mathchoice{\tilde{\nabla}^{{\mathchoice{\makebox[4.33765pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[4.33765pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.59009pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.85005pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}_{{{a}}}}{\tilde{\nabla}^{{\mathchoice{\makebox[4.33765pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[4.33765pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.59009pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.85005pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}_{{{a}}}}{\tilde{\nabla}^{{\mathchoice{\makebox[4.33765pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[4.33765pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.59009pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.85005pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}_{{{a}}}}{\tilde{\nabla}^{{\mathchoice{\makebox[4.33765pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[4.33765pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.59009pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.85005pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}_{{{a}}}}(\omega^{4}\mathchoice{n^{{{a}}}_{{\mathchoice{\makebox[4.33765pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[4.33765pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.59009pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.85005pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}}{n^{{{a}}}_{{\mathchoice{\makebox[4.33765pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[4.33765pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.59009pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.85005pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}}{n^{{{a}}}_{{\mathchoice{\makebox[4.33765pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[4.33765pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.59009pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.85005pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}}{n^{{{a}}}_{{\mathchoice{\makebox[4.33765pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[4.33765pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.59009pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.85005pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}})|_{\mathscr{I}^{+}}=0

(122)

and such that the integral curves of
\omega^{-1}\mathchoice{n^{{{a}}}_{{\mathchoice{\makebox[4.33765pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[4.33765pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.59009pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.85005pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}}{n^{{{a}}}_{{\mathchoice{\makebox[4.33765pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[4.33765pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.59009pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.85005pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}}{n^{{{a}}}_{{\mathchoice{\makebox[4.33765pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[4.33765pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.59009pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.85005pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}}{n^{{{a}}}_{{\mathchoice{\makebox[4.33765pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[4.33765pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.59009pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.85005pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}}
are complete on
\mathscr{I}^{+}
. This technical condition is meant to ensure that
\mathscr{I}^{+}\cong\mdmathbb{R}\times\mdmathbb{S}^{2}
.

Finally, we need the Riemann tensor to fall off sufficiently quickly near infinity. Thus, we ask that
(M,\mathchoice{g^{{\mathchoice{\makebox[4.33765pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[4.33765pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.59009pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.85005pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}\mathchoice{\makebox[3.51666pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[3.51666pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.1029pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.50208pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}_{{{a}{b}}}}{g^{{\mathchoice{\makebox[4.33765pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[4.33765pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.59009pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.85005pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}\mathchoice{\makebox[3.51666pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[3.51666pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.1029pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.50208pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}_{{{a}{b}}}}{g^{{\mathchoice{\makebox[4.33765pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[4.33765pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.59009pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.85005pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}\mathchoice{\makebox[3.51666pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[3.51666pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.1029pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.50208pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}_{{{a}{b}}}}{g^{{\mathchoice{\makebox[4.33765pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[4.33765pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.59009pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.85005pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}\mathchoice{\makebox[3.51666pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[3.51666pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.1029pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.50208pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}_{{{a}{b}}}})
satisfies the vacuum Einstein field equations on some neighborhood of the boundary of
\psi(M)
. This can be weakened to requiring that the vacuum Einstein field equations hold asymptotically
[
235
]
. The point is that at infinity we should get a vacuum solution, so that we are far away from any matter sources.

We now bring everything together to get to the following definition.

Definition 14

(Asymptotically Flat Spacetime at Future Null Infinity)

4.3
Case Study: Schwarzschild Spacetime

As a case study, let us show that Schwarzschild spacetime is asymptotically flat at future null infinity (and actually at past null infinity too). We follow
[
215
]
. I will not make an effort to prove all of the conditions of asymptotic flatness, but rather show the conformal compactification procedure.

We want to get to future null infinity, so it makes sense to employ a retarded time coordinate instead of the more usual Schwarzschild time coordinate. In this scenario,
u
is known as the retarded Eddington–Finkelstein coordinate. The Schwarzschild metric is written as

\differential{s}^{2}=-\quantity(1 - \frac{2M}{r})\differential{u}^{2}-2\differential{u}\differential{r}+r^{2}\differential{\Sph}^{2}.

(124)

M
is the black hole’s mass, and the coordinate ranges are
u\in\mdmathbb{R}
and
r>0
. Notice that
r=0
is
not
a part of spacetime, since it is a curvature singularity.

We proceed as with Minkowski spacetime. Define a new coordinate
l=1/r
, which is now defined on the entire spacetime, since
r>0
strictly. Using this new coordinate we get the line element

\differential{s}^{2}=-\quantity(1 - 2 M l)\differential{u}^{2}+2l^{-2}\differential{u}\differential{l}+l^{-2}\differential{\Sph}^{2}.

(125)

As with Minkowski spacetime, we have a divergence at
l\to 0^{+}
because the area of spheres tends to infinity. We solve this by multiplying the metric by
l^{2}
(which means our conformal factor is
\Omega=l
) to get to

\differential{\tilde{s}}^{2}=-l^{2}\quantity(1 - 2 M l)\differential{u}^{2}+2\differential{u}\differential{l}+\differential{\Sph}^{2}.

(126)

This unphysical metric can now be extended so that
l\in\mdmathbb{R}
. Through this procedure we get the unphysical spacetime
(\tilde{M},\mathchoice{\tilde{g}^{{\mathchoice{\makebox[4.33765pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[4.33765pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.59009pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.85005pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}\mathchoice{\makebox[3.51666pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[3.51666pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.1029pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.50208pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}_{{{a}{b}}}}{\tilde{g}^{{\mathchoice{\makebox[4.33765pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[4.33765pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.59009pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.85005pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}\mathchoice{\makebox[3.51666pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[3.51666pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.1029pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.50208pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}_{{{a}{b}}}}{\tilde{g}^{{\mathchoice{\makebox[4.33765pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[4.33765pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.59009pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.85005pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}\mathchoice{\makebox[3.51666pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[3.51666pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.1029pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.50208pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}_{{{a}{b}}}}{\tilde{g}^{{\mathchoice{\makebox[4.33765pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[4.33765pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.59009pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.85005pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}\mathchoice{\makebox[3.51666pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[3.51666pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.1029pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.50208pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}_{{{a}{b}}}})
. Since
r=0
was never a point in spacetime, we did not “give up” on that point when using the new coordinate
l
.

4.4
Case Study: Poincaré Transformations at Null Infinity

At this point, we can do a simple calculation that will help us to understand the results in the next section. Namely, we will now compute what the Poincaré transformations look like at null infinity.

We start by considering Lorentz transformations. These are the vector fields
\mathchoice{J^{{{a}}}_{{{\mu}{\nu}}}}{J^{{{a}}}_{{{\mu}{\nu}}}}{J^{{{a}}}_{{{\mu}{\nu}}}}{J^{{{a}}}_{{{\mu}{\nu}}}}
given on
Eq.

99
. These vectors induce vectors on
\mathscr{I}^{+}
. These induced vectors can be computed by considering the expressions on
Eq.

99
, changing coordinates from
(t,x,y,z)
to
(u,l,\zeta,\bar{\zeta})
(
l=1/r
), and then taking the
l\to 0^{+}
limit
10
10

10

Where did the pushforward go? It is hidden inside the new coordinates. Since the physical spacetime
M
is embedded in the unphysical spacetime
\tilde{M}
, we can use the same coordinates on
M
and on
\psi(M)
. The coordinate system
(u,l,\zeta,\bar{\zeta})
is useful here because it holds on a larger region of
\tilde{M}
, while
(t,x,y,z)
or even
(u,r,\zeta,\bar{\zeta})
would break down at null infinity.
.

Let me give an example. Take
\mathchoice{J^{{{a}}}_{{{x}{t}}}}{J^{{{a}}}_{{{x}{t}}}}{J^{{{a}}}_{{{x}{t}}}}{J^{{{a}}}_{{{x}{t}}}}
as defined on
Eq.

99
. This vector generates boosts along the

\displaystyle=\sqrt{4\pi}\mathchoice{Y^{{\mathchoice{\makebox[3.98613pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[3.98613pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.45pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.75pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}{0}}}_{{{0}\mathchoice{\makebox[3.98613pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[3.98613pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.45pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.75pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}}{Y^{{\mathchoice{\makebox[3.98613pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[3.98613pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.45pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.75pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}{0}}}_{{{0}\mathchoice{\makebox[3.98613pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[3.98613pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.45pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.75pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}}{Y^{{\mathchoice{\makebox[3.98613pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[3.98613pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.45pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.75pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}{0}}}_{{{0}\mathchoice{\makebox[3.98613pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[3.98613pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.45pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.75pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}}{Y^{{\mathchoice{\makebox[3.98613pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[3.98613pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.45pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.75pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}{0}}}_{{{0}\mathchoice{\makebox[3.98613pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[3.98613pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.45pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.75pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}}(\zeta,\bar{\zeta})\mathchoice{\quantity(\pdv{u})^{{{a}}}_{{\mathchoice{\makebox[4.33765pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[4.33765pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.59009pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.85005pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}}{\quantity(\pdv{u})^{{{a}}}_{{\mathchoice{\makebox[4.33765pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[4.33765pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.59009pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.85005pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}}{\quantity(\pdv{u})^{{{a}}}_{{\mathchoice{\makebox[4.33765pt][c]{$\displaystyle$ (131g)

\displaystyle\mathchoice{\mathcal{P}^{{{a}}}_{{{x}}}}{\mathcal{P}^{{{a}}}_{{{x}}}}{\mathcal{P}^{{{a}}}_{{{x}}}}{\mathcal{P}^{{{a}}}_{{{x}}}}=-\frac{\zeta+\bar{\zeta}}{1+\zeta\bar{\zeta}}\mathchoice{\quantity(\pdv{u})^{{{a}}}_{{\mathchoice{\makebox[4.33765pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[4.33765pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.59009pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.85005pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}}{\quantity(\pdv{u})^{{{a}}}_{{\mathchoice{\makebox[4.33765pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[4.33765pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.59009pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.85005pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}}{\quantity(\pdv{u})^{{{a}}}_{{\mathchoice{\makebox[4.33765pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[4.33765pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.59009pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.85005pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}}{\quantity(\pdv{u})^{{{a}}}_{{\mathchoice{\makebox[4.33765pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[4.33765pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.59009pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.85005pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}}

\displaystyle=\sqrt{\frac{2\pi}{3}}\quantity(\tensor{Y}{_1^1}(\zeta,\bar\zeta) - \tensor{Y}{_1^{-1}}(\zeta,\bar\zeta))\mathchoice{\quantity(\pdv{u})^{{{a}}}_{{\mathchoice{\makebox[4.33765pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[4.33765pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.59009pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.85005pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}}{\quantity(\pdv{u})^{{{a}}}_{{\mathchoice{\makebox[4.33765pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[4.33765pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.59009pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.85005pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}}{\quantity(\pdv{u})^{{{a}}}_{{\mathchoice{\makebox[4.33765pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[4.33765pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.59009pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.85005pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}}{\quantity(\pdv{u})^{{{a}}}_{{\mathchoice{\makebox[4.33765pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[4.33765pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.59009pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.85005pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}},

(131h)

\displaystyle\mathchoice{\mathcal{P}^{{{a}}}_{{{y}}}}{\mathcal{P}^{{{a}}}_{{{y}}}}{\mathcal{P}^{{{a}}}_{{{y}}}}{\mathcal{P}^{{{a}}}_{{{y}}}}=\frac{i(\zeta-\bar{\zeta})}{1+\zeta\bar{\zeta}}\mathchoice{\quantity(\pdv{u})^{{{a}}}_{{\mathchoice{\makebox[4.33765pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[4.33765pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.59009pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.85005pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}}{\quantity(\pdv{u})^{{{a}}}_{{\mathchoice{\makebox[4.33765pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[4.33765pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.59009pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.85005pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}}{\quantity(\pdv{u})^{{{a}}}_{{\mathchoice{\makebox[4.33765pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[4.33765pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.59009pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.85005pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}}{\quantity(\pdv{u})^{{{a}}}_{{\mathchoice{\makebox[4.33765pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[4.33765pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.59009pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.85005pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}}

\displaystyle=-i\sqrt{\frac{2\pi}{3}}\quantity(\tensor{Y}{_1^1}(\zeta,\bar\zeta) + \tensor{Y}{_1^{-1}}(\zeta,\bar\zeta))\mathchoice{\quantity(\pdv{u})^{{{a}}}_{{\mathchoice{\makebox[4.33765pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[4.33765pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.59009pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.85005pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}}{\quantity(\pdv{u})^{{{a}}}_{{\mathchoice{\makebox[4.33765pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[4.33765pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.59009pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.85005pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}}{\quantity(\pdv{u})^{{{a}}}_{{\mathchoice{\makebox[4.33765pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[4.33765pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.59009pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.85005pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}}{\quantity(\pdv{u})^{{{a}}}_{{\mathchoice{\makebox[4.33765pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[4.33765pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.59009pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.85005pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}},

(131i)

\displaystyle\mathchoice{\mathcal{P}^{{{a}}}_{{{z}}}}{\mathcal{P}^{{{a}}}_{{{z}}}}{\mathcal{P}^{{{a}}}_{{{z}}}}{\mathcal{P}^{{{a}}}_{{{z}}}}=\frac{1-\zeta\bar{\zeta}}{1+\zeta\bar{\zeta}}\mathchoice{\quantity(\pdv{u})^{{{a}}}_{{\mathchoice{\makebox[4.33765pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[4.33765pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.59009pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.85005pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}}{\quantity(\pdv{u})^{{{a}}}_{{\mathchoice{\makebox[4.33765pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[4.33765pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.59009pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.85005pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}}{\quantity(\pdv{u})^{{{a}}}_{{\mathchoice{\makebox[4.33765pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[4.33765pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.59009pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.85005pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}}{\quantity(\pdv{u})^{{{a}}}_{{\mathchoice{\makebox[4.33765pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[4.33765pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.59009pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.85005pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}}

\displaystyle=-\sqrt{\frac{4\pi}{3}}\mathchoice{Y^{{\mathchoice{\makebox[3.98613pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[3.98613pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.45pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.75pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}{0}}}_{{{1}\mathchoice{\makebox[3.98613pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[3.98613pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.45pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.75pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}}{Y^{{\mathchoice{\makebox[3.98613pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[3.98613pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.45pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.75pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}{0}}}_{{{1}\mathchoice{\makebox[3.98613pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[3.98613pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.45pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.75pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}}{Y^{{\mathchoice{\makebox[3.98613pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[3.98613pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.45pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.75pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}{0}}}_{{{1}\mathchoice{\makebox[3.98613pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[3.98613pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.45pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.75pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}}{Y^{{\mathchoice{\makebox[3.98613pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[3.98613pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.45pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.75pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}{0}}}_{{{1}\mathchoice{\makebox[3.98613pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[3.98613pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.45pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.75pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}}(\zeta,\bar{\zeta})\mathchoice{\quantity(\pdv{u})^{{{a}}}_{{\mathchoice{\makebox[4.33765pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[4.33765pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.59009pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.85005pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}}{\quantity(\pdv{u})^{{{a}}}_{{\mathchoice{\makebox[4.33765pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[4.33765pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.59009pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.85005pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}}{\quantity(\pdv{u})^{{{a}}}_{{\mathchoice{\makebox[4.33765pt][c]{$\di (131j)

Notice the coefficients are all linear combinations of spherical harmonics
\mathchoice{Y^{{\mathchoice{\makebox[2.56946pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[2.56946pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[1.55847pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.11319pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}{m}}}_{{{l}\mathchoice{\makebox[7.09612pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[7.09612pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[4.30226pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[3.07304pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}}{Y^{{\mathchoice{\makebox[2.56946pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[2.56946pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[1.55847pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.11319pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}{m}}}_{{{l}\mathchoice{\makebox[7.09612pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[7.09612pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[4.30226pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[3.07304pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}}{Y^{{\mathchoice{\makebox[2.56946pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[2.56946pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[1.55847pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.11319pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}{m}}}_{{{l}\mathchoice{\makebox[7.09612pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[7.09612pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[4.30226pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[3.07304pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}}{Y^{{\mathchoice{\makebox[2.56946pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[2.56946pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[1.55847pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.11319pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}{m}}}_{{{l}\mathchoice{\makebox[7.09612pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[7.09612pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[4.30226pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[3.07304pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}}(\zeta,\bar{\zeta})

. This hints on how supertranslations will occur on

5
: they will admit values with

. Similarly, on
Section

8
we will see how superrotations generalize the coefficients of the
\mathchoice{\mathcal{J}^{{{a}}}_{{{\mu}{\nu}}}}{\mathcal{J}^{{{a}}}_{{{\mu}{\nu}}}}{\mathcal{J}^{{{a}}}_{{{\mu}{\nu}}}}{\mathcal{J}^{{{a}}}_{{{\mu}{\nu}}}}
vectors to allow for other powers of
\zeta
and
\bar{\zeta}
.

4.5
The Night Sky as the Riemann Sphere

In
Section

3.4
we saw the conformal group of the two-dimensional sphere is the Lorentz group. At that point, this seemed a curious result with no obvious physical interpretation.
Eq.

131
, however, gives us some intuition on what is going on: we should look at what is happening in the sphere at infinity. We follow Sec. 1.3 of Ref.
\citeonline
penrose1984TwoSpinorCalculusRelativistic.

We have been working mostly with future null infinity
\mathscr{I}^{+}
, and
Eq.

131
is written at
\mathscr{I}^{+}
, but for this discussion it is best to consider past null infinity,
\mathscr{I}^{-}
. In this way, we can picture the sphere at infinity—often called the celestial sphere—as what an observer sees as the night sky. After all, for each fixed advanced time
v=t+r
, the observer sees the sphere
\mdmathbb{S}^{2}\subseteq\mathscr{I}^{-}
with that fixed value of
v
.

Consider then two observers, Alice and Bob, who observe the night sky at the same event. Their motion is related by a Lorentz transformation. For simplicity, we assume the Lorentz transformation is only a composition of a rotation and a boost along the same direction,
\boldsymbol{\hat{z}}
. This is an example of a four-screw
[
228
]
, and it holds that any Lorentz transformation can either be written as a four-screw along some axis or as another type of transformation known as null rotation. I will ignore the null rotations, which are discussed in Sec. 1.3 of Ref.
\citeonline
penrose1984TwoSpinorCalculusRelativistic.

The Lorentz matrix for a rotation by an angle
\psi
about the
\boldsymbol{\hat{z}}
axis is

\Lambda_{R}(\psi)=\matrixquantity(\lx@physics@matrix 1 & 0 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & \cos\psi& \sin\psi& 0 \\ 0 & -\sin\psi& \cos\psi& 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 & 1\endlx@physics@matrix).

(132)

The Lorentz matrix for a boost with velocity
\tanh\chi
is given by

\Lambda_{B}(\chi)=\matrixquantity(\lx@physics@matrix\cosh\chi& 0 & 0 & -\sinh\chi\\ 0 & 1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1 & 0 \\ -\sinh\chi& 0 & 0 & \cosh\chi\endlx@physics@matrix).

(133)

The parameter
\chi
is known as “rapidity”. Notice the boost and the rotation commute. A four-screw about the
\boldsymbol{\hat{z}}
axis is then represented by

\Lambda(\psi,\chi)=\matrixquantity(\lx@physics@matrix\cosh\chi& 0 & 0 & -\sinh\chi\\ 0 & \cos\psi& \sin\psi& 0 \\ 0 & -\sin\psi& \cos\psi& 0 \\ -\sinh\chi& 0 & 0 & \cosh\chi\endlx@physics@matrix).

(134)

If an event is labeled by Alice as
\mathchoice{x^{{{\mu}}}_{{\mathchoice{\makebox[5.25pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[5.25pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[3.67499pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[2.625pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}}{x^{{{\mu}}}_{{\mathchoice{\makebox[5.25pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[5.25pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[3.67499pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[2.625pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}}{x^{{{\mu}}}_{{\mathchoice{\makebox[5.25pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[5.25pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[3.67499pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[2.625pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}}{x^{{{\mu}}}_{{\mathchoice{\makebox[5.25pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[5.25pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[3.67499pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[2.625pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}}=(t,x,y,z)
, then Bob labels it as

\matrixquantity(\lx@physics@matrix t' \\ x' \\ y' \\ z'\endlx@physics@matrix)=\matrixquantity(\lx@physics@matrix\cosh\chi& 0 & 0 & -\sinh\chi\\ 0 & \cos\psi& \sin\psi& 0 \\ 0 & -\sin\psi& \cos\psi& 0 \\ -\sinh\chi& 0 & 0 & \cosh\chi\endlx@physics@matrix)\matrixquantity(\lx@physics@matrix t \\ x \\ y \\ z\endlx@physics@matrix).

(135)

Define now, for Alice, a new coordinate system
(v,l,\zeta,\bar{\zeta})
. The stereographic coordinates are given in terms of the Cartesian coordinates by

\zeta=\frac{z+r}{x-iy},

(136)

with inverse,

x=r\frac{\zeta+\bar{\zeta}}{1+\zeta\bar{\zeta}},\quad y=-ir\frac{\zeta-\bar{\zeta}}{1+\zeta\bar{\zeta}},\quad\mbox{and}\quad z=r\frac{-1+\zeta\bar{\zeta}}{1+\zeta\bar{\zeta}}.

(137)

As usual,
v=t+r
and
l=1/r
. We define
(v^{\prime},l^{\prime},\zeta^{\prime},\bar{\zeta}^{\prime})
similarly for Bob.

Using the previous equations, we can find the relation between
(v^{\prime},\zeta^{\prime},\bar{\zeta}^{\prime})
and
(v,\zeta,\bar{\zeta})
in the
l\to 0^{+}
limit (meaning we are interested in the celestial sphere, not on a finite sphere). We have the relations

\displaystyle v^{\prime}

\displaystyle=\frac{e^{\chi}(1+\zeta\bar{\zeta})}{1+e^{2\chi}\zeta\bar{\zeta}}v,

(138)

and

\displaystyle\zeta^{\prime}

\displaystyle=e^{\chi-i\psi}\zeta.

(139)

Physically, these relations answer the following question. Suppose Alice observes, at a given event, a light-ray incoming from the celestial sphere at past null infinity with angular coordinates
(\zeta,\bar{\zeta})
at advanced time
v
. At the same event, from which direction
(\zeta^{\prime},\bar{\zeta}^{\prime})
does Bob see the light-ray incoming and at which advanced time was the light-ray sent in?

It is particularly interesting to analyze how the Lorentz transformations affect, say, the positions of the stars on the night sky. This is answered by
Eq.

139
.

Consider first the case of a pure boost (
\psi=0
). In this case, the transformation is
\zeta^{\prime}=e^{\chi}\zeta
, meaning that Bob sees larger absolute values of the stereographic coordinate in comparison to Alice. Since
\zeta=\infty
is the North pole and
\zeta=0
is the South pole, this means Bob sees the stars in the sky closer to the North pole in comparison to Alice. By “North pole” I mean the direction in the sky to which Bob is moving relative to Alice.

The second case is that of a pure rotation (
\chi=0
). In this case, the transformation is
\zeta^{\prime}=e^{-i\psi}\zeta
, which is just a phase shift. One may recall from
Eq.

65
that the phase of
\zeta
is the azimuthal angle, and therefore a rotation simply shifts
\phi\to\phi^{\prime}=\phi-\psi
. This is just a rotation of the night sky about the same axis in which Bob is rotated relative to the
\boldsymbol{\hat{z}}
axis—as expected.

For a general four-screw, the effect is a combination of the two previous ones. All of these effects, and the separate case of a null rotation, are illustrated on
Fig.

6
. The lesson we take is that the night sky seen by Alice and the night sky seen by Bob—two observers in four-dimensional Minkowski spacetime related by a Lorentz transformation—are related by a conformal transformation. This is a physical interpretation for
\mathrm{SO}^{+}(3,1)
being the conformal group on the sphere.

Figure 6:
Effects of Lorentz transformations on the celestial sphere. If Alice saw a star in the sky at some point in the sphere, Bob (who is related to Alice by a Lorentz transformation) sees the star moved along the direction of the arrows. Top left: Bob is rotated relative to Alice. Top right: Bob is boosted relative to Alice (Alice sees Bob moving toward the North pole). Bottom left: Bob is related to Alice by a four-screw (a combination of the two previous cases). Bottom right: Bob is related to Alice by a null rotation. The pictures are drawn with
Mathematica

[
251
]
and are based on the figures on Sec. 1.3 of the book by
[
193
]
.

4.6
Bondi–Sachs Formalism

There are some important remarks to be made concerning the definitions I used so far. I chose to discuss asymptotic flatness in the language of conformal compactifications, which is a coordinate-free approach and finds many uses in relativity. Nevertheless, this is not the only way of thinking about asymptotic flatness. In fact, the original works of
[
35
,
212
,
211
]
thought of asymptotic flatness in terms of the existence of a particular coordinate system in which the metric components fall-off sufficiently fast. This approach is employed in many modern references on the
\gls
BMS group and its extensions
[
225
,
68
,
184
,
7
]
.

There is a good reason for avoiding the use of conformal compactifications: there are physically interesting spacetimes that can be understood as asymptotically flat in a broader sense, but do not admit smooth conformal compactifications
[
60
,
74
,
107
,
234
]
. This is due to the fact that the smoothness properties at null infinity are related to the decay properties of the Riemann tensor, which may be complicated in dynamical scenarios.

It is important to point out that there are very simple examples in which this sort of problem occurs. For instance, in Ref.
\citeonline
christodoulou2002GlobalInitialValue, Christodoulou considers the case of a system of
n
massive bodies interacting gravitationally in linearized gravity. In the far past the bodies are assumed to interact with each other through Newtonian interactions and to have asymptotically constant velocities. For convenience, a short review of linearized gravity is available in Appendix
C
.

For such a system, the quadrupole moment in the far past is given by

\mathchoice{Q^{{\mathchoice{\makebox[2.82928pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[2.82928pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[1.68811pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.2058pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}\mathchoice{\makebox[3.71356pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[3.71356pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.29834pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.64166pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}_{{{i}{j}}}}{Q^{{\mathchoice{\makebox[2.82928pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[2.82928pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[1.68811pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.2058pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}\mathchoice{\makebox[3.71356pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[3.71356pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.29834pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.64166pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}_{{{i}{j}}}}{Q^{{\mathchoice{\makebox[2.82928pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[2.82928pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[1.68811pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.2058pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}\mathchoice{\makebox[3.71356pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[3.71356pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.29834pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.64166pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}_{{{i}{j}}}}{Q^{{\mathchoice{\makebox[2.82928pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[2.82928pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[1.68811pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.2058pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}\mathchoice{\makebox[3.71356pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[3.71356pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.29834pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.64166pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}_{{{i}{j}}}}=\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}p\\
\text{incoming}\end{subarray}}m_{p}\mathchoice{x^{{{(p)}}}_{{{i}}}}{x^{{{(p)}}}_{{{i}}}}{x^{{{(p)}}}_{{{i}}}}{x^{{{(p)}}}_{{{i}}}}\mathchoice{x^{{{(p)}}}_{{{j}}}}{x^{{{(p)}}}_{{{j}}}}{x^{{{(p)}}}_{{{j}}}}{x^{{{(p)}}}_{{{j}}}},

(140)

where
m_{p}
is the mass of the
p
-th massive body and
\mathchoice{x^{{{(p)}}}_{{{i}}}}{x^{{{(p)}}}_{{{i}}}}{x^{{{(p)}}}_{{{i}}}}{x^{{{(p)}}}_{{{i}}}}
are the Cartesian coordinates of its position. In the far past, we know
\mathchoice{\dot{x}^{{{(p)}}}_{{{i}}}}{\dot{x}^{{{(p)}}}_{{{i}}}}{\dot{x}^{{{(p)}}}_{{{i}}}}{\dot{x}^{{{(p)}}}_{{{i}}}}=\mathchoice{v^{{{(p)}}}_{{{i}}}}{v^{{{(p)}}}_{{{i}}}}{v^{{{(p)}}}_{{{i}}}}{v^{{{(p)}}}_{{{i}}}}
, which are the constant incoming velocities (the dot denotes differentiation with respect to coordinate Cartesian time). In particular, notice that in the far past it holds that

\differential{s}^{2}=-\differential{u}^{2}-2\differential{u}\differential{r}+r^{2}\mathchoice{{}^{{\mathchoice{\makebox[6.01392pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[6.01392pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[3.675pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[2.625pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}\mathchoice{\makebox[6.383pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[6.383pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[3.96252pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[2.83037pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}_{{{A}{B}}}}{{}^{{\mathchoice{\makebox[6.01392pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[6.01392pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[3.675pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[2.625pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}\mathchoice{\makebox[6.383pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[6.383pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[3.96252pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[2.83037pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}_{{{A}{B}}}}{{}^{{\mathchoice{\makebox[6.01392pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[6.01392pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[3.675pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[2.625pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}\mathchoice{\makebox[6.383pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[6.383pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[3.96252pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[2.83037pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}_{{{A}{B}}}}{{}^{{\mathchoice{\makebox[6.01392pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[6.01392pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[3.675pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[2.625pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}\mathchoice{\makebox[6.383pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[6.383pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[3.96252pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[2.83037pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}_{{{A}{B}}}}\differential{\tensor{x}{^A}}\differential{\tensor{x}{^B}}.

(151)

, which is done with previous knowledge of the matter stress-energy tensor. We are implicitly assuming that there is no stress-energy reaching null infinity at early times and that the angular momentum aspect is constant at early times. We also assume the Bondi news tensor to decay sufficiently fast at early and late times.

In these lectures, I chose the conformal compactification approach because it gives a direct and coordinate-independent construction of null infinity, which I find pedagogical. Also, it is the most popular approach among relativists, despite its limitations. In practice, this difference will not play a significant role in our discussions, because the notion of null infinity can be defined even in the absence of a conformal compactification
[
63
]
. It will, however, be useful to have two definitions we can work with, depending on what we are doing. Indeed, some applications we will consider in
Section

6
are formulated using conformal compactifications.

4.7
\glsfmtlong
CK Spacetimes

An important development in the theory of asymptotically flat spacetimes came with the work of
[
61
,
62
,
63
]
, who were originally considering the study of spacetimes globally (not only asymptotically) similar to Minkowski spacetime. Their interest was mostly in proving the nonlinear stability of Minkowski spacetime, meaning that spacetimes that are similar to Minkowski at one specific instant of time are still similar to Minkowski after evolution.

To write their definition, let
\Sigma_{t}
be a spacelike surface in the spacetime
M

at every point (which we take to be unitary). We define the induced metric on each

to be
17
17

17

On a more formal level, given a submanifold

The symbol
o_{n}(r^{-k})
stands for any function
f
such that there are always constants
C_{l}
such that
\absolutevalue{f^{(l)}}\leq C_{l}r^{-k-l}
for
0\leq l\leq n
, where
f^{(l)}
is a shorthand for any
l
-order partial derivative. Any
\gls
CK spacetime satisfying a “global smallness condition”
[
61
,
62
,
63
]
is a geodesically complete solution. In this sense, Minkowski spacetime is nonlinearly stable—perturbing the initial conditions for Minkowski spacetime will still lead to a similar spacetime.

5
The
\glsfmtlong
BMS Group

We are almost ready to derive the
\gls
BMS group. The last prerequisite we should cover is the basic theory of Carrollian manifolds, which is the sort of structure present at null infinity. This language will provide the natural arena for us to discuss asymptotic symmetries.

5.1
Carrollian Structures

By going back to the examples we provided of Minkowski and Schwarzschild spacetimes, one can notice that the line element for the induced metric at
\mathscr{I}^{+}
appears to have the form given in
Eq.

105
,

\differential{\tilde{\sigma}}^{2}=0\differential{u}^{2}+\differential{\Sph}^{2}.

(177)

Notice this is not a pseudo-Riemannian metric, because it is degenerate. If we denote this metric by

Namely, in the coordinates we used before, we have

(179)

for both Minkowski and Schwarzschild spacetimes.

Spacetimes with degenerate metrics can be understood as limiting cases of Lorentzian spacetimes. Namely, consider the Minkowski metric

\differential{s}^{2}=-c^{2}\differential{t}^{2}+\differential{x}^{2}+\differential{y}^{2}+\differential{z}^{2},

(180)

where I intentionally wrote the
c
factors explicitly. Notice now that in the unusual limit
c\to 0
we get

\differential{s}^{2}=-0\differential{t}^{2}+\differential{x}^{2}+\differential{y}^{2}+\differential{z}^{2},

(181)

which is a degenerate metric. Hence, the sort of manifold we are interested in can be understood as the
c\to 0
limit of a Lorentzian manifold.

These sorts of limits were originally considered by
[
164
,
219
]
, who were interested in studying the
c\to 0
limit of the Poincaré group. Notice that in this limit the lightcones “close” around the time axis, and there is no propagation. Lévy-Leblond associated this strange causal behavior to some scenes in Lewis Carroll’s books
Alice’s Adventures in Wonderland
and
Through the Looking Glass and What Alice Found There
. Of particular notice are Chap. 7 of the former (in which the days of the month pass faster than the hours of the day) and Chap. 2 of the latter (in which the Red Queen states that “Here, you see, it takes all the running you can do to keep in the same place”). This prompts the name “Carrollian group” for the
c\to 0
limit of the Poincaré group. Similarly, we get “Carrollian manifold” for manifolds endowed with a metric that is degenerate along a specific direction—one cannot move, even when moving at the speed of light
c=0
.

The work of
[
164
]
was mostly focused on the Carroll group, which is the
c\to 0
limit of the Poincaré group. Carrollian structures in differential geometry were defined and studied by
[
95
,
93
,
94
]
. Following their work, I shall now review the basic ideas and definitions necessary for the study of
\gls
BMS symmetries.

is known as a weak Carrollian structure, or simply a Carrollian structure.

The adjective “weak” makes reference to the fact that one can strengthen the definition of a Carrollian structure by further specifying a covariant derivative. To understand why, recall that in a pseudo-Riemannian manifold the metric singles out a particular choice of covariant derivative by imposing that the Christoffel symbols are given by

Nevertheless, this is not applicable for a Carrollian metric. Since Carrollian metrics are degenerate, the inverse metric tensor
\mathchoice{g^{{{a}{b}}}_{{\mathchoice{\makebox[4.33765pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[4.33765pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.59009pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.85005pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}\mathchoice{\makebox[3.51666pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[3.51666pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.1029pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.50208pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}}{g^{{{a}{b}}}_{{\mathchoice{\makebox[4.33765pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[4.33765pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.59009pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.85005pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}\mathchoice{\makebox[3.51666pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[3.51666pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.1029pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.50208pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}}{g^{{{a}{b}}}_{{\mathchoice{\makebox[4.33765pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[4.33765pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.59009pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.85005pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}\mathchoice{\makebox[3.51666pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[3.51666pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.1029pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.50208pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}}{g^{{{a}{b}}}_{{\mathchoice{\makebox[4.33765pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[4.33765pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.59009pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.85005pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}\mathchoice{\makebox[3.51666pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[3.51666pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.1029pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.50208pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}}

then go further and ask that

To proceed, notice that there is a gauge freedom in the definition of future null infinity. Namely, if
(M,\mathchoice{g^{{\mathchoice{\makebox[4.33765pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[4.33765pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.59009pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.85005pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}\mathchoice{\makebox[3.51666pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[3.51666pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.1029pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.50208pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}_{{{a}{b}}}}{g^{{\mathchoice{\makebox[4.33765pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[4.33765pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.59009pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.85005pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}\mathchoice{\makebox[3.51666pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[3.51666pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.1029pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.50208pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}_{{{a}{b}}}}{g^{{\mathchoice{\makebox[4.33765pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[4.33765pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.59009pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.85005pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}\mathchoice{\makebox[3.51666pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[3.51666pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.1029pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.50208pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}_{{{a}{b}}}}{g^{{\mathchoice{\makebox[4.33765pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[4.33765pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.59009pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.85005pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}\mathchoice{\makebox[3.51666pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[3.51666pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.1029pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.50208pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}_{{{a}{b}}}})
is asymptotically flat with conformal factor
\Omega
, then the conformal factor
\omega\Omega
for
\omega\in\mathcal{C}^{\infty}(\tilde{M})
and
\omega>0
would work just as well. Using this freedom, the Carrollian structure of null infinity can be made into a strong Carrollian structure. As discussed in Chap. 11 of Ref.
\citeonline
wald1984GeneralRelativity, one can use this gauge freedom to impose that
\mathchoice{\tilde{\nabla}^{{\mathchoice{\makebox[4.33765pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[4.33765pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.59009pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.85005pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}_{{{a}}}}{\tilde{\nabla}^{{\mathchoice{\makebox[4.33765pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[4.33765pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.59009pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.85005pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}_{{{a}}}}{\tilde{\nabla}^{{\mathchoice{\makebox[4.33765pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[4.33765pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.59009pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.85005pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}_{{{a}}}}{\tilde{\nabla}^{{\mathchoice{\makebox[4.33765pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[4.33765pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.59009pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.85005pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}_{{{a}}}}\mathchoice{n^{{{b}}}_{{\mathchoice{\makebox[3.51666pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[3.51666pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.1029pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.50208pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}}{n^{{{b}}}_{{\mathchoice{\makebox[3.51666pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[3.51666pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.1029pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.50208pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}}{n^{{{b}}}_{{\mathchoice{\makebox[3.51666pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[3.51666pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.1029pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.50208pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}}{n^{{{b}}}_{{\mathchoice{\makebox[3.51666pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[3.51666pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.1029pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.50208pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}}=0
. Notice that this condition is equivalent to imposing that
\mathchoice{\tilde{\nabla}^{{\mathchoice{\makebox[4.33765pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[4.33765pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.59009pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.85005pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}_{{{a}}}}{\tilde{\nabla}^{{\mathchoice{\makebox[4.33765pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[4.33765pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.59009pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.85005pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}_{{{a}}}}{\tilde{\nabla}^{{\mathchoice{\makebox[4.33765pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[4.33765pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.59009pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.85005pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}_{{{a}}}}{\tilde{\nabla}^{{\mathchoice{\makebox[4.33765pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[4.33765pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.59009pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.85005pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}_{{{a}}}}\mathchoice{\tilde{\nabla}^{{\mathchoice{\makebox[3.51666pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[3.51666pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.1029pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.50208pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}_{{{b}}}}{\tilde{\nabla}^{{\mathchoice{\makebox[3.51666pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[3.51666pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.1029pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.50208pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}_{{{b}}}}{\tilde{\nabla}^{{\mathchoice{\makebox[3.51666pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[3.51666pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.1029pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.50208pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}_{{{b}}}}{\tilde{\nabla}^{{\mathchoice{\makebox[3.51666pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[3.51666pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.1029pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.50208pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}_{{{b}}}}\Omega=0
, which does not need to hold in general. However, one can always find a choice of
\Omega
for which this holds.

The strong Carrollian structure ends up being too strong for our purposes. Hence, we will work mostly with the weak Carrollian structure of null infinity and only comment later on the role the strong Carrollian structure can play.

5.2
Symmetries at Null Infinity

We are now ready to discuss the symmetry group of future null infinity. To do so, consider the gauge freedom mentioned at the end of the last section, which consists of exchanging the conformal factor
\Omega
according to
\Omega\to\omega\Omega
for smooth
\omega>0
. Using that

We shall begin our discussion by taking a coordinate approach. Using the gauge freedom in the definition of future null infinity one can always choose a coordinate system near

in which (see,

(185)

(\mathscr{I}^{+},\omega^{2}\mathchoice{\tilde{h}^{{\mathchoice{\makebox[4.33765pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[4.33765pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.59009pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.85005pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}\mathchoice{\makebox[3.51666pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[3.51666pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.1029pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.50208pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}_{{{a}{b}}}}{\tilde{h}^{{\mathchoice{\makebox[4.33765pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[4.33765pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.59009pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.85005pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}\mathchoice{\makebox[3.51666pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[3.51666pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.1029pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.50208pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}_{{{a}{b}}}}{\tilde{h}^{{\mathchoice{\makebox[4.33765pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[4.33765pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.59009pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.85005pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}\mathchoice{\makebox[3.51666pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[3.51666pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.1029pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.50208pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}_{{{a}{b}}}}{\tilde{h}^{{\mathchoice{\makebox[4.33765pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[4.33765pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.59009pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.85005pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}\mathchoice{\makebox[3.51666pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[3.51666pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.1029pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.50208pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}_{{{a}{b}}}})
we see that this is the group of confomorphisms of
(\mathscr{I}^{+},\mathchoice{\tilde{h}^{{\mathchoice{\makebox[4.33765pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[4.33765pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.59009pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.85005pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}\mathchoice{\makebox[3.51666pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[3.51666pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.1029pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.50208pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}_{{{a}{b}}}}{\tilde{h}^{{\mathchoice{\makebox[4.33765pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[4.33765pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.59009pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.85005pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}\mathchoice{\makebox[3.51666pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[3.51666pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.1029pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.50208pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}_{{{a}{b}}}}{\tilde{h}^{{\mathchoice{\makebox[4.33765pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[4.33765pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.59009pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.85005pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}\mathchoice{\makebox[3.51666pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[3.51666pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.1029pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.50208pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}_{{{a}{b}}}}{\tilde{h}^{{\mathchoice{\makebox[4.33765pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[4.33765pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.59009pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.85005pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}\mathchoice{\makebox[3.51666pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[3.51666pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.1029pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.50208pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}_{{{a}{b}}}})
. In the canonical triplet, we have

(\mathscr{I}^{+},\mathchoice{\tilde{h}^{{\mathchoice{\makebox[4.33765pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[4.33765pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.59009pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.85005pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}\mathchoice{\makebox[3.51666pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[3.51666pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.1029pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.50208pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}_{{{a}{b}}}}{\tilde{h}^{{\mathchoice{\makebox[4.33765pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[4.33765pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.59009pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.85005pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}\mathchoice{\makebox[3.51666pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[3.51666pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.1029pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.50208pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}_{{{a}{b}}}}{\tilde{h}^{{\mathchoice{\makebox[4.33765pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[4.33765pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.59009pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.85005pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}\mathchoice{\makebox[3.51666pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[3.51666pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.1029pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.50208pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}_{{{a}{b}}}}{\tilde{h}^{{\mathchoice{\makebox[4.33765pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[4.33765pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.59009pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.85005pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}\mathchoice{\makebox[3.51666pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[3.51666pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.1029pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.50208pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}_{{{a}{b}}}})=(\mathscr{I}^{+},\differential{\Sph}^{2}).

(189)

Hence, we want transformations that are confomorphisms of the sphere (since we have the metric of a sphere) and change
u
in an arbitrary way. We know from
Section

3.4
that the confomorphisms on the sphere are the Möbius transformations, which in stereographic coordinates can be written as

\zeta\to\frac{a\zeta+b}{c\zeta+d}

(190)

with

\matrixquantity(\lx@physics@matrix a & b \\ c & d\endlx@physics@matrix)\in\mathrm{SL}(2,\mdmathbb{C})/\mdmathbb{Z}_{2}\cong\mathrm{SO}^{+}(3,1).

(191)

Furthermore, we have to assign a general transformation law for
u
. Since
u
does not occur in the metric, we can preserve the conformal structure of the metric by perfoming any transformation of the form

u\to F(u,\zeta,\bar{\zeta})

(192)

with
u\mapsto F(u,\zeta,\bar{\zeta})
being a diffeomorphism.

We thus get the general coordinate transformations

\left\{\begin{aligned} \zeta&\to\frac{a\zeta+b}{c\zeta+d},\\
u&\to F(u,\zeta,\bar{\zeta}).\end{aligned}\right.

(193)

This collection of transformations form a group known as the Newman–Unti group
[
179
]
. As a set, the Newman–Unti group is given by a subset of
\mathrm{SO}^{+}(3,1)\times\mathcal{C}^{\infty}(\mdmathbb{R}\times\mdmathbb{S}^{2})
, but it has a complicated Lie group structure
[
202
]
.

For completeness, I mention that under the Möbius transformation

\zeta\to\zeta^{\prime}=\frac{a\zeta+b}{c\zeta+d}

(194)

the metric of the sphere transforms according to (recall
Eq.

67
)

2{}_{\zeta^{\prime}\bar{\zeta}^{\prime}}\differential{\zeta}\differential{\bar{\zeta}'}=2K(\zeta,\bar{\zeta})^{2}{}_{\zeta\bar{\zeta}}\differential{\zeta}\differential{\bar{\zeta}}

(195)

with

K(\zeta,\bar{\zeta})=\frac{1+\zeta\bar{\zeta}}{(a\zeta+b)(\bar{a}\bar{\zeta}+\bar{b})+(c\zeta+d)(\bar{c}\bar{\zeta}+\bar{d})}.

(196)

Now we impose that the Carrollian structure is preserved as a whole. This means we also must have that
\mathchoice{n^{{{a}}}_{{\mathchoice{\makebox[4.33765pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[4.33765pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.59009pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.85005pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}}{n^{{{a}}}_{{\mathchoice{\makebox[4.33765pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[4.33765pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.59009pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.85005pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}}{n^{{{a}}}_{{\mathchoice{\makebox[4.33765pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[4.33765pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.59009pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.85005pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}}{n^{{{a}}}_{{\mathchoice{\makebox[4.33765pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[4.33765pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.59009pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.85005pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}}\to\omega^{-1}\mathchoice{n^{{{a}}}_{{\mathchoice{\makebox[4.33765pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[4.33765pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.59009pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.85005pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}}{n^{{{a}}}_{{\mathchoice{\makebox[4.33765pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[4.33765pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.59009pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.85005pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}}{n^{{{a}}}_{{\mathchoice{\makebox[4.33765pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[4.33765pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.59009pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.85005pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}}{n^{{{a}}}_{{\mathchoice{\makebox[4.33765pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[4.33765pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.59009pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.85005pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}}
. We know already that
\omega=K(\zeta,\bar{\zeta})
because we have already restricted the set of possible transformations to the Newman–Unti group. To further restrict the transformations, we notice that the
u
parameter is defined by the equation

\mathchoice{n^{{{a}}}_{{\mathchoice{\makebox[4.33765pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[4.33765pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.59009pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.85005pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}}{n^{{{a}}}_{{\mathchoice{\makebox[4.33765pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[4.33765pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.59009pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.85005pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}}{n^{{{a}}}_{{\mathchoice{\makebox[4.33765pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[4.33765pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.59009pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.85005pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}}{n^{{{a}}}_{{\mathchoice{\makebox[4.33765pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[4.33765pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.59009pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.85005pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}}\mathchoice{\tilde{\nabla}^{{\mathchoice{\makebox[4.33765pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[4.33765pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.59009pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.85005pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}_{{{a}}}}{\tilde{\nabla}^{{\mathchoice{\makebox[4.33765pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[4.33765pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.59009pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.85005pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}_{{{a}}}}{\tilde{\nabla}^{{\mathchoice{\makebox[4.33765pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[4.33765pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.59009pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.85005pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}_{{{a}}}}{\tilde{\nabla}^{{\mathchoice{\makebox[4.33765pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[4.33765pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.59009pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.85005pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}_{{{a}}}}u=1,

(197)

and this equation is gauge-independent. Hence, since the normal vector is known to transform as
\mathchoice{n^{{{a}}}_{{\mathchoice{\makebox[4.33765pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[4.33765pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.59009pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.85005pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}}{n^{{{a}}}_{{\mathchoice{\makebox[4.33765pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[4.33765pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.59009pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.85005pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}}{n^{{{a}}}_{{\mathchoice{\makebox[4.33765pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[4.33765pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.59009pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.85005pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}}{n^{{{a}}}_{{\mathchoice{\makebox[4.33765pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[4.33765pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.59009pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.85005pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}}\to\omega^{-1}\mathchoice{n^{{{a}}}_{{\mathchoice{\makebox[4.33765pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[4.33765pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.59009pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.85005pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}}{n^{{{a}}}_{{\mathchoice{\makebox[4.33765pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[4.33765pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.59009pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.85005pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}}{n^{{{a}}}_{{\mathchoice{\makebox[4.33765pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[4.33765pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.59009pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.85005pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}}{n^{{{a}}}_{{\mathchoice{\makebox[4.33765pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[4.33765pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.59009pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.85005pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}}
, it follows that we must have

\mathchoice{\tilde{\nabla}^{{\mathchoice{\makebox[4.33765pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[4.33765pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.59009pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.85005pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}_{{{a}}}}{\tilde{\nabla}^{{\mathchoice{\makebox[4.33765pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[4.33765pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.59009pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.85005pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}_{{{a}}}}{\tilde{\nabla}^{{\mathchoice{\makebox[4.33765pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[4.33765pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.59009pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.85005pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}_{{{a}}}}{\tilde{\nabla}^{{\mathchoice{\makebox[4.33765pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[4.33765pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.59009pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.85005pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}_{{{a}}}}u\to\omega\mathchoice{\tilde{\nabla}^{{\mathchoice{\makebox[4.33765pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[4.33765pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.59009pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.85005pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}_{{{a}}}}{\tilde{\nabla}^{{\mathchoice{\makebox[4.33765pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[4.33765pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.59009pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.85005pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}_{{{a}}}}{\tilde{\nabla}^{{\mathchoice{\makebox[4.33765pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[4.33765pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.59009pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.85005pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}_{{{a}}}}{\tilde{\nabla}^{{\mathchoice{\makebox[4.33765pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[4.33765pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.59009pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.85005pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}_{{{a}}}}u.

(198)

This is better expressed in the notation of differential forms, in which case we find that the transformation for
u
must be such that

\differential{u}\to\differential{u'}=K(\zeta,\bar{\zeta})\differential{u},

(199)

where we used
\omega=K(\zeta,\bar{\zeta})
. Integrating
Eq.

199
allows us to conclude that the allowed transformations for
u
are those with the form

u\to u^{\prime}=K(\zeta,\bar{\zeta})(u+f(\zeta,\bar{\zeta})),

(200)

where
f\in\mathcal{C}^{\infty}(\mdmathbb{S}^{2})
is an arbitrary function that occurs as an integration constant. We assume it to be smooth because we are working in a smooth manifold.

The transformations that preserve the (weak) Carrollian structure are thus given by

\left\{\begin{aligned} \zeta&\to\frac{a\zeta+b}{c\zeta+d},\\
u&\to K(\zeta,\bar{\zeta})(u+f(\zeta,\bar{\zeta})),\end{aligned}\right.

(201)

where
K
is given by
Eq.

196
. These are known as
\glsxtrfull
BMS transformations and they form the (restricted)
\gls
BMS group in four dimensions
[
35
,
212
,
211
]
, which I will denote as
\mathrm{BMS}_{4}
. The adjective “restricted” refers to the fact that we are ignoring time and space reflections.

Notice that a
\gls
BMS transformation is characterized by a pair
(\Lambda,f)\in\mathrm{SO}^{+}(3,1)\times\mathcal{C}^{\infty}(\mdmathbb{S}^{2})
, where
\Lambda
relates to the coefficients
a
,
b
,
c
, and
d
in
Eq.

201
by

\Pi^{-1}(\Lambda)=\matrixquantity(\lx@physics@matrix a & b \\ c & d\endlx@physics@matrix),

(202)

with
\Pi\colon\mathrm{SL}(2,\mdmathbb{C})/\mdmathbb{Z}_{2}\to\mathrm{SO}^{+}(3,1)
being the isomorphism between the two groups. We denote the function
K
associated to
\Lambda
by
K_{\Lambda}
. Using this notation, the group product
\odot
is given by

(\Lambda^{\prime},f^{\prime})\odot(\Lambda,f)=(\Lambda^{\prime}\Lambda,f+(K_{\Lambda^{-1}}\circ\Lambda)\cdot(f^{\prime}\circ\Lambda)),

(203)

where
\circ
denotes composition of mappings and
\cdot
denotes the pointwise product of functions.

Notice that
\mathrm{SO}^{+}(3,1)
is isomorphic to the subgroup

\mathcal{L}=\quantity{(\Lambda,0); \Lambda\in\SO*(3,1)}

(204)

of the
\gls
BMS group. Similarly,
\mathcal{C}^{\infty}(\mdmathbb{S}^{2})
(with the pointwise sum of functions as the group product) is isomorphic to

\mathcal{T}=\quantity{(\Eins,f); f \in\ck[\infty](\Sph^2)}.

(205)

Eq.

203
allows us to conclude that
\mathcal{T}
is a normal subgroup of the
\gls
BMS group, but
\mathcal{L}
is not.

Notice that these two subgroups satisfy

\mathcal{L}\cap\mathcal{T}=\quantity{(\Eins,0)},

(206)

which means their intersection is given by the
\gls
BMS group’s identity. Furthermore, using
Eq.

203
we can see that any element
(\Lambda,f)
of the
\gls
BMS group can be written in the form

(\Lambda,f)=(\Lambda,0)\odot(\text{1},f).

(207)

Hence, we can write the
\gls
BMS group as
\mathcal{L}\odot\mathcal{T}
. These results allow us to conclude that the
\gls
BMS group is the semidirect product of
\mathcal{L}
and
\mathcal{T}
. Hence, the
\gls
BMS group is given by
\mathcal{L}\ltimes\mathcal{T}
. Using the isomorphisms
\mathcal{L}\cong\mathrm{SO}^{+}(3,1)
and
\mathcal{T}\cong\mathcal{C}^{\infty}(\mdmathbb{S}^{2})
, we can write that the
\gls
BMS group is given by the semidirect product
\mathrm{SO}^{+}(3,1)\ltimes\mathcal{C}^{\infty}(\mdmathbb{S}^{2})
.

5.3
Alternative Derivation with Conformal Killing Vector Fields

Let us now derive the
\gls
BMS group once again, but this time employing vector field methods. In other words, we want to find which vector fields generate the
\gls
BMS transformations. This will make it easier for us to compare the results with those of the Poincaré group.

We know we want to consider confomorphisms. Furthermore, these confomorphisms should also preserve (in a conformal sense) the normal vector
\mathchoice{n^{{{a}}}_{{\mathchoice{\makebox[4.33765pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[4.33765pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.59009pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.85005pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}}{n^{{{a}}}_{{\mathchoice{\makebox[4.33765pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[4.33765pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.59009pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.85005pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}}{n^{{{a}}}_{{\mathchoice{\makebox[4.33765pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[4.33765pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.59009pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.85005pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}}{n^{{{a}}}_{{\mathchoice{\makebox[4.33765pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[4.33765pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.59009pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.85005pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}}
. We can state these conditions mathematically by stating that we are looking for diffeomorphisms generated by vector fields
\mathchoice{\xi^{{{a}}}_{{\mathchoice{\makebox[4.33765pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[4.33765pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.59009pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.85005pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}}{\xi^{{{a}}}_{{\mathchoice{\makebox[4.33765pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[4.33765pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.59009pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.85005pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}}{\xi^{{{a}}}_{{\mathchoice{\makebox[4.33765pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[4.33765pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.59009pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.85005pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}}{\xi^{{{a}}}_{{\mathchoice{\makebox[4.33765pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[4.33765pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.59009pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.85005pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}}
such that
