To understand the role that the cosmological constant, matter, and radiation play at each point in the evolution of the Universe we can make plots of the quantities

\displaystyle{}_{\Lambda}(\tau)

\displaystyle=\frac{{}_{\Lambda,0}}{{}_{\Lambda,0}+{}_{m,0}\quantity(\frac{a_0}{a(\tau)})^{3}+{}_{r,0}\quantity(\frac{a_0}{a(\tau)})^{4}},

(471a)

\displaystyle{}_{m}(\tau)

\displaystyle=\frac{{}_{m,0}a_{0}^{3}a(\tau)^{-3}}{{}_{\Lambda,0}+{}_{m,0}\quantity(\frac{a_0}{a(\tau)})^{3}+{}_{r,0}\quantity(\frac{a_0}{a(\tau)})^{4}},

(471b)

\displaystyle{}_{r}(\tau)

\displaystyle=\frac{{}_{r,0}a_{0}^{4}a(\tau)^{-4}}{{}_{\Lambda,0}+{}_{m,0}\quantity(\frac{a_0}{a(\tau)})^{3}+{}_{r,0}\quantity(\frac{a_0}{a(\tau)})^{4}}.

(471c)

These three quantities add to one. Hence, they can be used to understand which fraction of the matter of the Universe is comprised by a cosmological constant, by cold matter, or by radiation. Indeed, as attested by
Eq.

468
, the largest of them at each time is responsible for dictating the approximate evolution of the Universe. They are plotted on
Fig.

10

Figure 10:
Values of the density parameters
i
defined on
Eq.

471
as functions of cosmic time. A dashed line indicates present-day.

As one can read from
Fig.

10
, for
\tau\lesssim$10\,000\text{\,}\mathrm{\text{yr}}$
radiation dominates and dictates the evolution of the early Universe. Later, for
$10\,000\text{\,}\mathrm{\text{yr}}$\lesssim\tau\lesssim$10\text{\,}\mathrm{G\text{yr}}$
matter dominates. At late times (
\tau\gtrsim$10\text{\,}\mathrm{G\text{yr}}$
), the cosmological constant dominates and the evolution of the Universe is essentially equal to that of a vacuum spacetime with a cosmological constant. In this region, the Friedmann equation becomes

\frac{\dot{a}^{2}}{a^{2}}\approx H_{0}^{2}{}_{\Lambda,0}=\frac{\Lambda}{3}>0,

(472)

where we used
Eq.

466
with
\rho=0
. The inequality follows from the experimental values of
H_{0}
and
�,0
.

Eq.

472
can be solved exactly and yields

a(\tau)=a_{0}\exp(\sqrt{\frac{\Lambda}{3}} (\tau- \tau_0)),

(473)

where
a(\tau_{0})=a_{0}
(present-day). In this case, the metric is given by

\differential{s}^{2}=-\differential{\tau}^{2}+a_{0}^{2}\exp(2 \sqrt{\frac{\Lambda}{3}} (\tau- \tau_0))\differential{\ell}^{2}.

(474)

This is the metric for de Sitter spacetime in planar coordinates
[
222
]
.

To get a global picture of the geometry of the Universe, let us compute the Carter–Penrose diagram. To do this, it is useful to begin by changing the time coordinate from cosmic time
\tau
to conformal time
t
, which is defined by

t(\tau)=a_{0}\int_{0}^{\tau}\frac{\differential{\tau'}}{a(\tau^{\prime})}.

(475)

It is possible to choose a different initial condition for
t
, but we will work with the assumption that
t(0)=0
. This means conformal time vanishes at the Big Bang.
Fig.

11
shows the dependence of conformal time with respect to cosmic time for the experimental data given in
Eq.

470
. It is interesting to notice that
t
tends to a finite value as
\tau\to+\infty
.

Figure 11:
Conformal time as a function of cosmic time for the
\Lambda
CDM model. Present-day is indicated by a dashed line. For large values of cosmic time, we get the asymptotic value of
t\approx$63.06$a_{0}
.

The usefulness of conformal time is that the spatially flat
\gls
FLRW geometry can now be written as

\differential{s}^{2}=a(t)^{2}\quantity[-\dd{t}^2 + \dd{\ell}^2],

(476)

and it is now clear that the spacetime metric is related to that of Minkowski spacetime by a conformal transformation. This holds for any spatially flat
\gls
FLRW geometry. By repeating the analysis of
Section

4.1
we can find the expression

\differential{s}^{2}=4a(t)^{2}\sec[2](\frac{T-R}{2})\sec[2](\frac{T+R}{2})\quantity[-\dd{T}^2 + \dd{R}^2 + \sin^2{R} \dd{\Sph}^2],

(477)

where conformal time is given by

t=\frac{1}{2}\quantity[\tan(\frac{T-R}{2}) + \tan(\frac{T+R}{2})]

(478)

and the compactified coordinates
T
and
R
obey

0<T<\pi\quad\mbox{and}\quad 0\leq R<\pi-T.

(479)

This holds for any scale factor
a(t)
. However, if for a specific geometry we have that conformal time is bounded in the interval
t\in(t_{0},t_{f})
, then we also have the constraints

t_{0}<t=\frac{1}{2}\quantity[\tan(\frac{T-R}{2}) + \tan(\frac{T+R}{2})]<t_{f}.

(480)

As attested by
Fig.

11
, our model of the Universe has
t_{0}=0
and
t_{f}\approx$63.06$a_{0}
. The Carter–Penrose diagram can then be obtained by plotting the ranges of
T
and
R
. The result is shown on
Fig.

12
.

Figure 12:
Carter–Penrose diagram for the
\Lambda
CDM spacetime. The zigzag line (representing the Big Bang) is a singularity. The
t=t_{f}
line denotes timelike and null infinity.

We can also compute the Carter–Penrose diagram for de Sitter spacetime. In this case, conformal time is given by

\displaystyle t

\displaystyle=a_{0}\int\frac{\differential{\tau}}{a(\tau)},

(481a)

\displaystyle=\int\exp(-\sqrt{\frac{\Lambda}{3}}(\tau- \tau_0))\differential{\tau},

(481b)

\displaystyle=-\sqrt{\frac{3}{\Lambda}}\quantity[\exp(-\sqrt{\frac{\Lambda}{3}}(\tau- \tau_0))-1]+t_{0},

(481c)

with
t(\tau_{0})=t_{0}
. Notice then that, since
\tau\in\mathbb{R}
(de Sitter spacetime does not present a Big Bang), we have

-\infty<t<t_{0}+\sqrt{\frac{3}{\Lambda}}.

(482)

It is harmless and convenient to pick
t_{0}=-\sqrt{{3}/{\Lambda}}
. In this case, we find that the coordinates
T
and
R
obey

-\pi<T<0\quad\mbox{and}\quad 0\leq R<\pi+T.

(483)

Plotting the ranges of
T
and
R
gives the Carter–Penrose diagram for the cosmological patch of de Sitter spacetime,
i.e.
, for the metric we originally considered as de Sitter spacetime without any extensions. It is shown on
Fig.

13
. It is important to notice that the
t=0
boundary in de Sitter spacetime corresponds to the
t=t_{f}
boundary in the
\Lambda
CDM spacetime. They look different in
Figs.

12
and
13
because in de Sitter spacetime we had the freedom of using a conformal transformation to “flatten” the boundary, but in the
\Lambda
CDM spacetime we had already used this freedom when dealing with the Big Bang.

Figure 13:
Carter–Penrose diagram for the cosmological patch of de Sitter spacetime.

We can extend the original de Sitter spacetime. When dealing with the Schwarzschild spacetime, one can extend the exterior Schwarzschild geometry to obtain the full Kruskal extension. This extension includes not only the asymptotically flat region, but also the black hole region and two other regions corresponding to a white hole and to a “parallel universe”
[
235
,
57
,
64
,
51
]
. We can do a similar procedure with de Sitter spacetime.

The first step to seeing this is computing the scale factor as a function of conformal time. Using
Eqs.

473
and
481
we see that

a(t)=-\sqrt{\frac{3}{\Lambda}}\frac{1}{t}.

(484)

Using this result on
Eq.

477
and rewriting
t
in terms of
T
and
R
we find that the de Sitter metric can be written as

\differential{s}^{2}=\frac{3\csc^{2}T}{\Lambda}\quantity[-\dd{T}^2 + \dd{R}^2 + \sin^2{R} \dd{\Sph}^2].

(485)

From this expression it is clear that we can extend the original coordinate ranges on
Eq.

483
to allow
0\leq R\leq\pi
. In this case,
R
is now an angular variable on a three-dimensional sphere
\mathbb{S}^{3}
. The Carter–Penrose diagram for this extended spacetime (which is the full de Sitter spacetime) is shown in
Fig.

14
.

Figure 14:
Global Carter–Penrose diagram for de Sitter spacetime. The thin lines depict spatially flat planes foliating the cosmological patch. These planes asymptote to the hypersurface
\mathscr{H}^{-}
, which is a cosmological horizon. Figure adapted from Ref.
\citeonline
aguiaralves2025NullInfinityKilling.

We notice that the boundary of the original cosmological patch is now a hypersurface on the full de Sitter spacetime. This hypersurface, indicated as
\mathscr{H}^{-}
on
Fig.

14
, is known as a (past) particle horizon
[
206
,
205
]
for the cosmic observer sitting at
R=0
—this observer cannot send any information to the events beyond the horizon. In fact, for de Sitter spacetime this statement is even stronger: no cosmic observer can send any information beyond the horizon and the notion of cosmic observer as we originally defined does not make sense beyond the horizon.

For this reason,
\mathscr{H}^{-}
will be referred to as a cosmological horizon: it is a distinguished null hypersurface in the spacetime that can be interpreted as the boundary of the cosmological patch of de Sitter spacetime. It seems fair then that we consider the original cosmological patch as the “bulk” and the global de Sitter spacetime as an extension.
\mathscr{H}^{-}
is then understood as a boundary similar to
\mathscr{I}^{+}
(or, even better,
\mathscr{I}^{-}
) in asymptotically flat spacetimes. Our expectation is then that studying this cosmological horizon we may find results similar to those we found when working with null infinity.

There is, however, an important point to be addressed: is this horizon physically meaningful? As
Fig.

12
clearly shows, the global structure of the
\Lambda
CDM universe is very different from that of de Sitter spacetime. In particular, we cannot make a past extension to get a past cosmological horizon, because the Big Bang prevents us from doing so.

In spite of this, at late times we know that the cosmological constant gives the most relevant contribution to the Universe’s evolution. Hence, at late times, we can say the Universe is asymptotically de Sitter. It seems fair then that we can consider the past cosmological horizon of de Sitter spacetime as an auxiliary structure to understand the behavior of the Universe at late times. In fact, this does not seem so different from what we do with asymptotically flat spacetimes: we know the Universe is not asymptotically flat in large scales, but we can still use the concept of null infinity to obtain information about the behavior of regions of spacetime. In fact, the Weinberg soft graviton theorem shows that we can even use the notion of null infinity to obtain insights into the behavior of elementary particles in a locally flat patch.

9.2
Inflation

There is still a second reason to consider “asymptotically de Sitter” spacetimes: it is believed that, near its beginning, the Universe underwent a stage of very fast expansion known as inflation. This period of fast expansion is very similar to a de Sitter solution. In this sense, the de Sitter solution is interesting at very early times in the history of the Universe, just as at very late times. In this section, I will very briefly review some ideas behind inflation as a motivation for considering asymptotically de Sitter spacetimes. Further information can be found in any modern book on cosmology—such as Refs.
\citeonline
baumann2022Cosmology,weinberg2008Cosmology—or on specialized reviews such as Refs.
\citeonline
baumann2012TASILecturesInflation,kinney2009TASILecturesInflation.

While the
\Lambda
CDM model is very successful, it has a few drawbacks. For instance, one may inquire why we see no magnetic monopoles, even though they are a standard prediction of
\glspl
GUT
[
139
,
198
,
243
,
245
]
. Alternatively, one may inquire how the universe is spatially flat, given that spatial flatness can be an extremely unstable feature in
\gls
FLRW cosmologies
[
21
,
245
]
.

I will focus on a different aspect, known as the horizon problem. We observe the Universe as being extremely homogeneous and isotropic
[
2
]
. For instance, the relative variations on the temperature of the
\gls
CMB are of the order of
{10}^{-5}
over the whole sky
[
2
]
. This suggests regions of the sky that are very far away from each other were once in contact.

Let us then draw a Carter–Penrose diagram of the universe and, in particular, draw the lightcones of two different points in the sky at the time of emission of the
\gls
CMB. For them to be in thermal equilibrium, they should have been in causal contact before. This is shown in
Fig.

15
for a radiation-filled universe—
i.e.
, ignoring the late-time behavior of the
\Lambda
CDM model, which is irrelevant for this discussion anyway. One sees in the diagram that regions farther and closer to the Earth were not in causal contact, despite observational data suggesting otherwise.

Figure 15:
Carter–Penrose diagram for a radiation-filled, spatially flat universe. The zigzag at the bottom of the diagram indicates the Big Bang. The dashed line indicates the cosmic time at photon decoupling. Two light cones on different regions of the universe are indicated. Notice they are not in causal contact. Since the Carter–Penrose diagram omits the angular variables, this does not illustrate the causal relations between different regions in the night sky, but rather between regions closer and farther from Earth.

[
121
]
noticed this behavior (and the other problems I briefly mentioned) could be remedied if the universe had undergone a stage of rapid expansion before entering the radiation era. The radiation era involves most of the observable predictions of the Big Bang theory (formation of nuclei, formation of the first few elements, and so on), but it can be modified at very early times without affecting the predictions that match with experiment.

If one constructs a
\gls
FLRW geometry in which the universe starts with an approximately constant Hubble parameter—thus mimicking a cosmological constant—then the diagram on
Fig.

15
gets considerably altered. This can happen if the universe is dominated by some matter type with
\rho+3P<0
(it is said that this matter type violates the
\gls
SEC), such as a scalar field with a suitably chosen potential. If this is the case, the diagram may become as in
Fig.

16
. Notice how the diagrams on
Figs.

13
and
16
are similar apart from the Big Bang on the latter.

Figure 16:
Carter–Penrose diagram for a spatially flat universe dominated by a single component violating the
\gls
SEC (but different from curvature or a cosmological constant). The zigzag at the bottom of the diagram indicates the Big Bang, which has been pushed to conformal infinity. The dashed line indicates the cosmic time at photon decoupling. Two light cones on different regions of the universe are indicated. Notice they now are in causal contact. Since the Carter–Penrose diagram omits the angular variables, this does not illustrate the causal relations between different regions in the night sky, but rather between regions closer and farther from Earth.

These sorts of theoretical motivations inspire the consideration of a de Sitter-like era at the beginning of the universe. Quantum effects are particularly relevant during this stage. In fact, many of the modern cosmological observations are based on the perturbations of the
\gls
FLRW metric, which can be explained by quantum fluctuations of a scalar field during inflation (this is often called an inflaton). See Refs.
\citeonline
baumann2022Cosmology,weinberg2008Cosmology,lesgourgues2013TASILecturesCosmological, for example for discussions on this. Hence, it would be extremely interesting to understand the behavior of gravity and of
\gls
QFT in regions of the universe similar to de Sitter spacetime.

With these motivations, we may then proceed to the study of spacetimes with cosmological horizons with the goal of understanding their
\gls
IR symmetries.

9.3
\glsfmtshort
FLRW Spacetimes with Cosmological Horizons

Our present goal is to get to an appropriate definition of an “expanding universe with cosmological horizon”. This definition was provided by Dappiaggi, Moretti, and Pinamonti
[
81
]
(see also their review, Ref.
\citeonline
dappiaggi2017HadamardStatesLightlike). To gain some intuition, we will start by considering
\gls
FLRW spacetimes resembling de Sitter spacetime. After studying this particular case we will be able to give a more general definition—analogous to the definition of asymptotic flatness—which will no longer depend on the symmetry assumptions that lie behind
\gls
FLRW. Refs.
\citeonline
dappiaggi2009CosmologicalHorizonsReconstruction,dappiaggi2017HadamardStatesLightlike are our main references.

We start by choosing the spacetime manifold. We want a universe with flat spatial sections, since this is the most relevant case from a cosmological perspective. We may thus prescribe the manifold

M=(t_{0},t_{f})\times\mathbb{R}^{3},

(486)

with
-\infty\leq t_{0}<t_{f}\leq+\infty
.
M
is diffeomorphic to
\mathbb{R}^{4}
, but we write
(t_{0},t_{f})
instead of
\mathbb{R}
to make explicit the range of conformal time. We will require that either
(t_{0},t_{f})=(0,+\infty)
or
(t_{0},t_{f})=(-\infty,0)
. The latter case is the one we had with expanding de Sitter spacetime, while the former would be given by a different coordinate patch of de Sitter spacetime corresponding to a contracting universe. This is the patch below
\mathscr{H}^{-}
on
Fig.

14
.

The metric is given by a spatially flat
\gls
FLRW metric. In terms of conformal time
t
, we write

\differential{s}^{2}=a(t)^{2}\quantity[-\dd{t}^2 + \dd{\ell}^2],

(487)

with
\differential{\ell}^{2}
standing for the flat Euclidean metric as before. To get a spacetime resembling de Sitter spacetime we ask that there is a constant
H
such that

a(t)=-\frac{1}{Ht}+\order{\frac{1}{t^2}}

(488)

as
t\to\pm\infty
(according to whether
(t_{0},t_{f})=(0,+\infty)
or
(t_{0},t_{f})=(-\infty,0)
). If conformal time ranges over
(t_{0},t_{f})=(0,+\infty)
we demand
H<0
, while for
(t_{0},t_{f})=(-\infty,0)
we ask that
H>0
. This is intended to keep the scale factor positive. Notice that
Eq.

488
is intended to resemble
Eq.

484
.

This class of
\gls
FLRW geometries is a very general family that still is asymptotically de Sitter at late (or early) conformal time, which is enforced by the condition (
488
) on the scale factor. This decay property will be sufficient to ensure the presence of a cosmological horizon.

From this point onward, I shall focus on the
(t_{0},t_{f})=(-\infty,0)
case for concreteness. The other case can be dealt with in a completely analogous manner, and hence we are not losing any generality.

Let us show we have a past cosmological horizon. To do this, we work as before and write the metric in null coordinates
(U,V)
as defined on
Section

4.1
. The metric is then, as in the previous section,

\differential{s}^{2}=4a(t)^{2}\sec[2](\frac{T-R}{2})\sec[2](\frac{T+R}{2})\quantity[-\dd{T}^2 + \dd{R}^2 + \sin^2{R} \dd{\Sph}^2],

(489)

with

t=\frac{1}{2}\quantity[\tan(\frac{T-R}{2}) + \tan(\frac{T+R}{2})],

(490)

and the coordinates
T
and
R
respect

-\pi<T<0\quad\mbox{and}\quad 0\leq R<\pi+T.

(491)

This is identical to what we had with de Sitter space, except for the expression of the scale factor itself. This time, it is only asymptotically de Sitter, rather than exactly de Sitter. This means we get

\differential{s}^{2}=\quantity(\frac{\csc^2 T}{H^2} + \order{\frac{1}{t^3}})\quantity[-\dd{T}^2 + \dd{R}^2 + \sin^2{R} \dd{\Sph}^2].

(492)

We thus see that the metric is well-behaved in the
t\to-\infty
limit and we can extend it beyond the original patch. This means we can take
R\geq\pi+T
, but we cannot know how far
R
can be extended without further knowledge of the metric: it may happen that the behavior of the extension of the spacetime across the boundary
R-T=\pi
(or, less rigorously,
t=-\infty
) is very different from what we had in de Sitter spacetime (although it is similar to de Sitter in a neighborhood of
R-T=\pi
).

This ambiguity in the extension is expected: the physical spacetime is to be taken only as the original manifold
M
. What we have now found is an extended spacetime
\tilde{M}
, with

\mathscr{H}^{-}=\quantity{(T,R,\zeta,\bar{\zeta}) \in\tilde{M} \mid R-T=\pi}

(493)

being the boundary of the original spacetime inside this extension. We see this extension as unphysical for two main reasons:

1.

the cosmic observers on the spacetime can only probe the original spacetime
M
and are unable to reach beyond
\mathscr{H}^{-}
, which is a particle horizon for all cosmic observers;

2.

since the horizon
\mathscr{H}^{-}
is unreachable (and in fact an idealization arising from the assumption that
t_{0}=-\infty
), it is possible to obtain multiple different extensions
(\tilde{M},\mathchoice{\tilde{g}^{{\mathchoice{\makebox[4.33765pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[4.33765pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.59009pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.85005pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}\mathchoice{\makebox[3.51666pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[3.51666pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.1029pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.50208pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}_{{{a}{b}}}}{\tilde{g}^{{\mathchoice{\makebox[4.33765pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[4.33765pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.59009pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.85005pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}\mathchoice{\makebox[3.51666pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[3.51666pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.1029pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.50208pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}_{{{a}{b}}}}{\tilde{g}^{{\mathchoice{\makebox[4.33765pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[4.33765pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.59009pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.85005pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}\mathchoice{\makebox[3.51666pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[3.51666pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.1029pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.50208pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}_{{{a}{b}}}}{\tilde{g}^{{\mathchoice{\makebox[4.33765pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[4.33765pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.59009pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.85005pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}\mathchoice{\makebox[3.51666pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[3.51666pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.1029pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.50208pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}_{{{a}{b}}}})
and none of them should be preferred over the others, for they are experimentally undistinguishable.

Notice then that the extended spacetime
\tilde{M}
plays a role similar to that of the unphysical spacetime considered in asymptotically flat spacetimes—it is experimentally inaccessible, and therefore should be understood as a mere mathematical abstraction.

At this point, it is interesting to notice that, in fact,
(\tilde{M},\mathchoice{\tilde{g}^{{\mathchoice{\makebox[4.33765pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[4.33765pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.59009pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.85005pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}\mathchoice{\makebox[3.51666pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[3.51666pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.1029pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.50208pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}_{{{a}{b}}}}{\tilde{g}^{{\mathchoice{\makebox[4.33765pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[4.33765pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.59009pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.85005pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}\mathchoice{\makebox[3.51666pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[3.51666pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.1029pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.50208pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}_{{{a}{b}}}}{\tilde{g}^{{\mathchoice{\makebox[4.33765pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[4.33765pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.59009pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.85005pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}\mathchoice{\makebox[3.51666pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[3.51666pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.1029pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.50208pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}_{{{a}{b}}}}{\tilde{g}^{{\mathchoice{\makebox[4.33765pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[4.33765pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.59009pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.85005pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}\mathchoice{\makebox[3.51666pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[3.51666pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.1029pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.50208pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}_{{{a}{b}}}})
is a conformal completion of the asymptotically flat spacetime
(M,a^{-2}\mathchoice{g^{{\mathchoice{\makebox[4.33765pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[4.33765pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.59009pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.85005pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}\mathchoice{\makebox[3.51666pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[3.51666pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.1029pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.50208pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}_{{{a}{b}}}}{g^{{\mathchoice{\makebox[4.33765pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[4.33765pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.59009pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.85005pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}\mathchoice{\makebox[3.51666pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[3.51666pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.1029pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.50208pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}_{{{a}{b}}}}{g^{{\mathchoice{\makebox[4.33765pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[4.33765pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.59009pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.85005pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}\mathchoice{\makebox[3.51666pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[3.51666pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.1029pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.50208pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}_{{{a}{b}}}}{g^{{\mathchoice{\makebox[4.33765pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[4.33765pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.59009pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.85005pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}\mathchoice{\makebox[3.51666pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[3.51666pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.1029pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.50208pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}_{{{a}{b}}}})
, which is just a submanifold of Minkowski spacetime. In this point of view, we notice that the past cosmological horizon
\mathscr{H}^{-}
of
(M,\mathchoice{g^{{\mathchoice{\makebox[4.33765pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[4.33765pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.59009pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.85005pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}\mathchoice{\makebox[3.51666pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[3.51666pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.1029pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.50208pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}_{{{a}{b}}}}{g^{{\mathchoice{\makebox[4.33765pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[4.33765pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.59009pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.85005pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}\mathchoice{\makebox[3.51666pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[3.51666pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.1029pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.50208pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}_{{{a}{b}}}}{g^{{\mathchoice{\makebox[4.33765pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[4.33765pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.59009pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.85005pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}\mathchoice{\makebox[3.51666pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[3.51666pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.1029pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.50208pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}_{{{a}{b}}}}{g^{{\mathchoice{\makebox[4.33765pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[4.33765pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.59009pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.85005pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}\mathchoice{\makebox[3.51666pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[3.51666pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.1029pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.50208pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}_{{{a}{b}}}})
coincides with the past null infinity of
(M,a^{-2}\mathchoice{g^{{\mathchoice{\makebox[4.33765pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[4.33765pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.59009pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.85005pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}\mathchoice{\makebox[3.51666pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[3.51666pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.1029pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.50208pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}_{{{a}{b}}}}{g^{{\mathchoice{\makebox[4.33765pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[4.33765pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.59009pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.85005pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}\mathchoice{\makebox[3.51666pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[3.51666pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.1029pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.50208pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}_{{{a}{b}}}}{g^{{\mathchoice{\makebox[4.33765pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[4.33765pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.59009pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.85005pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}\mathchoice{\makebox[3.51666pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[3.51666pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.1029pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.50208pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}_{{{a}{b}}}}{g^{{\mathchoice{\makebox[4.33765pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[4.33765pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.59009pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.85005pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}\mathchoice{\makebox[3.51666pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[3.51666pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.1029pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.50208pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}_{{{a}{b}}}})

This establishes the existence of cosmological horizons on this class of
\gls
FLRW spacetimes. It will still be useful, however, to show a few extra properties these spacetimes enjoy.

First we define the vector

(494)

An explicit computation shows that

\displaystyle=-H\mathchoice{\quantity(\pdv{t})^{{{b}}}_{{\mathchoice{\makebox[3.51666pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[3.51666pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.1029pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.50208pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}}{\quantity(\pdv{t})^{{{b}}}_{{\mathchoice{\makebox[3.51666pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[3.51666pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.1029pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.50208pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}}{\quantity(\pdv{t})^{{{b}}}_{{\mathchoice{\makebox[3.51666pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[3.51666pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.1029pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.50208pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}}{\quantity(\pdv{t})^{{{b}}}_{{\mathchoice{\makebox[3.51666pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[3.51666pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.1029pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.50208pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}}+\order{\frac{1}{t}},

(498a)

\displaystyle=-\mathchoice{X^{{{b}}}_{{\mathchoice{\makebox[3.51666pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[3.51666pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.1029pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.50208pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}}{X^{{{b}}}_{{\mathchoice{\makebox[3.51666pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[3.51666pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.1029pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.50208pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}}{X^{{{b}}}_{{\mathchoice{\makebox[3.51666pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[3.51666pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.1029pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.50208pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}}{X^{{{b}}}_{{\mathchoice{\makebox[3.51666pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[3.51666pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.1029pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.50208pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}}+\order{\frac{1}{t}}.

(498b)

At last, we will check what is the form of the metric on
\mathscr{H}^{-}
. We will write the metric near
\mathscr{H}^{-}
as

\displaystyle\differential{s}^{2}

\displaystyle=a(t)^{2}\quantity[- \dd{t}^2 + \dd{r}^2 + r^2 \dd{\Sph}^2],

(499a)

\displaystyle=a(t)^{2}\quantity[- 2\dd{t}\dd{v} + \dd{v}^2 + (t-v)^2 \dd{\Sph}^2],

(499b)

\displaystyle=\frac{1}{H^{2}t^{2}}\quantity[- 2\dd{t}\dd{v} + \dd{v}^2 + (t-v)^2 \dd{\Sph}^2]+\cdots,

(499c)

\displaystyle=\frac{1}{H^{2}}\quantity[- \frac{2}{t^2}\dd{t}\dd{v} + \frac{1}{t^2}\dd{v}^2 + \qty(1-\frac{v}{t})^2 \dd{\Sph}^2]+\cdots,

(499d)

\displaystyle=\frac{1}{H^{2}}\quantity[- 2H a'\dd{t}\dd{v} + H^2 a^2 \dd{v}^2 + \qty(1+H v a)^2 \dd{\Sph}^2]+\cdots,

(499e)

\displaystyle=\frac{1}{H^{2}}\quantity[- 2H \dd{a}\dd{v} + H^2 a^2 \dd{v}^2 + \qty(1+H v a)^2 \dd{\Sph}^2]+\cdots,

(499f)

\displaystyle=\frac{1}{H^{2}}\quantity[- 2H \dd{a}\dd{v} + \dd{\Sph}^2]+\cdots,

(499g)

\displaystyle=\frac{1}{H^{2}}\quantity[- 2 \dd{a}\dd{\tilde{v}} + \dd{\Sph}^2]+\cdots.

(499h)

Above we introduced advanced time
v=t+r
, neglected the subleading terms in
a
(indicated by the trailing dots), and defined
\tilde{v}=Hv
at the end. The conclusion is that the extended metric
\mathchoice{\tilde{g}^{{\mathchoice{\makebox[4.33765pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[4.33765pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.59009pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.85005pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}\mathchoice{\makebox[3.51666pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[3.51666pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.1029pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.50208pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}_{{{a}{b}}}}{\tilde{g}^{{\mathchoice{\makebox[4.33765pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[4.33765pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.59009pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.85005pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}\mathchoice{\makebox[3.51666pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[3.51666pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.1029pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.50208pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}_{{{a}{b}}}}{\tilde{g}^{{\mathchoice{\makebox[4.33765pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[4.33765pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.59009pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.85005pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}\mathchoice{\makebox[3.51666pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[3.51666pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.1029pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.50208pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}_{{{a}{b}}}}{\tilde{g}^{{\mathchoice{\makebox[4.33765pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[4.33765pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.59009pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.85005pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}\mathchoice{\makebox[3.51666pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[3.51666pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.1029pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.50208pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}_{{{a}{b}}}}
restricted to
\mathscr{H}^{-}
can be written as

\differential{\tilde{s}}^{2}|_{\mathscr{H}^{-}}=\frac{1}{H^{2}}\quantity[- 2 \dd{a}\dd{\tilde{v}} + \dd{\Sph}^2].

(500)

Up to the factor of
H
, this is the Bondi form of the metric. Notice that the induced metric is given by

\differential{\tilde{\sigma}}^{2}|_{\mathscr{H}^{-}}=\frac{1}{H^{2}}\differential{\Sph}^{2}.

(501)

Finally, one should notice that

\mathchoice{X^{{{a}}}_{{\mathchoice{\makebox[4.33765pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[4.33765pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.59009pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.85005pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}}{X^{{{a}}}_{{\mathchoice{\makebox[4.33765pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[4.33765pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.59009pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.85005pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}}{X^{{{a}}}_{{\mathchoice{\makebox[4.33765pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[4.33765pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.59009pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.85005pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}}{X^{{{a}}}_{{\mathchoice{\makebox[4.33765pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[4.33765pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.59009pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.85005pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}}\mathchoice{\nabla^{{\mathchoice{\makebox[4.33765pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[4.33765pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.59009pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.85005pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}_{{{a}}}}{\nabla^{{\mathchoice{\makebox[4.33765pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[4.33765pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.59009pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.85005pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}_{{{a}}}}{\nabla^{{\mathchoice{\makebox[4.33765pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[4.33765pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.59009pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.85005pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}_{{{a}}}}{\nabla^{{\mathchoice{\makebox[4.33765pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[4.33765pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.59009pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.85005pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}_{{{a}}}}\tilde{v}=H^{2},

(502)

and hence
\tilde{v}
can be understood as the parameter along the integral lines of

on

.

Notice this definition is intended to mimic the behavior of
\gls
FLRW spacetimes with cosmological horizons, but lifts the requirements of homogeneity and isotropy that are present in the
\gls
FLRW case. Hence, this definition is much more general.

9.5
Case Study: de Sitter Spacetime

Before moving on to studying the
\gls
DMP group of symmetries on expanding universes with cosmological horizons, we should make a case study to gain some intuition about the symmetries we expect to find. Since our model universe is de Sitter spacetime (just as Minkowski spacetime was the model for asymptotically flat geometries), we should first study the isometries of de Sitter spacetime.

Since de Sitter spacetime is conformally Minkowskian, they share the same conformal Killing vector fields. Furthermore, we know all Killing vector fields for de Sitter spacetime must be conformal Killing vector fields as well—which follows from the definition of (conformal) Killing vector fields. Hence, we can compute the conformal Killing vector fields of Minkowski spacetime and then check by explicit computation which of them yield Killing vector fields for de Sitter spacetime.

In any spacetime dimension
n>2
the conformal Killing vector fields for Minkowski spacetime are spanned by

with
a,b=-2,\ldots,n
and
\mathchoice{\tilde{\eta}^{{\mathchoice{\makebox[4.33765pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[4.33765pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.59009pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.85005pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}\mathchoice{\makebox[3.51666pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[3.51666pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.1029pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.50208pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}_{{{a}{b}}}}{\tilde{\eta}^{{\mathchoice{\makebox[4.33765pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[4.33765pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.59009pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.85005pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}\mathchoice{\makebox[3.51666pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[3.51666pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.1029pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.50208pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}_{{{a}{b}}}}{\tilde{\eta}^{{\mathchoice{\makebox[4.33765pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[4.33765pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.59009pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.85005pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}\mathchoice{\makebox[3.51666pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[3.51666pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.1029pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.50208pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}_{{{a}{b}}}}{\tilde{\eta}^{{\mathchoice{\makebox[4.33765pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[4.33765pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.59009pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.85005pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}\mathchoice{\makebox[3.51666pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[3.51666pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.1029pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.50208pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}_{{{a}{b}}}}
being the Minkowski metric with signature
(p+1,q+1)
(where
(p,q)
is the signature of the original space). One may notice from
Eq.

425
that, for a four-dimensional Lorentzian spacetime, this is precisely the Lorentz algebra
\mathfrak{so}^{+}(4,2)
.

To get to the de Sitter isometries, we need to figure out which of these conformal transformations are isometries of de Sitter spacetime. Through explicit computation, one finds the answer is
\mathchoice{P^{{{a}}}_{{{i}}}}{P^{{{a}}}_{{{i}}}}{P^{{{a}}}_{{{i}}}}{P^{{{a}}}_{{{i}}}}
,
\mathchoice{J^{{{a}}}_{{{i}{j}}}}{J^{{{a}}}_{{{i}{j}}}}{J^{{{a}}}_{{{i}{j}}}}{J^{{{a}}}_{{{i}{j}}}}
,
\mathchoice{D^{{{a}}}}{D^{{{a}}}}{D^{{{a}}}}{D^{{{a}}}}
, and
\mathchoice{K^{{{a}}}_{{{i}}}}{K^{{{a}}}_{{{i}}}}{K^{{{a}}}_{{{i}}}}{K^{{{a}}}_{{{i}}}}
for
i,j=1,2,3
. Hence, we find that the isometry algebra for de Sitter spacetime is given by (
510
) for
a,b,c,d\neq 0
. This means the algebra is given by
\mathfrak{so}^{+}(4,1)
. One can then integrate the Killing vector fields to find that the isometry group is
\mathrm{SO}^{+}(4,1)
, known as the de Sitter group. This is a ten-dimensional group, corresponding to the fact that de Sitter spacetime is maximally symmetric.

There is still an unaddressed subtlety: while
\mathrm{SO}^{+}(4,1)
is indeed the (or, in fact, a) Lie group with Lie algebra
\mathfrak{so}^{+}(4,1)
, it may happen that the Lie algebra of Killing vector fields does not integrate to a
\mathrm{SO}^{+}(4,1)
isometry group. In fact, integrating the transformation generated by
\mathchoice{P^{{{a}}}_{{{i}}}}{P^{{{a}}}_{{{i}}}}{P^{{{a}}}_{{{i}}}}{P^{{{a}}}_{{{i}}}}
,
\mathchoice{J^{{{a}}}_{{{i}{j}}}}{J^{{{a}}}_{{{i}{j}}}}{J^{{{a}}}_{{{i}{j}}}}{J^{{{a}}}_{{{i}{j}}}}
, and
\mathchoice{D^{{{a}}}}{D^{{{a}}}}{D^{{{a}}}}{D^{{{a}}}}

(512)

for
c\in\mathbb{R}^{3}
. Greek indices are contracted with the Minkowski metric.
c
yields a
\gls
SCT. Notice, however, that this transformation takes some points to infinity. This is not a problem, and is the reason one usually considers a conformal compactification when discussing conformal symmetry.

The true issue we have is that
\glspl
SCT map points in the cosmological patch to other regions of de Sitter spacetime. In other words, they take points from the physical region of de Sitter spacetime—which is the relevant region in cosmology—and take them to the unphysical region. For our purposes, we are only focusing in symmetries of the cosmological patch, and hence transformations that do not preserve the cosmological patch are not of interest.

To see this it will be useful to employ coordinates appropriate to the almost-Bondi gauge we are using at
\mathscr{H}^{-}
. This is due to two reasons: Bondi-like coordinates extend from the cosmological patch to a neighborhood of
\mathscr{H}^{-}
(and hence we can see which transformations preserve the cosmological patch), and later this coordinate system is the one we will employ when discussing asymptotic symmetries. In Bondi gauge, with
a=-(Ht)^{-1}
and
v=H(t+r)
, the de Sitter metric is written as

\differential{s}^{2}=H^{-2}\quantity[a^2 \dd{v}^2 - 2 \dd{a} \dd{v} + (1 + a v)^2 \dd{\Sph}^2].

The nomenclature and notations for the cosmological de Sitter algebra and group are not standard in the literature.

\mathfrak{cds}(3,1)
for the “cosmological de Sitter algebra in
3+1
dimensions”. The group of isometries is then the “cosmological de Sitter group in
3+1
dimensions”

\mathrm{CdS}(3,1)=\mathrm{SO}(3)\ltimes\quantity(\R\ltimes\R^3).

(516)

\mathrm{SO}(3)
corresponds to spatial rotations,
\mathbb{R}^{3}
corresponds to spatial translations, and
\mathbb{R}
corresponds to dilations.

It is interesting to notice that even though de Sitter spacetime is a maximally symmetric spacetime, the cosmological patch of de Sitter spacetime is not maximally symmetric. This is meant in the sense that not all of the de Sitter group
\mathrm{SO}^{+}(4,1)
preserves the cosmological patch. Instead, only the subgroup
\mathrm{CdS}(3,1)
does.

9.6
The
\glsfmtlong
DMP Group

The
\gls
BMS group is constructed by considering the behavior at infinity of asymptotically flat spacetimes. It is based on studying the Carrollian manifold obtained at future (or past) null infinity. However, what happens if we now consider an expanding universe with cosmological horizon?

[
81
,
80
,
83
]
considered this problem and proved the existence of an infinite-dimensional symmetry group at the cosmological horizon analogous to the
\gls
BMS group. I will refer to this group as the
\glsxtrfull
DMP group and denote it by
\mathrm{DMP}_{4}
. Our present goal is to derive this group by working with the framework of Carrollian manifolds we previously employed.

We first need to identify what is the Carrollian structure of
\mathscr{H}^{-}
. By considering
Definition

21
we see that the Carrollian manifold is
\mathscr{H}^{-}=\mathbb{R}\times\mathbb{S}^{2}
(up to diffeomorphism) and the induced Carrollian metric is always the round metric on the sphere with radius
H^{-1}
. One natural candidate for the vector
\mathchoice{n^{{{a}}}_{{\mathchoice{\makebox[4.33765pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[4.33765pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.59009pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.85005pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}}{n^{{{a}}}_{{\mathchoice{\makebox[4.33765pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[4.33765pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.59009pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.85005pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}}{n^{{{a}}}_{{\mathchoice{\makebox[4.33765pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[4.33765pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.59009pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.85005pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}}{n^{{{a}}}_{{\mathchoice{\makebox[4.33765pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[4.33765pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.59009pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.85005pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}}
giving the kernel of the Carrollian metric is the vector
\mathchoice{\tilde{\nabla}^{{{b}}}_{{\mathchoice{\makebox[3.51666pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[3.51666pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.1029pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.50208pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}}{\tilde{\nabla}^{{{b}}}_{{\mathchoice{\makebox[3.51666pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[3.51666pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.1029pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.50208pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}}{\tilde{\nabla}^{{{b}}}_{{\mathchoice{\makebox[3.51666pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[3.51666pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.1029pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.50208pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}}{\tilde{\nabla}^{{{b}}}_{{\mathchoice{\makebox[3.51666pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[3.51666pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.1029pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.50208pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}}a
.

What are the allowed symmetries of the Carrollian structure? The basic transformation we are allowed to make that will affect the Carrollian structure is a “gauge transformation”
a\to\omega a
, where
\omega\in\mathcal{C}^{\infty}(\tilde{M})
does not vanish at
\mathscr{H}^{-}
. Such a transformation will act on the standard Carrollian triple according to

(517)

c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.85005pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}\mathchoice{\makebox[3.51666pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[3.51666pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.1029pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.50208pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}_{{{a}{b}}}}{\tilde{g}^{{\mathchoice{\makebox[4.33765pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[4.33765pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.59009pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.85005pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}\mathchoice{\makebox[3.51666pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[3.51666pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.1029pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.50208pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}_{{{a}{b}}}}.

(520b)

This then implies that
\mathchoice{X^{{{c}}}_{{\mathchoice{\makebox[3.57375pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[3.57375pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.1205pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.51463pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}}{X^{{{c}}}_{{\mathchoice{\makebox[3.57375pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[3.57375pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.1205pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.51463pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}}{X^{{{c}}}_{{\mathchoice{\makebox[3.57375pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[3.57375pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.1205pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.51463pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}}{X^{{{c}}}_{{\mathchoice{\makebox[3.57375pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[3.57375pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.1205pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.51463pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}}\mathchoice{\nabla^{{\mathchoice{\makebox[3.57375pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[3.57375pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.1205pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.51463pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}_{{{c}}}}{\nabla^{{\mathchoice{\makebox[3.57375pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[3.57375pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.1205pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.51463pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}_{{{c}}}}{\nabla^{{\mathchoice{\makebox[3.57375pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[3.57375pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.1205pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.51463pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}_{{{c}}}}{\nabla^{{\mathchoice{\makebox[3.57375pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[3.57375pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.1205pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.51463pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}_{{{c}}}}(\log\omega)=0
. It then follows from
Eq.

506
that
\omega
cannot depend on
v
. We now see that
\differential{v}\to\omega^{-1}\differential{v}
implies

v\to\exp(f(\theta,\phi))v+g(\theta,\phi),

(521)

with
f,g\in\mathcal{C}^{\infty}(\mathbb{S}^{2})
(I defined
f(\theta,\phi)=-\log\omega(\theta,\phi)
).

We thus conclude that the most general transformation that preserves the cosmological horizon is given by

v\to\exp(f(\theta,\phi))v+g(\theta,\phi),\quad(\theta,\phi)\to R(\theta,\phi),

(522)

with
R\in\mathrm{SO}(3)
and
f,g\in\mathcal{C}^{\infty}(\mathbb{S}^{2})
.

The transformation (
522
) can be written in a more compact notation as the triple
(R,f,g)
. It can be seen then that the composition law for these transformations is

(R,f,g)\odot(R^{\prime},f^{\prime},g^{\prime})=(R\circ R^{\prime},f+f^{\prime}\circ R,\exp(f' \circ R)\cdot g+g^{\prime}),

(523)

where
\circ
denotes composition and
\cdot
denotes the pointwise product of functions. This product defines a Lie group structure on the manifold
\mathrm{SO}(3)\times\mathcal{C}^{\infty}(\mathbb{S}^{2})\times\mathcal{C}^{\infty}(\mathbb{S}^{2})
. The identity is given by
(\text{1},0,0)
. The inverse is given by

(R,f,g)^{-1}=(R^{-1},-f\circ R^{-1},-\exp(-f)\cdot g).

(524)

This group is the
\gls
DMP group, henceforth denoted by
\mathrm{DMP}_{4}
.

Next we notice that

\displaystyle(\text{1},f,g)\odot(\text{1},0,g^{\prime})\odot(\text{1},f,g)^{-1}

\displaystyle=(\text{1},f,g+g^{\prime})\odot(\text{1},f,g)^{-1},

(525a)

\displaystyle=(\text{1},f,g+g^{\prime})\odot(\text{1},-f,-e^{-f}\cdot g),

(525b)

\displaystyle=(\text{1},0,e^{-f}\cdot g+e^{-f}\cdot g^{\prime}-e^{-f}\cdot g),

(525c)

\displaystyle=(\text{1},0,e^{-f}\cdot g^{\prime}).

(525d)

This shows
\quantity{(\Eins, 0, g) | g \in\ck[\infty](\Sph^2)}
is a normal subgroup of
\quantity{(\Eins, f, g) | f, g \in\ck[\infty](\Sph^2)}
. We also notice that

(\text{1},f,0)\odot(\text{1},0,g)=(\text{1},f,g).

(526)

By adding in the fact that

\quantity{(\Eins, f, 0) | f \in\ck[\infty](\Sph^2)}\cap\quantity{(\Eins, 0, g) | g \in\ck[\infty](\Sph^2)}=\quantity{(\Eins,0,0)}

(527)

we conclude that

\displaystyle\quantity{(\Eins, f, g) | f, g \in\ck[\infty](\Sph^2)}

\displaystyle=\quantity{(\Eins, f, 0) | f \in\ck[\infty](\Sph^2)}\ltimes\quantity{(\Eins, 0, g) | g \in\ck[\infty](\Sph^2)},

(528a)

\displaystyle=\mathcal{C}^{\infty}(\mathbb{S}^{2})\ltimes\mathcal{C}^{\infty}(\mathbb{S}^{2}).

(528b)

This still does not yield the full structure of
\mathrm{DMP}_{4}
, which has the manifold structure
\mathrm{SO}(3)\times\mathcal{C}^{\infty}(\mathbb{S}^{2})\times\mathcal{C}^{\infty}(\mathbb{S}^{2})
. To get to this, we must now consider the behavior of the rotations. We find that

\displaystyle(R,f,g)\odot(\text{1},f^{\prime},g^{\prime})

\displaystyle\odot(R,f,g)^{-1},

\displaystyle=(R,f,g)\odot(\text{1},f^{\prime},g^{\prime})\odot(R^{-1},-f\circ R^{-1},-\exp(-f)\cdot g),

(529a)

\displaystyle=(R,f+f^{\prime}\circ R,\exp(f' \circ R)\cdot g+g^{\prime})\odot(R^{-1},-f\circ R^{-1},-\exp(-f)\cdot g),

(529b)

\displaystyle=(\text{1},f^{\prime}\circ R,\exp(f' \circ R - f)\cdot g+\exp(-f)g^{\prime}-\exp(-f)\cdot g),

(529c)

which means
\mathcal{C}^{\infty}(\mathbb{S}^{2})\ltimes\mathcal{C}^{\infty}(\mathbb{S}^{2})
is a normal subgroup of
\mathrm{DMP}_{4}
. Furthermore, we notice that

(R,0,0)\odot(\text{1},f,g)=(R,f,g).

(530)

Furthermore,

\quantity{(R,0,0) \mid R \in\SO(3)}\cap(\mathcal{C}^{\infty}(\mathbb{S}^{2})\ltimes\mathcal{C}^{\infty}(\mathbb{S}^{2}))=\quantity{(\Eins,0,0)}.

(531)

Therefore, we conclude that the
\gls
DMP group has the structure of an iterated semidirect product,

\mathrm{DMP}_{4}=\mathrm{SO}(3)\ltimes(\mathcal{C}^{\infty}(\mathbb{S}^{2})\ltimes\mathcal{C}^{\infty}(\mathbb{S}^{2})).

(532)

This generalizes the cosmological de Sitter group
\mathrm{CdS}(3,1)
presented in
Eq.

516
. It is interesting to notice that it would not be possible to find a similar decomposition for the de Sitter group
\mathrm{SO}^{+}(4,1)
, because it does not admit nontrivial normal subgroups (it is said to be a simple Lie group).

We may also perform the symmetry analysis using conformal Killing vector fields, which will yield us immediately the
\gls
DMP algebra
\mathfrak{dmp}_{4}
. The calculation is completely analogous to the calculation we performed when studying the
\gls
BMS algebra in
Section

5
.

on

such that

and

9.7
Hadamard States in Expanding Universes with Cosmological Horizons

The analysis by
[
81
,
80
,
83
]
was directed at the construction of Hadamard states in expanding universes with cosmological horizons. The core ideas are analogous to the asymptotically flat case, discussed in
Section

6.7
.

One considers a boundary algebra of observables
\mathcal{A}_{\text{bound.}}
defined on the cosmological horizon
\mathscr{H}^{-}
. Simultaneously, one considers a bulk algebra of observables
\mathcal{A}_{\text{bulk}}
defined on the cosmological patch of the spacetime. It is then possible to construct a
\gls
DMP-invariant state on the boundary and pull-it-back to the bulk. Within
\gls
FLRW spacetimes, this state can be shown to be Hadamard. In the particular case of de Sitter spacetime this construction yields the so-called Bunch–Davies vacuum
[
45
]
. In particular, this provides a way of constructing physically meaningful quantum states in inflationary scenarios.

10
The Sky as a Killing Horizon

As a final topic, I would like to discuss the work I am currently developing in collaboration with Landulfo
[
6
]
and try to unify the perspectives we had so far toward null infinity in asymptotically flat spacetimes and cosmological horizons in expanding universes.

When dealing with null infinity in asymptotically flat spacetimes, the natural globally-defined group we encountered was the
\gls
BMS group,

\mathrm{BMS}_{4}=\mathrm{SO}^{+}(3,1)\ltimes\mathcal{C}^{\infty}(\mathbb{S}^{2}),

(539)

which we discussed at length in
Section

5
. Nevertheless, in
Section

9
we considered the case of expanding universes with cosmological horizons and found the
\gls
DMP group,

\mathrm{DMP}_{4}=\mathrm{SO}(3)\ltimes(\mathcal{C}^{\infty}(\mathbb{S}^{2})\ltimes\mathcal{C}^{\infty}(\mathbb{S}^{2})).

(540)

While these groups look similar, they are also still quite different. The
\gls
BMS group considers the conformal group on the sphere,
\mathrm{SO}^{+}(3,1)
, which on
Section

8
led us to the notion of superrotations.
\gls
DMP, however, only allows isometries on the sphere, meaning we are stuck with
\mathrm{SO}(3)
. There is no such thing as a “local isometry on the sphere”, so we cannot promote
\mathrm{SO}(3)
to a larger group in a similar way
42
42

42

A possible alternative would be to consider the group
\mathrm{Diff}(\mathbb{S}^{2})
of sphere diffeomorphisms, as some authors do
[
48
,
49
,
69
]
, but this makes no use of the metric or conformal structure on the sphere.
. On the other hand,
\mathrm{DMP}_{4}
has two factors of
\mathcal{C}^{\infty}(\mathbb{S}^{2})
, while
\mathrm{BMS}_{4}
has only one. It is at least curious that the two groups are so similar, yet so different.

One reason for this to be an interesting problem is precisely how the presence of
\mathrm{SO}^{+}(3,1)
in
\mathrm{BMS}_{4}
calls for superrotations. The fact we were able to move from
\mathrm{BMS}_{4}
to
\mathfrak{ebms}_{4}
on
Section

8
meant we suddenly were in the realm of two-dimensional
\gls
CFT, which opens up many new possible developments and techniques. It would be interesting to try to replicate this in expanding universes, but
\mathrm{SO}(3)
is not large enough for us to do that.

A natural question is then how to unify the definitions of the
\gls
BMS and
\gls
DMP groups in a manner that clarifies their similarities and differences. This is, in a sense, a quest to extend the definitions of asymptotic symmetries to a wider class of null hypersurfaces with the goal of keeping the original setups (null infinity and cosmological horizons) as particular cases of interest.

There have been many efforts along these lines (although not necessarily with the same motivation). The works of
[
95
,
93
,
94
]
—which based our discussions of Carrollian manifolds—discuss precisely how to consider these sorts of “conformal Carroll groups” on null hypersurfaces. Other notable efforts are the works by
[
54
]
—who extend the
\gls
DMP group by replacing
\mathrm{SO}(3)
with
\mathrm{Diff}(\mathbb{S}^{2})
—and
[
70
,
210
]
—who use a Lie algebroid
[
171
]
to obtain a structure in (anti) de Sitter spacetime that recovers the
\gls
BMS results in the limit in which the cosmological constant tends to zero.

The approach I took with Landulfo
[
6
]
is heavily inspired by structures and results found in
\gls
GR and
\gls
QFTCS. The existence of Killing vector fields often leads to interesting null hypersurfaces known as Killing horizons. This notion was originally introduced by
[
52
,
53
]
and is defined as a null hypersurface tangent to a Killing vector field. These structures will be at the core of our discussion for the rest of this section, and hence we will now take a moment to discuss them in more depth.

10.1
Killing Horizons

Let us begin by defining what we mean by a Killing horizon.

Definition 22

(Killing Horizon)
.

Let

.

A few examples are in place. Let us begin with Minkowski spacetime. We will consider the boost-generating vector field (see

)

(541)

This is a Killing vector field, as we derived on

. Notice, though, that

(542)

which means the vector field is null on the hyperplanes with

. These are Killing horizons. This behavior is illustrated on

.

Figure 17:
Minkowski diagram exhibiting the flow of the Killing vector field
\mathchoice{J^{{{a}}}_{{{x}{t}}}}{J^{{{a}}}_{{{x}{t}}}}{J^{{{a}}}_{{{x}{t}}}}{J^{{{a}}}_{{{x}{t}}}}
, which represents a boost. Notice the vector field is null precisely at the surfaces shown in black, which are the hypersurfaces with
x^{2}=t^{2}
. These are Killing horizons.

One may notice from
Fig.

17
that the boost vector field is timelike on the right wedge of the spacetime (known as the right Rindler wedge). This means we can consider a family of observers whose worldlines are precisely the orbits of the Killing field. These turn out to be uniformly accelerated observers. An important prediction of
\gls
QFTCS is that these observers perceive the standard Minkowski vacuum in Minkowski spacetime as a thermal state at temperature

T=\frac{a}{2\pi},

(543)

where
a
is their acceleration. This is known as the (Fulling–Davies–)Unruh effect
[
108
,
84
,
232
]
, reviewed, for example, in Refs.
\citeonline
aguiaralves2023NonperturbativeAspectsQuantum,birrell1982QuantumFieldTheory,crispino2008UnruhEffectIts,mukhanov2007IntroductionQuantumEffects,parker2009QuantumFieldTheory,wald1994QuantumFieldTheory.

Notice that there are two Killing horizons on
Fig.

17
—one is given by the hypersurface
x=t
, and the other by the hypersurface
x=-t
. These two horizons cross at a bifurcation surface in which
x=t=0
. Notice this is indeed a surface, since it is a two-dimensional plane in the
(y,z)
-directions. We say the full structure is a bifurcate Killing horizon. This notion was originally introduced by
[
39
]
and often occurs when there is a fixed point of an isometry group in spacetime. As the next examples will show, this is an important structure in
\gls
QFTCS.

Let us consider Schwarzschild spacetime. We will work in the full Kruskal extension and consider the action of the vector field locally defined in Schwarzschild coordinates as

\mathchoice{K^{{{a}}}_{{\mathchoice{\makebox[4.33765pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[4.33765pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.59009pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.85005pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}}{K^{{{a}}}_{{\mathchoice{\makebox[4.33765pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[4.33765pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.59009pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.85005pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}}{K^{{{a}}}_{{\mathchoice{\makebox[4.33765pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[4.33765pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.59009pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.85005pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}}{K^{{{a}}}_{{\mathchoice{\makebox[4.33765pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[4.33765pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.59009pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.85005pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}}=\mathchoice{\quantity(\pdv{t})^{{{a}}}_{{\mathchoice{\makebox[4.33765pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[4.33765pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.59009pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.85005pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}}{\quantity(\pdv{t})^{{{a}}}_{{\mathchoice{\makebox[4.33765pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[4.33765pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.59009pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.85005pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}}{\quantity(\pdv{t})^{{{a}}}_{{\mathchoice{\makebox[4.33765pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[4.33765pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.59009pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.85005pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}}{\quantity(\pdv{t})^{{{a}}}_{{\mathchoice{\makebox[4.33765pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[4.33765pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.59009pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.85005pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}}.

(544)

The resulting orbits are shown in
Fig.

18
. Notice, in particular, that the Killing vector field is timelike on the right wedge (where it is parallel to the worldlines of stationary observers), but near the horizon the field becomes null. Hence, the event horizon of the black (and white) hole(s) is a bifurcate Killing horizon.

Figure 18:
Orbits of the Killing vector field
\mathchoice{\quantity(\pdv*{t})^{{{a}}}_{{\mathchoice{\makebox[4.33765pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[4.33765pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.59009pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.85005pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}}{\quantity(\pdv*{t})^{{{a}}}_{{\mathchoice{\makebox[4.33765pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[4.33765pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.59009pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.85005pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}}{\quantity(\pdv*{t})^{{{a}}}_{{\mathchoice{\makebox[4.33765pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[4.33765pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.59009pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.85005pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}}{\quantity(\pdv*{t})^{{{a}}}_{{\mathchoice{\makebox[4.33765pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[4.33765pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.59009pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.85005pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}}
in the maximally extended Schwarzschild spacetime. Notice how the Killing field is similar to the boost field we considered in
Fig.

17
. This time, the (bifurcate) Killing horizon is the event horizon for the white and black hole regions in the spacetime.

As in Minkowski spacetime, we have a thermal behavior for observers in this spacetime. Namely, stationary observers on the right wedge perceive the natural vacuum on this spacetime—known as the Hartle–Hawking vacuum
[
124
]
—as being thermal at temperature

T=\frac{1}{8\pi M}.

(545)

In this sense, the black hole is “hot”. This particular quantum state is similar to a black hole in a radiation box at the temperature (
545
). This phenomenon is a curved spacetime version of the Unruh effect, and it is similar (but conceptually different from) the Hawking effect
[
126
,
127
]
, which concerns a black hole formed from gravitational collapse as opposed to an eternal black hole.

. Consider the vector field

The pattern between bifurcate Killing horizons and thermal effects is general. It has been shown by
[
148
]
that, if there is a stationary Hadamard state, then this state is unique and observers following the Killing orbits perceive it as a thermal state. Here, “stationary” refers to the state being invariant under the action of the Killing vector field.

The temperature of this quantum state is naturally defined by the geometric structure of the Killing horizon. Namely, at the horizon the Killing vector field
\mathchoice{K^{{{a}}}_{{\mathchoice{\makebox[4.33765pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[4.33765pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.59009pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.85005pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}}{K^{{{a}}}_{{\mathchoice{\makebox[4.33765pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[4.33765pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.59009pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.85005pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}}{K^{{{a}}}_{{\mathchoice{\makebox[4.33765pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[4.33765pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.59009pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.85005pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}}{K^{{{a}}}_{{\mathchoice{\makebox[4.33765pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[4.33765pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.59009pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.85005pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}}
satisfies

\mathchoice{K^{{{a}}}_{{\mathchoice{\makebox[4.33765pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[4.33765pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.59009pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.85005pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}}{K^{{{a}}}_{{\mathchoice{\makebox[4.33765pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[4.33765pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.59009pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.85005pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}}{K^{{{a}}}_{{\mathchoice{\makebox[4.33765pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[4.33765pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.59009pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.85005pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}}{K^{{{a}}}_{{\mathchoice{\makebox[4.33765pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[4.33765pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.59009pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.85005pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}}\mathchoice{\nabla^{{\mathchoice{\makebox[4.33765pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[4.33765pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.59009pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.85005pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}_{{{a}}}}{\nabla^{{\mathchoice{\makebox[4.33765pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[4.33765pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.59009pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.85005pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}_{{{a}}}}{\nabla^{{\mathchoice{\makebox[4.33765pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[4.33765pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.59009pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.85005pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}_{{{a}}}}{\nabla^{{\mathchoice{\makebox[4.33765pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[4.33765pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.59009pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.85005pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}_{{{a}}}}\mathchoice{K^{{{b}}}_{{\mathchoice{\makebox[3.51666pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[3.51666pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.1029pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.50208pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}}{K^{{{b}}}_{{\mathchoice{\makebox[3.51666pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[3.51666pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.1029pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.50208pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}}{K^{{{b}}}_{{\mathchoice{\makebox[3.51666pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[3.51666pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.1029pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.50208pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}}{K^{{{b}}}_{{\mathchoice{\makebox[3.51666pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[3.51666pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.1029pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.50208pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}}=\kappa\mathchoice{K^{{{b}}}_{{\mathchoice{\makebox[3.51666pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[3.51666pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.1029pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.50208pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}}{K^{{{b}}}_{{\mathchoice{\makebox[3.51666pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[3.51666pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.1029pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.50208pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}}{K^{{{b}}}_{{\mathchoice{\makebox[3.51666pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[3.51666pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.1029pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.50208pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}}{K^{{{b}}}_{{\mathchoice{\makebox[3.51666pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[3.51666pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.1029pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.50208pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}}

(548)

for some function
\kappa
. When properly normalized (typically by imposing that the Killing vector field is a unit timelike vector field at spatial infinity), we say this function
\kappa
is the “surface gravity” of the Killing horizon. For black holes, this is similar to a “renormalized” measurement of the gravitational acceleration at the horizon. In
\gls
BHT, the temperature of the horizon is given by

T=\frac{\kappa}{2\pi}.

(549)

See Refs.
\citeonline
wald1994QuantumFieldTheory,witten2024IntroductionBlackHole,wald2001ThermodynamicsBlackHoles,wall2018SurveyBlackHole for further information on
\gls
BHT and related topics.

Hence, Killing horizons are intimately related to the thermal phenomena we encounter when studying
\gls
QFTCS. The interest in them does not stop at that. Recently, it has been shown by
[
75
,
76
]
that Killing horizons decohere quantum superpositions. In a very short description, once a quantum particle with nonvanishing charge and/or mass is put into spatial superposition, the Coulombic electromagnetic and/or gravitational field induced by the particle is also put in superposition. The quantum state of the background quantum field is thus put into superposition, and this can be shown to lead to a flow of soft radiation into a black hole (or other Killing horizon). These soft particles carry information about the superposition across the Killing horizon, causing the decoherence of the original system. See Refs.
\citeonline
danielson2022BlackHolesDecohere,danielson2022KillingHorizonsDecohere for further details, and Refs.
\citeonline
danielson2022BlackHolesDecohere,danielson2022KillingHorizonsDecohere,gralla2024DecoherenceHorizonsGeneral,danielson2025LocalDescriptionDecoherence,danielson2025HowMinimizeDecoherence for further developments on this topic.

With these ideas in mind, it becomes apparent that Killing horizons play a key role in gravitational physics. They encode the symmetries of spacetime in distinguished null hypersurfaces, and thus provide natural places for us to understand asymptotic symmetries. In fact, the works of
[
75
,
76
]
already exhibit interesting physics associated with very low energy particles occurring on Killing horizons. This suggests we should look at Killing horizons to learn more about infrared physics.

This has been pursued before. For instance,
[
152
]
had considered
\gls
BMS-like symmetries on Killing horizons and found a group similar to the Newman–Unti group. Later, these ideas were employed by
[
131
,
132
]
, for example, in understanding soft hair in black holes. Nevertheless, a very interesting observation is that the notion of Killing horizon can be suitably modified to encompass null infinity as well. This will lead us to the notion of
\glsxtrfull
ACKH introduced in Ref.
\citeonline
aguiaralves2025NullInfinityKilling.

10.2
Asymptotic (Conformal) Killing Horizons

Under this construction, we see that
\mathchoice{X^{{{a}}}_{{\mathchoice{\makebox[4.33765pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[4.33765pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.59009pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.85005pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}}{X^{{{a}}}_{{\mathchoice{\makebox[4.33765pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[4.33765pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.59009pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.85005pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}}{X^{{{a}}}_{{\mathchoice{\makebox[4.33765pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[4.33765pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.59009pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.85005pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}}{X^{{{a}}}_{{\mathchoice{\makebox[4.33765pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[4.33765pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.59009pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.85005pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}}
is not necessarily a genuine Killing vector field away from the horizon, but becomes a Killing vector field asymptotically. We thus get a notion of Killing horizon which holds at the horizon itself, but it is not too constraining elsewhere. Hence, while the horizon itself still has a rich symmetry structure (as we will soon see), we do not need to assume the spacetime itself to enjoy a symmetry on an open set.

This idea can be generalized to a domain far beyond that of expanding universes with cosmological horizons. Following Ref.
\citeonline
aguiaralves2025NullInfinityKilling, we define an
\gls
AKH in the following manner.

.

\mathchoice{g^{{\mathchoice{\makebox[4.33765pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[4.33765pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.59009pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.85005pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}\mathchoice{\makebox[3.51666pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[3.51666pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.1029pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.50208pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}_{{{a}{b}}}}{g^{{\mathchoice{\makebox[4.33765pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[4.33765pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.59009pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.85005pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}\mathchoice{\makebox[3.51666pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[3.51666pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.1029pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.50208pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}_{{{a}{b}}}}{g^{{\mathchoice{\makebox[4.33765pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[4.33765pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.59009pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.85005pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}\mathchoice{\makebox[3.51666pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[3.51666pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.1029pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.50208pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}_{{{a}{b}}}}{g^{{\mathchoice{\makebox[4.33765pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[4.33765pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.59009pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.85005pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}\mathchoice{\makebox[3.51666pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[3.51666pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.1029pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.50208pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}_{{{a}{b}}}}
, meaning in particular that it preserves the conformal structure in the way we would like.

When referring to either an
\gls
AKH or an
\gls
ACKH, I like to write “
\gls
A(C)KH”.
\Glspl
A(C)KH pose natural structures on which we can consider asymptotic symmetries, and as we shall see they lead to very natural extensions of the
\gls
BMS and
\gls
DMP groups.

10.3
Symmetries on Asymptotic Horizons

We are now ready to discuss asymptotic symmetry groups on
\glspl
A(C)KH. The procedure is completely analogous to how we discussed the
\gls
BMS and
\gls
DMP groups in terms of Carrollian structures.

We start with
\glspl
AKH. Given an
\gls
AKH, we want to obtain a Carrollian structure associated to it. This means a manifold
N
, a Carrollian metric
\mathchoice{h^{{\mathchoice{\makebox[4.33765pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[4.33765pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.59009pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.85005pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}\mathchoice{\makebox[3.51666pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[3.51666pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.1029pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.50208pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}_{{{a}{b}}}}{h^{{\mathchoice{\makebox[4.33765pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[4.33765pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.59009pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.85005pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}\mathchoice{\makebox[3.51666pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[3.51666pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.1029pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.50208pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}_{{{a}{b}}}}{h^{{\mathchoice{\makebox[4.33765pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[4.33765pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.59009pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.85005pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}\mathchoice{\makebox[3.51666pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[3.51666pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.1029pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.50208pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}_{{{a}{b}}}}{h^{{\mathchoice{\makebox[4.33765pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[4.33765pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.59009pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.85005pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}\mathchoice{\makebox[3.51666pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[3.51666pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.1029pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.50208pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}_{{{a}{b}}}}
, and a normal vector
\mathchoice{n^{{{a}}}_{{\mathchoice{\makebox[4.33765pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[4.33765pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.59009pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.85005pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}}{n^{{{a}}}_{{\mathchoice{\makebox[4.33765pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[4.33765pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.59009pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.85005pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}}{n^{{{a}}}_{{\mathchoice{\makebox[4.33765pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[4.33765pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.59009pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.85005pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}}{n^{{{a}}}_{{\mathchoice{\makebox[4.33765pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[4.33765pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.59009pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.85005pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}}
. Since an
\gls
AKH is a submanifold of an isometric extension of the original spacetime, we already have one natural choice for the manifold structure (this will be the horizon itself) and for the metric (this will be the induced metric of the extended spacetime on the horizon). Notice these choices are unique up to isometries.

It remains to choose a normal vector. While in principle the asymptotic Killing vector
\mathchoice{X^{{{a}}}_{{\mathchoice{\makebox[4.33765pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[4.33765pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.59009pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.85005pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}}{X^{{{a}}}_{{\mathchoice{\makebox[4.33765pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[4.33765pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.59009pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.85005pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}}{X^{{{a}}}_{{\mathchoice{\makebox[4.33765pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[4.33765pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.59009pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.85005pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}}{X^{{{a}}}_{{\mathchoice{\makebox[4.33765pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[4.33765pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.59009pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.85005pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}}
may seem like an interesting choice, picking it would not give any information about the ambient spacetime metric along the null direction—and this information is also not provided by the induced metric. For this reason, Ref.
\citeonline
aguiaralves2025NullInfinityKilling prefers to choose the normal null vector

\mathchoice{n^{{{a}}}_{{\mathchoice{\makebox[4.33765pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[4.33765pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.59009pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.85005pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}}{n^{{{a}}}_{{\mathchoice{\makebox[4.33765pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[4.33765pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.59009pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.85005pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}}{n^{{{a}}}_{{\mathchoice{\makebox[4.33765pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[4.33765pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.59009pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.85005pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}}{n^{{{a}}}_{{\mathchoice{\makebox[4.33765pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[4.33765pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.59009pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.85005pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}}=\sigma\mathchoice{X^{{{a}}}_{{\mathchoice{\makebox[4.33765pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[4.33765pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.59009pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.85005pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}}{X^{{{a}}}_{{\mathchoice{\makebox[4.33765pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[4.33765pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.59009pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.85005pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}}{X^{{{a}}}_{{\mathchoice{\makebox[4.33765pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[4.33765pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.59009pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.85005pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}}{X^{{{a}}}_{{\mathchoice{\makebox[4.33765pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[4.33765pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.59009pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.85005pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}},

(557)

where
\sigma
is a solution to the differential equation

\text{\textsterling}_{X}\sigma=-\kappa\sigma,
