(\Sigma,\mathchoice{h^{{\mathchoice{\makebox[4.33765pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[4.33765pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.59009pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.85005pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}\mathchoice{\makebox[3.51666pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[3.51666pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.1029pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.50208pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}_{{{a}{b}}}}{h^{{\mathchoice{\makebox[4.33765pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[4.33765pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.59009pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.85005pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}\mathchoice{\makebox[3.51666pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[3.51666pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.1029pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.50208pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}_{{{a}{b}}}}{h^{{\mathchoice{\makebox[4.33765pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[4.33765pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.59009pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.85005pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}\mathchoice{\makebox[3.51666pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[3.51666pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.1029pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.50208pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}_{{{a}{b}}}}{h^{{\mathchoice{\makebox[4.33765pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[4.33765pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.59009pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.85005pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}\mathchoice{\makebox[3.51666pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[3.51666pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.1029pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.50208pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}_{{{a}{b}}}})
. Notice that
\mathrm{Isom}(\Sigma)
is only defined in the first place because we are working with an
\gls
AKH, and a more general null hypersurface could have cross sections that are not isometric.

For
\glspl
ACKH we can perform a very similar procedure. A null geodesic is a null geodesic in any spacetime related by a confomorphism. Hence, the key difference is that now the induced metric is only defined up to a confomorphism. Hence, we get the equivalence relation

which leads to the equations

(567a)

\displaystyle\text{\textsterling}_{\xi}\mathchoice{\tilde{n}^{{{a}}}_{{\mathchoice{\makebox[4.33765pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[4.33765pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.59009pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.85005pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}}{\tilde{n}^{{{a}}}_{{\mathchoice{\makebox[4.33765pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[4.33765pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.59009pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.85005pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}}{\tilde{n}^{{{a}}}_{{\mathchoice{\makebox[4.33765pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[4.33765pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.59009pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.85005pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}}{\tilde{n}^{{{a}}}_{{\mathchoice{\makebox[4.33765pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[4.33765pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.59009pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.85005pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}}

\displaystyle=\lambda\mathchoice{\tilde{n}^{{{a}}}_{{\mathchoice{\makebox[4.33765pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[4.33765pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.59009pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.85005pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}}{\tilde{n}^{{{a}}}_{{\mathchoice{\makebox[4.33765pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[4.33765pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.59009pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.85005pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}}{\tilde{n}^{{{a}}}_{{\mathchoice{\makebox[4.33765pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[4.33765pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.59009pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.85005pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}}{\tilde{n}^{{{a}}}_{{\mathchoice{\makebox[4.33765pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[4.33765pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.59009pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.85005pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}},

(567b)

for
\mu,\lambda\in\mathcal{C}^{\infty}(\Sigma)
. This time we get to the vector field

+ f(\tensor{x}{^A}))\mathchoice{n^{{{a}}}_{{\mathchoice{\makebox[4.33765pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[4.33765pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.59009pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.85005pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}}{n^{{{a}}}_{{\mathchoice{\makebox[4.33765pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[4.33765pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.59009pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.85005pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}}{n^{{{a}}}_{{\mathchoice{\makebox[4.33765pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[4.33765pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.59009pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.85005pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}}{n^{{{a}}}_{{\mathchoice{\makebox[4.33765pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[4.33765pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.59009pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.85005pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}},

(568)

with
\mathchoice{Y^{{{a}}}_{{\mathchoice{\makebox[4.33765pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[4.33765pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.59009pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.85005pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}}{Y^{{{a}}}_{{\mathchoice{\makebox[4.33765pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[4.33765pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.59009pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.85005pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}}{Y^{{{a}}}_{{\mathchoice{\makebox[4.33765pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[4.33765pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.59009pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.85005pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}}{Y^{{{a}}}_{{\mathchoice{\makebox[4.33765pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[4.33765pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.59009pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.85005pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}}
a
conformal
Killing vector field as opposed to a genuine Killing vector field. We are thus led to the
\gls
ACKH group

G_{\text{ACKH}}=\mathrm{Conf}(\Sigma)\ltimes(\mathcal{C}^{\infty}(\Sigma)\ltimes\mathcal{C}^{\infty}(\Sigma)),

(569)

where
\mathrm{Conf}(\Sigma)
is the confomorphism group of
(\Sigma,\mathchoice{\tilde{h}^{{\mathchoice{\makebox[4.33765pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[4.33765pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.59009pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.85005pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}\mathchoice{\makebox[3.51666pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[3.51666pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.1029pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.50208pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}_{{{a}{b}}}}{\tilde{h}^{{\mathchoice{\makebox[4.33765pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[4.33765pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.59009pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.85005pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}\mathchoice{\makebox[3.51666pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[3.51666pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.1029pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.50208pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}_{{{a}{b}}}}{\tilde{h}^{{\mathchoice{\makebox[4.33765pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[4.33765pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.59009pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.85005pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}\mathchoice{\makebox[3.51666pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[3.51666pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.1029pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.50208pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}_{{{a}{b}}}}{\tilde{h}^{{\mathchoice{\makebox[4.33765pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[4.33765pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.59009pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.85005pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}\mathchoice{\makebox[3.51666pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[3.51666pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.1029pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.50208pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}_{{{a}{b}}}})
. As with
\glspl
AKH,
\mathrm{Conf}(\Sigma)
is only defined because we are working with an
\gls
ACKH—and a more general null hypersurface could have cross sections that are not confomorphic.

For
\Sigma=\mathbb{S}^{2}
we find

G_{\text{AKH}}=\mathrm{SO}(3)\ltimes(\mathcal{C}^{\infty}(\mathbb{S}^{2})\ltimes\mathcal{C}^{\infty}(\mathbb{S}^{2}))=\mathrm{DMP}_{4}

(570)

and

G_{\text{ACKH}}=\mathrm{SO}^{+}(3,1)\ltimes(\mathcal{C}^{\infty}(\mathbb{S}^{2})\ltimes\mathcal{C}^{\infty}(\mathbb{S}^{2})).

(571)

G_{\text{ACKH}}
is larger than the
\gls
BMS group, but smaller than the Newman–Unti group. In Ref.
\citeonline
aguiaralves2025NullInfinityKilling, the additional transformations are called “superdilations”, for they are direction-dependent dilations.

10.4
Superdilations

The original motivation for considering
\glspl
A(C)KH was to find a bridge between the
\gls
BMS and
\gls
DMP groups. In particular, this was motivated by a search for a notion of superrotation in the de Sitter cosmological horizon. By providing a unified definition of the
\gls
BMS and
\gls
DMP groups, it would be possible to attempt at an extension of the
\gls
DMP group.

Curiously, the
\gls
AKH group is exactly the same as the
\gls
DMP group, and leaves no clear room for extensions. There is no such thing as a “local isometry”, so we cannot trade the isometry group of the cross section for a local isometry algebra. In this sense, we cannot get a notion of superrotation in the cosmological horizon. Meanwhile, the
\gls
ACKH group provides a new extension of the
\gls
BMS group in the form of superdilations. These transformations were already present in the
\gls
DMP group (due to its double semidirect product structure), but had not been seriously considered as a symmetry at infinity.

Other authors had stumbled upon transformations similar to superdilations. For instance, as previously mentioned, the
\gls
ACKH group is smaller than the Newman–Unti group
[
179
]
, and the original analysis of superrotations by
[
16
,
15
]
also addressed the possibility of considering the extra Newman–Unti transformations. However, these approaches consider transformations much more general than superdilations, because one does not restrict the conformal scaling of the normal vector
\mathchoice{\tilde{n}^{{{a}}}_{{\mathchoice{\makebox[4.33765pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[4.33765pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.59009pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.85005pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}}{\tilde{n}^{{{a}}}_{{\mathchoice{\makebox[4.33765pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[4.33765pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.59009pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.85005pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}}{\tilde{n}^{{{a}}}_{{\mathchoice{\makebox[4.33765pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[4.33765pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.59009pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.85005pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}}{\tilde{n}^{{{a}}}_{{\mathchoice{\makebox[4.33765pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[4.33765pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.59009pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.85005pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}}
in any way.

If on the one hand one may not constrain the conformal scaling of
\mathchoice{\tilde{n}^{{{a}}}_{{\mathchoice{\makebox[4.33765pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[4.33765pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.59009pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.85005pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}}{\tilde{n}^{{{a}}}_{{\mathchoice{\makebox[4.33765pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[4.33765pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.59009pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.85005pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}}{\tilde{n}^{{{a}}}_{{\mathchoice{\makebox[4.33765pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[4.33765pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.59009pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.85005pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}}{\tilde{n}^{{{a}}}_{{\mathchoice{\makebox[4.33765pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[4.33765pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.59009pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.85005pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}}
, on the other hand it is possible to overconstrain it and remove the superdilations altogether. This is what is typically done in the derivation of the
\gls
BMS group, in which the conformal scaling of
\mathchoice{\tilde{n}^{{{a}}}_{{\mathchoice{\makebox[4.33765pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[4.33765pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.59009pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.85005pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}}{\tilde{n}^{{{a}}}_{{\mathchoice{\makebox[4.33765pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[4.33765pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.59009pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.85005pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}}{\tilde{n}^{{{a}}}_{{\mathchoice{\makebox[4.33765pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[4.33765pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.59009pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.85005pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}}{\tilde{n}^{{{a}}}_{{\mathchoice{\makebox[4.33765pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[4.33765pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.59009pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.85005pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}}
is tied to that of the induced metric
\mathchoice{\tilde{h}^{{\mathchoice{\makebox[4.33765pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[4.33765pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.59009pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.85005pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}\mathchoice{\makebox[3.51666pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[3.51666pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.1029pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.50208pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}_{{{a}{b}}}}{\tilde{h}^{{\mathchoice{\makebox[4.33765pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[4.33765pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.59009pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.85005pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}\mathchoice{\makebox[3.51666pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[3.51666pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.1029pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.50208pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}_{{{a}{b}}}}{\tilde{h}^{{\mathchoice{\makebox[4.33765pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[4.33765pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.59009pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.85005pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}\mathchoice{\makebox[3.51666pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[3.51666pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.1029pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.50208pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}_{{{a}{b}}}}{\tilde{h}^{{\mathchoice{\makebox[4.33765pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[4.33765pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.59009pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.85005pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}\mathchoice{\makebox[3.51666pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[3.51666pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.1029pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.50208pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}_{{{a}{b}}}}
. In asymptotically flat spacetimes, this occurs due to the role played by the conformal factor
\Omega
. In the
\gls
ACKH approach, however, we never imposed any conditions about asymptotic flatness, but rather focused on the more general geometric structure of an
\gls
ACKH. This invites us to keep this freedom and consider superdilations more seriously. Other authors, such as
[
67
]
, also worked in more general setups and decided to tie the conformal scalings of
\mathchoice{\tilde{n}^{{{a}}}_{{\mathchoice{\makebox[4.33765pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[4.33765pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.59009pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.85005pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}}{\tilde{n}^{{{a}}}_{{\mathchoice{\makebox[4.33765pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[4.33765pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.59009pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.85005pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}}{\tilde{n}^{{{a}}}_{{\mathchoice{\makebox[4.33765pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[4.33765pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.59009pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.85005pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}}{\tilde{n}^{{{a}}}_{{\mathchoice{\makebox[4.33765pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[4.33765pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.59009pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.85005pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}}
and
\mathchoice{\tilde{h}^{{\mathchoice{\makebox[4.33765pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[4.33765pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.59009pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.85005pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}\mathchoice{\makebox[3.51666pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[3.51666pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.1029pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.50208pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}_{{{a}{b}}}}{\tilde{h}^{{\mathchoice{\makebox[4.33765pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[4.33765pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.59009pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.85005pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}\mathchoice{\makebox[3.51666pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[3.51666pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.1029pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.50208pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}_{{{a}{b}}}}{\tilde{h}^{{\mathchoice{\makebox[4.33765pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[4.33765pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.59009pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.85005pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}\mathchoice{\makebox[3.51666pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[3.51666pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.1029pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.50208pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}_{{{a}{b}}}}{\tilde{h}^{{\mathchoice{\makebox[4.33765pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[4.33765pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.59009pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.85005pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}\mathchoice{\makebox[3.51666pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[3.51666pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.1029pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.50208pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}_{{{a}{b}}}}
together to preserve a residual form of conformal invariance and exclude the superdilations.

At the end of the day, the usefulness of a definition comes through its implications. In the case of superdilations, it seems natural to pursue further connections by means of an infrared triangle. For example,
\glspl
GW in
\gls
GR are always transverse and traceless, because so are the two graviton degrees of freedom. Nevertheless, modified theories of gravity may include extra degrees of freedom
[
96
,
97
,
246
]
. In particular, some theories may include a “transverse breathing mode”, which corresponds to a transverse, but “tracefull”, polarization. Instead of causing shears on an array of inertial detectors, this polarization causes the array to expand and contract. This is illustrated on
Fig.

20
.

Figure 20:
Gravitons are transverse and traceless, and thus it follows that
\glspl
GW in
\gls
GR passing through an array of inertial detectors (orange lines) can only cause it to shear in the
+
and
\times
polarizations (top row). However, modified theories of gravity may involve other polarizations, such as a transverse breathing mode. Such a polarization would affect the array of inertial detectors by making it expand and contract (bottom row). Figure taken from Ref.
\citeonline
aguiaralves2025NullInfinityKilling.

Since the
\gls
ACKH approach is purely geometrical and makes no assumptions about the underlying theory of gravity, superdilations could be a hint at a modified theory of gravity, in the sense it is possible they could be mapped to a memory effect in the transverse breathing mode. A guess would be that such a theory can be described by including an extra scalar field, which is what happens in Brans–Dicke gravity
[
42
]
. Some aspects of the infrared behavior of Brans–Dicke gravity have been investigated
[
142
,
220
,
92
]
, and it is known that massless scalar fields also enjoy an interesting infrared structure
[
47
,
50
]
. Hence, by modifying
\gls
GR in a suitable manner, superdilations could be manifested in memory effects and
\glspl
GW in general, which could lead to observable effects
[
96
,
97
,
92
]
.

The interest in this approach is that we use geometry and symmetry considerations and infrared physics to guess (or “bootstrap”) what should be the degrees of freedom of gravity. The existence of a new scalar mode is suggested by considerations that arise from pure Lorentzian geometry, and may later be tested through
\gls
GW observations.

10.5
Applications

In addition to the exploration of modified gravity theories, the
\gls
A(C)KH approach has a few other prospective applications.

First and foremost, it disfavors the idea of generalizing superrotations to de Sitter spacetime in a
\gls
CFT-friendly manner. This means it may be difficult (or incorrect) to pursue a conformally-invariant holographic duality in the cosmological horizon.

Secondly, we may now come back to the notion of bifurcate Killing horizons and wonder what could happen with a bifurcate
\gls
ACKH. With an appropriate definition, it could be that we may understand the relation between
\mathscr{I}^{+}
and
\mathscr{I}^{-}
is terms of a bifurcate horizon, and thus shed more light into Strominger’s antipodal matching condition
[
224
]
, which was essential for us to identify
\gls
BMS symmetries and the Weinberg soft graviton theorem in
Section

6.4
.

\Glspl

A(C)KH are still too young to be fully understood, but it is exciting to see how purely geometric insights may bring new inspiration and results into high-energy physics.

11
Final Remarks

The
\glsxtrlong
IR structure of gravity is fascinating. While a first glance could make it seem that very large distances have a simple or almost boring behavior, this guess could not be further from the truth. As we have seem, there is a very rich structure hiding away at the infinitely distant sky.

In these notes, we have only managed to scratch the surface of these topics. While I wanted to cover many more topics and make this a much more comprehensive reference, there is an old saying—attributed to far too many people to have a single author—that texts are never finished, only abandoned. Since this particular text starts with basic group theory, it seemed an overreach to aim at even more cutting edge topics.

There are many directions one could pursue after finishing these notes. Some of the ones that draw my attention the most are the following, in no particular order.

•

The covariant phase space formalism
[
160
,
144
,
145
]
, which allows for a deeper understanding of what are asymptotic symmetries and their associated conserved charges
[
239
,
12
,
17
]
. See, for example, Refs.
\citeonline
gieres2023CovariantCanonicalFormulations,compere2019AdvancedLecturesGeneral,fiorucci2021LeakyCovariantPhase for introductions. In particular, one sees that a supertranslation is more than a diffeomorphism due to its nontrivial action on the boundary of the spacetime, where it does not behave as a mere gauge transformation.

•

The celestial holography program
[
187
,
7
,
203
,
186
,
185
,
86
]
, which pursues a dual
\gls
CFT to quantum gravity in asymptotically flat spacetimes by exploiting the infrared structure of gravity and gauge theory. It investigates how to formulate quantum gravity in asymptotically flat spacetimes in terms of a two-dimensional Euclidean
\gls
CFT living on the celestial sphere.

•

The Carrollian holography program
[
88
,
89
,
10
]
, which also pursues a holographic formulation of quantum gravity, but through a three-dimensional Carrollian
\gls
CFT at null infinity.

•

The study of infrared finite scattering theory in the algebraic approach
[
201
,

,
200
]
, which attempts at understanding how to avoid harmful infrared divergences that keep one from defining an
S
-matrix.

•

The deeper relations between scattering amplitudes and classical physics
[

,

,

]
, which is the fundamental reason for why soft theorems and memory effects must be related.

•

The behavior of asymptotic flatness and the memory effect in higher-dimensional spacetimes
[

,

,

,

]
, which exhibits, for example, how the notion of
\gls
BMS transformations appears to be special in four-dimensional spacetimes.

•

Improving on the construction of Carrollian manifolds by viewing them as fiber bundles
[

]
, thus mimicking what one has in Newton–Cartan theory (see,
e.g.
, Ref.
\citeonline

•

Studying in more depth the symmetries and degrees of freedom of null hypersurfaces in the bulk of spacetime
[

,

,

,

]
. In particular, our definition of expanding universe with cosmological horizon imposes a time-independent metric on the horizon, which forbids the passage of gravitational radiation. This can be quite different from the behavior at null infinity—
Eq.

, for example, shows how the Bondi mass aspect changes as radiation “leaks” through
\mathscr{I}^{+}
—and taking these effects into account can be relevant in general scenarios.

•

The relevance of soft gravitons in the quantum decoherence of spatial superpositions by Killing horizons

,

.

Of course, there are still many topics I could barely scratch along the notes, such as
\gls
CK spacetimes, the construction of Hadamard states in spacetimes with distinguished null hypersurfaces, and much more. What I hope to have shown is that infinity has never been closer, and the sky has never looked so promising.

Appendix A
Complex Analysis

In a few points throughout the text we need to employ some results from complex analysis, which involves Wirtinger derivatives and surface integrals over the complex plane. In this appendix I briefly summarize these ideas. The main reference is the book by Hörmander
[
140
]
. I assume the reader is familiar with more elementary facts about complex analysis, such as the general notions of what is a a holomorphic function, the Cauchy–Riemann equations, and so on. These topics are well discussed in Ref.
\citeonline
brown2014ComplexVariablesApplications.

We will often identify the complex plane
\mathbb{C}
with the real plane
\mathbb{R}^{2}
. Given some function
f
on
\mathbb{C}
(which is not necessarily holomorphic), we can write its differential as

\differential{f}=\partialderivative{f}{x}\differential{x}+\partialderivative{f}{y}\differential{y}.

(572)

This is real analysis. To get to the complex domain, we introduce the complex coordinates

\zeta=x+iy\quad\mbox{and}\quad\bar{\zeta}=x-iy.

(573)

If we define the Wirtinger derivatives by

\partialderivative{\zeta}=\frac{1}{2}\quantity(\pdv{x} - i \pdv{y})\quad\mbox{and}\quad\partialderivative{\bar{\zeta}}=\frac{1}{2}\quantity(\pdv{x} + i \pdv{y}),

(574)

then we can also write the differential of a function of a complex variable as

\differential{f}=\partialderivative{f}{\zeta}\differential{\zeta}+\partialderivative{f}{\bar{\zeta}}\differential{\bar{\zeta}}.

(575)

Hence, we see
\zeta
and its conjugate
\bar{\zeta}
as coordinates on the plane. It is convenient to treat these coordinates as independent, which intrinsically means extending
x,y\in\mathbb{R}
to
x,y\in\mathbb{C}
, so that
(\zeta,\bar{\zeta})\in\mathbb{C}^{2}
. At the end of the day, we remember the physical results fix
\bar{\zeta}
as the complex conjugate of
\zeta
.

The advantage of taking this point of view is that we can now discuss functions which are differentiable in the real plane, but still not holomorphic. For a function to be holomorphic, it must satisfy the Cauchy–Riemann equations, and in this notation this means that

\partialderivative{f}{\bar{\zeta}}=0.

(576)

Hence, if this condition holds,
f
is holomorphic and we are dealing with the usual notions of complex analysis. For this reason, it is common—for example in the
\gls
CFT literature—to write
f(\zeta)
for holomorphic
f
, but
f(\zeta,\bar{\zeta})
for more general functions. Notice that if
Eq.

576
does not hold, we can still talk about derivatives and calculus by borrowing the concepts from the real plane, but we are no longer discussing holomorphic functions. Therefore, this approach allows us to discuss and do calculus with more functions than the more usual notions of complex analysis would allow.

Now let us discuss integrals. Consider some bounded open set
\Omega\subseteq\mathbb{C}
. Notice that Green’s theorem allows us to write

\displaystyle\oint_{\partial\Omega}f\differential{\zeta}

\displaystyle=\oint_{\partial\Omega}f\differential{x}+if\differential{y},

(577a)

\displaystyle=\int\quantity(i \pdv{f}{x} - \pdv{f}{y})\differential{x}\wedge\differential{y},

(577b)

\displaystyle=i\int\quantity(\pdv{f}{x} + i\pdv{f}{y})\differential{x}\wedge\differential{y},

(577c)

\displaystyle=2i\int\partialderivative{f}{\bar{\zeta}}\differential{x}\wedge\differential{y},

(577d)

\displaystyle=2i\int\partialderivative{f}{\bar{\zeta}}\frac{\differential{\bar{\zeta}}\wedge\differential{\zeta}}{2i},

(577e)

\displaystyle=\int\partialderivative{f}{\bar{\zeta}}\differential{\bar{\zeta}}\wedge\differential{\zeta},

(577f)

\displaystyle\equiv\int\partialderivative{f}{\bar{\zeta}}\differential{\zeta}\differential{\bar{\zeta}}.

(577g)

In particular, the integral vanishes if
f
is holomorphic (a standard result). The correct way of writing these integrals would be in the language of differential forms (making the wedge products explicit, as in the previous calculation). This, however, can overload the notation. I will typically write
\differential{\zeta}\differential{\bar{\zeta}}
and it should be implicitly understood that this means
\differential{\bar{\zeta}}\wedge\differential{\zeta}
(as opposed to
\differential{\zeta}\wedge\differential{\bar{\zeta}}
, which differs by a sign). This is common in the
\gls
CFT literature.

For holomorphic
f
, we know the Cauchy integral formula holds. It states that, for
\chi\in\Omega
,

f(\chi)=\frac{1}{2\pi i}\oint_{\partial\Omega}\frac{f(\zeta)}{\zeta-\chi}\differential{\zeta}.

(578)

What about non-holomorphic functions?

Suppose
f
is real-differentiable in
\Omega
, but not necessarily holomorphic. We pick
\chi\in\Omega
and let
d_{\chi}
be the distance from
\chi
to
\mathbb{C}\setminus\Omega
. We may now define the sets

{}_{\epsilon}=\quantity{\zeta\in\Omega\mid\abs{\zeta- \chi} > \epsilon}

(579)

for all
0<\epsilon<d_{\chi}
. Notice that

\frac{1}{\zeta-\chi}

(580)

is holomorphic away from
\chi
. Hence, its
\bar{\zeta}
derivative vanishes in
�
. We can thus use
Eq.

577
to write

\displaystyle\int_{{}_{\epsilon}}\partialderivative{f}{\bar{\zeta}}\frac{1}{\zeta-\chi}\differential{\zeta}\differential{\bar{\zeta}}

\displaystyle=\int_{{}_{\epsilon}}\partialderivative{\bar{\zeta}}(\frac{f(\zeta,\bar{\zeta})}{\zeta- \chi})\differential{\zeta}\differential{\bar{\zeta}},

(581a)

\displaystyle=\oint_{\partial{}_{\epsilon}}\frac{f(\zeta,\bar{\zeta})}{\zeta-\chi}\differential{\zeta},

(581b)

\displaystyle=\oint_{\partial\Omega}\frac{f(\zeta,\bar{\zeta})}{\zeta-\chi}\differential{\zeta}-\oint_{\absolutevalue{\zeta-\chi}=\epsilon}\frac{f(\zeta,\bar{\zeta})}{\zeta-\chi}\differential{\zeta},

(581c)

\displaystyle=\oint_{\partial\Omega}\frac{f(\zeta,\bar{\zeta})}{\zeta-\chi}\differential{\zeta}-\int_{0}^{2\pi}\frac{f(\chi+\epsilon e^{i\phi},\bar{\chi}+\epsilon e^{-i\phi})}{\epsilon e^{i\phi}}\epsilon ie^{i\phi}\differential{\phi},

(581d)

\displaystyle=\oint_{\partial\Omega}\frac{f(\zeta,\bar{\zeta})}{\zeta-\chi}\differential{\zeta}-i\int_{0}^{2\pi}f(\chi+\epsilon e^{i\phi},\bar{\chi}+\epsilon e^{-i\phi})\differential{\phi}.

(581e)

1/(\zeta-\chi)
is integrable over
\Omega
and
\partialderivative*{f}{\bar{\zeta}}
is continuous on the same set. We can then take the
\epsilon\to 0
limit and find

f(\chi,\bar{\chi})=\frac{1}{2\pi i}\oint_{\partial\Omega}\frac{f(\zeta,\bar{\zeta})}{\zeta-\chi}\differential{\zeta}-\frac{1}{2\pi i}\int\partialderivative{f}{\bar{\zeta}}\frac{1}{\zeta-\chi}\differential{\zeta}\differential{\bar{\zeta}}.

(582)

This is known as the Cauchy–Pompeiu formula.

We can still manipulate the Cauchy–Pompeiu formula to an expression that will serve us better. Using
Eqs.

577
and
582
, we see that

\displaystyle f(\chi,\bar{\chi})

\displaystyle=\frac{1}{2\pi i}\oint_{\partial\Omega}\frac{f(\zeta,\bar{\zeta})}{\zeta-\chi}\differential{\zeta}-\frac{1}{2\pi i}\int\partialderivative{f}{\bar{\zeta}}\frac{1}{\zeta-\chi}\differential{\zeta}\differential{\bar{\zeta}},

(583a)

\displaystyle=\frac{1}{2\pi i}\int\partialderivative{\bar{\zeta}}\quantity(\frac{f(\zeta,\bar{\zeta})}{\zeta- \chi})\differential{\zeta}\differential{\bar{\zeta}}-\frac{1}{2\pi i}\int\partialderivative{f}{\bar{\zeta}}\frac{1}{\zeta-\chi}\differential{\zeta}\differential{\bar{\zeta}},

(583b)

\displaystyle=\frac{1}{2\pi i}\int f(\zeta,\bar{\zeta})\partialderivative{\bar{\zeta}}\quantity(\frac{1}{\zeta- \chi})\differential{\zeta}\differential{\bar{\zeta}}.

(583c)

The derivative is meant in a distributional sense, since it vanishes everywhere but at
(\chi,\bar{\chi})
. We may then write

\partialderivative{\bar{\zeta}}\quantity(\frac{1}{\zeta- \chi})=2\pi i\delta^{(2)}(\zeta-\chi),

(584)

where the Dirac delta is defined by the condition that, for any real-differentiable
44
44

44

To discuss distributions we actually need smooth functions, but if one refrains from differentiating the Dirac delta we can still consider this wider class of differentiable functions.
(but not necessarily holomorphic) function

\int f(\zeta,\bar{\zeta})\delta^{(2)}\quantity(\zeta- \chi)\differential{\zeta}\differential{\bar{\zeta}}=f(\chi,\bar{\chi}).

(585)

I mention some authors—especially in the
\gls
CFT literature—may omit the
i
factor in
Eq.

584
, but they then omit other factors of
i
that would occur in the integrals. I choose to keep both factors of
i
.

Appendix B
The Double Cover of the Lorentz Group

In this appendix I prove
Eq.

86
,

\mathrm{SL}(2,\mathbb{C})/\mathbb{Z}_{2}\cong\mathrm{SO}^{+}(3,1),

(586)

in order to establish that the conformal group of the two-sphere indeed is the Lorentz group.
\mathbb{Z}_{2}
is the two-element group
\quantity{-1,1}
with the product given by multiplication. Since this group only has two elements,
\mathrm{SL}(2,\mathbb{C})/\mathbb{Z}_{2}\cong\mathrm{SO}^{+}(3,1)
has the meaning that there are two elements of
\mathrm{SL}(2,\mathbb{C})
for each element of
\mathrm{SO}^{+}(3,1)
.
\mathrm{SL}(2,\mathbb{C})
is said to be the double cover of
\mathrm{SO}^{+}(3,1)
. This topic has many aspects studied in algebraic topology
[
125
,
165
]
and spin geometry
[
123
,
157
]
, but I will keep the discussion to the bare essentials and focus only on the group theoretic aspects. Our discussion mimics those of Refs.
\citeonline
zee2016GroupTheoryNutshell,weinberg1995Foundations,hamilton2017MathematicalGaugeTheory.

Let
x\in\mathbb{R}^{4}
be a point in Minkowski spacetime and let
L\in\mathrm{SL}(2,\mathbb{C})
. This means, for our purposes, that
L
is a
2\times 2
complex matrix with unit determinant. Using the Cartesian coordinates of
x
, consider the matrix

\mathchoice{x^{{{\mu}}}_{{\mathchoice{\makebox[5.25pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[5.25pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[3.67499pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[2.625pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}}{x^{{{\mu}}}_{{\mathchoice{\makebox[5.25pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[5.25pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[3.67499pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[2.625pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}}{x^{{{\mu}}}_{{\mathchoice{\makebox[5.25pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[5.25pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[3.67499pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[2.625pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}}{x^{{{\mu}}}_{{\mathchoice{\makebox[5.25pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[5.25pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[3.67499pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[2.625pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}}\sigma_{\mu},

(587)

where
\sigma_{0}=\text{1}
and
\sigma_{i}
are the Pauli matrices,

\sigma_{1}=\matrixquantity(\lx@physics@matrix 0 & 1 \\ 1 & 0\endlx@physics@matrix),\quad\sigma_{2}=\matrixquantity(\lx@physics@matrix 0 & -i \\ i & 0\endlx@physics@matrix),\quad\mbox{and}\quad\sigma_{3}=\matrixquantity(\lx@physics@matrix 1 & 0 \\ 0 & -1\endlx@physics@matrix).

(588)

Eq.

587
, with
\mathchoice{x^{{{\mu}}}_{{\mathchoice{\makebox[5.25pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[5.25pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[3.67499pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[2.625pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}}{x^{{{\mu}}}_{{\mathchoice{\makebox[5.25pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[5.25pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[3.67499pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[2.625pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}}{x^{{{\mu}}}_{{\mathchoice{\makebox[5.25pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[5.25pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[3.67499pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[2.625pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}}{x^{{{\mu}}}_{{\mathchoice{\makebox[5.25pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[5.25pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[3.67499pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[2.625pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}}
understood to be real, is the most general expression for a
2\times 2
Hermitian matrix with complex entries.

Consider now

X^{\prime}=L\mathchoice{x^{{{\mu}}}_{{\mathchoice{\makebox[5.25pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[5.25pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[3.67499pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[2.625pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}}{x^{{{\mu}}}_{{\mathchoice{\makebox[5.25pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[5.25pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[3.67499pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[2.625pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}}{x^{{{\mu}}}_{{\mathchoice{\makebox[5.25pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[5.25pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[3.67499pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[2.625pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}}{x^{{{\mu}}}_{{\mathchoice{\makebox[5.25pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[5.25pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[3.67499pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[2.625pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}}\sigma_{\mu}L^{\dagger},

(589)

where
\dagger
denotes Hermitian conjugation.
X^{\prime}
is surely a
2\times 2
complex matrix, and it is still Hermitian as one can show by direct computation. We can thus write

\mathchoice{x^{{{\prime}{\mu}}}_{{\mathchoice{\makebox[2.30556pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[2.30556pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[1.34749pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[0.9625pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}\mathchoice{\makebox[5.25pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[5.25pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[3.67499pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[2.625pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}}{x^{{{\prime}{\mu}}}_{{\mathchoice{\makebox[2.30556pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[2.30556pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[1.34749pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[0.9625pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}\mathchoice{\makebox[5.25pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[5.25pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[3.67499pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[2.625pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}}{x^{{{\prime}{\mu}}}_{{\mathchoice{\makebox[2.30556pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[2.30556pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[1.34749pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[0.9625pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}\mathchoice{\makebox[5.25pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[5.25pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[3.67499pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[2.625pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}}{x^{{{\prime}{\mu}}}_{{\mathchoice{\makebox[2.30556pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[2.30556pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[1.34749pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[0.9625pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}\mathchoice{\makebox[5.25pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[5.25pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[3.67499pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[2.625pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}}\sigma_{\mu}=L\mathchoice{x^{{{\mu}}}_{{\mathchoice{\makebox[5.25pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[5.25pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[3.67499pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[2.625pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}}{x^{{{\mu}}}_{{\mathchoice{\makebox[5.25pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[5.25pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[3.67499pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[2.625pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}}{x^{{{\mu}}}_{{\mathchoice{\makebox[5.25pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[5.25pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[3.67499pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[2.625pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}}{x^{{{\mu}}}_{{\mathchoice{\makebox[5.25pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[5.25pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[3.67499pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[2.625pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}}\sigma_{\mu}L^{\dagger}.

(590)

Since
L
has unit determinant, we find that

\mathchoice{x^{{{\prime}{\mu}}}_{{\mathchoice{\makebox[2.30556pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[2.30556pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[1.34749pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[0.9625pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}\mathchoice{\makebox[5.25pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[5.25pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[3.67499pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[2.625pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}}{x^{{{\prime}{\mu}}}_{{\mathchoice{\makebox[2.30556pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[2.30556pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[1.34749pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[0.9625pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}\mathchoice{\makebox[5.25pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[5.25pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[3.67499pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[2.625pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}}{x^{{{\prime}{\mu}}}_{{\mathchoice{\makebox[2.30556pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[2.30556pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[1.34749pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[0.9625pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}\mathchoice{\makebox[5.25pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[5.25pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[3.67499pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[2.625pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}}{x^{{{\prime}{\mu}}}_{{\mathchoice{\makebox[2.30556pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[2.30556pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[1.34749pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[0.9625pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}\mathchoice{\makebox[5.25pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[5.25pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[3.67499pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[2.625pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}}\mathchoice{x^{{{\prime}}}_{{{\mu}}}}{x^{{{\prime}}}_{{{\mu}}}}{x^{{{\prime}}}_{{{\mu}}}}{x^{{{\prime}}}_{{{\mu}}}}=-\det(\tensor{x}{^\prime^\mu} \sigma_\mu)=-\det L\det(\tensor{x}{^\mu} \sigma_\mu)\det L^{\dagger}=-\det(\tensor{x}{^\mu} \sigma_\mu)=\mathchoice{x^{{{\mu}}}_{{\mathchoice{\makebox[5.25pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[5.25pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[3.67499pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[2.625pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}}{x^{{{\mu}}}_{{\mathchoice{\makebox[5.25pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[5.25pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[3.67499pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[2.625pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}}{x^{{{\mu}}}_{{\mathchoice{\makebox[5.25pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[5.25pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[3.67499pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[2.625pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}}{x^{{{\mu}}}_{{\mathchoice{\makebox[5.25pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[5.25pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[3.67499pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[2.625pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}}\mathchoice{x^{{\mathchoice{\makebox[5.25pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[5.25pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[3.67499pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[2.625pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}_{{{\mu}}}}{x^{{\mathchoice{\makebox[5.25pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[5.25pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[3.67499pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[2.625pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}_{{{\mu}}}}{x^{{\mathchoice{\makebox[5.25pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[5.25pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[3.67499pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[2.625pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}_{{{\mu}}}}{x^{{\mathchoice{\makebox[5.25pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[5.25pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[3.67499pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[2.625pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}_{{{\mu}}}}.

(591)

Hence, the map
x\mapsto x^{\prime}
is a Lorentz transformation, because it preserves the invariant interval, and thus the Minkowski metric. We can write

L\mathchoice{x^{{{\mu}}}_{{\mathchoice{\makebox[5.25pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[5.25pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[3.67499pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[2.625pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}}{x^{{{\mu}}}_{{\mathchoice{\makebox[5.25pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[5.25pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[3.67499pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[2.625pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}}{x^{{{\mu}}}_{{\mathchoice{\makebox[5.25pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[5.25pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[3.67499pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[2.625pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}}{x^{{{\mu}}}_{{\mathchoice{\makebox[5.25pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[5.25pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[3.67499pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[2.625pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}}\sigma_{\mu}L^{\dagger}=\mathchoice{\Lambda(L)^{{{\mu}\mathchoice{\makebox[5.25pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[5.25pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[3.67499pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[2.625pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}_{{\mathchoice{\makebox[5.25pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[5.25pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[3.67499pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[2.625pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}{\nu}}}}{\Lambda(L)^{{{\mu}\mathchoice{\makebox[5.25pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[5.25pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[3.67499pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[2.625pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}_{{\mathchoice{\makebox[5.25pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[5.25pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[3.67499pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[2.625pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}{\nu}}}}{\Lambda(L)^{{{\mu}\mathchoice{\makebox[5.25pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[5.25pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[3.67499pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[2.625pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}_{{\mathchoice{\makebox[5.25pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[5.25pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[3.67499pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[2.625pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}{\nu}}}}{\Lambda(L)^{{{\mu}\mathchoice{\makebox[5.25pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[5.25pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\ (592)

Hence, we found a map
\Lambda
from
\mathrm{SL}(2,\mathbb{C})
to
\mathrm{O}(3,1)
. We now need to show that

1.

it is a homomorphism,

2.

its range is
\mathrm{SO}^{+}(3,1)
,

3.

it is two-to-one.

It is direct to show it is a homomorphism. Let
M\in\mathrm{SL}(2,\mathbb{C})
. Then

(593d)

(593e)

Since
\Lambda(ML)=\Lambda(M)\Lambda(L)
, we conclude
\Lambda
is indeed a homomorphism.

Next we want to show that
\Ran\Lambda=\mathrm{SO}^{+}(3,1)
. An inner product in the space of
2\times 2
complex Hermitian matrices can be introduced by defining the Frobenius inner product

\innerproduct{X}{Y}=\frac{1}{2}\Tr[X^{\dagger}Y]=\frac{1}{2}\Tr[XY].

(594)

The identity matrix and the Pauli matrices then establish an orthonormal basis with respect to this inner product. Exploiting this fact we see that

\mathchoice{x^{{{\prime}{\mu}}}_{{\mathchoice{\makebox[2.30556pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[2.30556pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[1.34749pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[0.9625pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}\mathchoice{\makebox[5.25pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[5.25pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[3.67499pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[2.625pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}}{x^{{{\prime}{\mu}}}_{{\mathchoice{\makebox[2.30556pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[2.30556pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[1.34749pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[0.9625pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}\mathchoice{\makebox[5.25pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[5.25pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[3.67499pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[2.625pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}}{x^{{{\prime}{\mu}}}_{{\mathchoice{\makebox[2.30556pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[2.30556pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[1.34749pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[0.9625pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}\mathchoice{\makebox[5.25pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[5.25pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[3.67499pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[2.625pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}}{x^{{{\prime}{\mu}}}_{{\mathchoice{\makebox[2.30556pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[2.30556pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[1.34749pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[0.9625pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}\mathchoice{\makebox[5.25pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[5.25pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[3.67499pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[2.625pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}}=\frac{\mathchoice{x^{{{\nu}}}_{{\mathchoice{\makebox[5.25pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[5.25pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[3.67499pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[2.625pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}}{x^{{{\nu}}}_{{\mathchoice{\makebox[5.25pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[5.25pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[3.67499pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[2.625pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}}{x^{{{\nu}}}_{{\mathchoice{\makebox[5.25pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[5.25pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[3.67499pt][c]{ (595)

where
\bar{\sigma}^{0}=-\sigma^{0}=\text{1}
and
\bar{\sigma}^{i}=\sigma^{i}
(we raise the indices of
\sigma_{\mu}
with the Minkowski metric). Therefore, the Lorentz matrix
\Lambda(L)
associated to
L
is given by

\mathchoice{\Lambda(L)^{{{\mu}\mathchoice{\makebox[5.25pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[5.25pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[3.67499pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[2.625pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}_{{\mathchoice{\makebox[5.25pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[5.25pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[3.67499pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[2.625pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}{\nu}}}}{\Lambda(L)^{{{\mu}\mathchoice{\makebox[5.25pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[5.25pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[3.67499pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[2.625pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}_{{\mathchoice{\makebox[5.25pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[5.25pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[3.67499pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[2.625pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}{\nu}}}}{\Lambda(L)^{{{\mu}\mathchoice{\makebox[5.25pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[5.25pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[3.67499pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[2.625pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}_{{\mathchoice{\makebox[5.25pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[5.25pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[3.67499pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[2.625pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}{\nu}}}}{\Lambda(L)^{{{\mu}\mathchoice{\makebox[5.25pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[5.25pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[3.67499pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[2.625pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}_{{\mathchoice{\makebox[5.25pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[5.25pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[3.67499pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[2.625pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}{\nu}}}}=\frac{1}{2}\Tr[L\sigma_{\nu}L^{\dagger}\bar{\sigma}^{\mu}].

(596)

Notice

\mathchoice{\Lambda(L)^{{{0}\mathchoice{\makebox[3.98613pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[3.98613pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.45pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.75pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}_{{\mathchoice{\makebox[3.98613pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[3.98613pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.45pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.75pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}{0}}}}{\Lambda(L)^{{{0}\mathchoice{\makebox[3.98613pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[3.98613pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.45pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.75pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}_{{\mathchoice{\makebox[3.98613pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[3.98613pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.45pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.75pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}{0}}}}{\Lambda(L)^{{{0}\mathchoice{\makebox[3.98613pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[3.98613pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.45pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.75pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}_{{\mathchoice{\makebox[3.98613pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[3.98613pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.45pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.75pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}{0}}}}{\Lambda(L)^{{{0}\mathchoice{\makebox[3.98613pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[3.98613pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.45pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.75pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}_{{\mathchoice{\makebox[3.98613pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[3.98613pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.45pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.75pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}{0}}}}=\frac{1}{2}\Tr[LL^{\dagger}]>0,

(597)

and hence
\Lambda(L)\in\mathrm{O}^{+}(3,1)
.

It will be a bit more difficult to prove
\Lambda(L)\in\mathrm{SO}(3,1)
. To do so, notice that any
2\times 2
complex matrix can be written as

\mathchoice{z^{{{\mu}}}_{{\mathchoice{\makebox[5.25pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[5.25pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[3.67499pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[2.625pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}}{z^{{{\mu}}}_{{\mathchoice{\makebox[5.25pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[5.25pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[3.67499pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[2.625pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}}{z^{{{\mu}}}_{{\mathchoice{\makebox[5.25pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[5.25pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[3.67499pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[2.625pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}}{z^{{{\mu}}}_{{\mathchoice{\makebox[5.25pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[5.25pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[3.67499pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[2.625pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}}\sigma_{\mu},

(598)

with complex
\mathchoice{z^{{{\mu}}}_{{\mathchoice{\makebox[5.25pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[5.25pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[3.67499pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[2.625pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}}{z^{{{\mu}}}_{{\mathchoice{\makebox[5.25pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[5.25pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[3.67499pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[2.625pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}}{z^{{{\mu}}}_{{\mathchoice{\makebox[5.25pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[5.25pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[3.67499pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[2.625pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}}{z^{{{\mu}}}_{{\mathchoice{\makebox[5.25pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[5.25pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[3.67499pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[2.625pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}}
. It follows that
\det(\tensor{z}{^\mu} \sigma_{\mu})=-\mathchoice{z^{{{\mu}}}_{{\mathchoice{\makebox[5.25pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[5.25pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[3.67499pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[2.625pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}}{z^{{{\mu}}}_{{\mathchoice{\makebox[5.25pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[5.25pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[3.67499pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[2.625pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}}{z^{{{\mu}}}_{{\mathchoice{\makebox[5.25pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[5.25pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[3.67499pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[2.625pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}}{z^{{{\mu}}}_{{\mathchoice{\makebox[5.25pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[5.25pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[3.67499pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[2.625pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}}\mathchoice{z^{{\mathchoice{\makebox[5.25pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[5.25pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[3.67499pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[2.625pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}_{{{\mu}}}}{z^{{\mathchoice{\makebox[5.25pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[5.25pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[3.67499pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[2.625pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}_{{{\mu}}}}{z^{{\mathchoice{\makebox[5.25pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[5.25pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[3.67499pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[2.625pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}_{{{\mu}}}}{z^{{\mathchoice{\makebox[5.25pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[5.25pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[3.67499pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[2.625pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}_{{{\mu}}}}
. Hence, we can always write
L\in\mathrm{SL}(2,\mathbb{C})
as

L=\mathchoice{z^{{{\mu}}}_{{\mathchoice{\makebox[5.25pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[5.25pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[3.67499pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[2.625pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}}{z^{{{\mu}}}_{{\mathchoice{\makebox[5.25pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[5.25pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[3.67499pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[2.625pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}}{z^{{{\mu}}}_{{\mathchoice{\makebox[5.25pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[5.25pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[3.67499pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[2.625pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}}{z^{{{\mu}}}_{{\mathchoice{\makebox[5.25pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[5.25pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[3.67499pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[2.625pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}}\sigma_{\mu}

(599)

with
\mathchoice{z^{{{\mu}}}_{{\mathchoice{\makebox[5.25pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[5.25pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[3.67499pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[2.625pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}}{z^{{{\mu}}}_{{\mathchoice{\makebox[5.25pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[5.25pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[3.67499pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[2.625pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}}{z^{{{\mu}}}_{{\mathchoice{\makebox[5.25pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[5.25pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[3.67499pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[2.625pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}}{z^{{{\mu}}}_{{\mathchoice{\makebox[5.25pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[5.25pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[3.67499pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[2.625pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}}\mathchoice{z^{{\mathchoice{\makebox[5.25pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[5.25pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[3.67499pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[2.625pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}_{{{\mu}}}}{z^{{\mathchoice{\makebox[5.25pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[5.25pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[3.67499pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[2.625pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}_{{{\mu}}}}{z^{{\mathchoice{\makebox[5.25pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[5.25pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[3.67499pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[2.625pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}_{{{\mu}}}}{z^{{\mathchoice{\makebox[5.25pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[5.25pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[3.67499pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[2.625pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}_{{{\mu}}}}=-1
. Using this, we notice that

\mathchoice{\Lambda(L)^{{{\mu}\mathchoice{\makebox[5.25pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[5.25pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[3.67499pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[2.625pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}_{{\mathchoice{\makebox[5.25pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[5.25pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[3.67499pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[2.625pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}{\nu}}}}{\Lambda(L)^{{{\mu}\mathchoice{\makebox[5.25pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[5.25pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[3.67499pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[2.625pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}_{{\mathchoice{\makebox[5.25pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[5.25pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[3.67499pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[2.625pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}{\nu}}}}{\Lambda(L)^{{{\mu}\mathchoice{\makebox[5.25pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[5.25pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[3.67499pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[2.625pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}_{{\mathchoice{\makebox[5.25pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[5.25pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[3.67499pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[2.625pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}{\nu}}}}{\Lambda(L)^{{{\mu}\mathchoice{\makebox[5.25pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[5.25pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[3.67499pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[2.625pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}_{{\mathchoice{\makebox[5.25pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[5.25pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[3.67499pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[2.625pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}{\nu}}}}=\frac{\mathchoice{z^{{{\alpha}}}_{{\mathchoice{\makebox[5.25pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[5.25pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[3.67499pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[2.625pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}}{z^{{{\alpha}}}_{{\mathchoice{\makebox[5.25pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[5.25pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[3.67499pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[2.625pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}}{z^{{{\alpha}}}_{{\mathchoice{\makebox[5.25pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[5.25pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[3.67499pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[2.625pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}}{z^{{{\alpha}}}_{{\mathchoice{\makebox[5.25pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[5.25pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[3.67499pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[2.625pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}}\mathchoice{\bar{z}^{{{\beta}}}_{{\mathchoice{\makebox[5.25pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[5.25pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[3.67499pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[2.625pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}}{\bar{z}^{{{\beta}}}_{{\mathchoice{\makebox[5.25pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[5.25pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[3.67499pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[2.625pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}}{\bar{z}^{{{\beta}}}_{{\mathchoice{\makebox[5.25pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[5.25pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[3.67499pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[2.625pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}}{\bar{z}^{{{\beta}}}_{{\mathchoice{\makebox[5.25pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[5.25pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[3.67499pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[2.625pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}}}{2}\Tr[\sigma_{\alpha}\sigma_{\nu}\sigma_{\beta}\bar{\sigma}^{\mu}].

(600)

Using this expression, we can compute the elements of
\Lambda(L)
explicitly and compute the determinant by brute force. The result is

\det\Lambda(L)=\mathchoice{z^{{{\mu}}}_{{\mathchoice{\makebox[5.25pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[5.25pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[3.67499pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[2.625pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}}{z^{{{\mu}}}_{{\mathchoice{\makebox[5.25pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[5.25pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[3.67499pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[2.625pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}}{z^{{{\mu}}}_{{\mathchoice{\makebox[5.25pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[5.25pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[3.67499pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[2.625pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}}{z^{{{\mu}}}_{{\mathchoice{\makebox[5.25pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[5.25pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[3.67499pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[2.625pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}}\mathchoice{z^{{\mathchoice{\makebox[5.25pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[5.25pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[3.67499pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[2.625pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}_{{{\mu}}}}{z^{{\mathchoice{\makebox[5.25pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[5.25pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[3.67499pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[2.625pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}_{{{\mu}}}}{z^{{\mathchoice{\makebox[5.25pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[5.25pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[3.67499pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[2.625pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}_{{{\mu}}}}{z^{{\mathchoice{\makebox[5.25pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[5.25pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[3.67499pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[2.625pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}_{{{\mu}}}}\mathchoice{\bar{z}^{{{\nu}}}_{{\mathchoice{\makebox[5.25pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[5.25pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[3.67499pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[2.625pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}}{\bar{z}^{{{\nu}}}_{{\mathchoice{\makebox[5.25pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[5.25pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[3.67499pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[2.625pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}}{\bar{z}^{{{\nu}}}_{{\mathchoice{\makebox[5.25pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[5.25pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[3.67499pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[2.625pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}}{\bar{z}^{{{\nu}}}_{{\mathchoice{\makebox[5.25pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[5.25pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[3.67499pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[2.625pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}}\mathchoice{\bar{z}^{{\mathchoice{\makebox[5.25pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[5.25pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[3.67499pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[2.625pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}_{{{\nu}}}}{\bar{z}^{{\mathchoice{\makebox[5.25pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[5.25pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[3.67499pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[2.625pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}_{{{\nu}}}}{\bar{z}^{{\mathchoice{\makebox[5.25pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[5.25pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[3.67499pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[2.625pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}_{{{\nu}}}}{\bar{z}^{{\mathchoice{\makebox[5.25pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[5.25pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[3.67499pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[2.625pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}_{{{\nu}}}}=1,

(601)

and hence
\Lambda(L)\in\mathrm{SO}(3,1)
. We already knew
\Lambda(L)\in\mathrm{O}^{+}(3,1)
, and thus we conclude
\Ran\Lambda\subseteq\mathrm{SO}^{+}(3,1)
. One can show that
\Ran\Lambda=\mathrm{SO}^{+}(3,1)
by constructing some key elements of the Lorentz group, such as rotations and boosts centered at each Cartesian axis, explicitly.

Finally, we want to see that
\Lambda\colon\mathrm{SL}(2,\mathbb{C})\to\mathrm{SO}^{+}(3,1)
is two-to-one. This can be seen by noticing that

\displaystyle\mathchoice{\Lambda(-L)^{{{\mu}\mathchoice{\makebox[5.25pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[5.25pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[3.67499pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[2.625pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}_{{\mathchoice{\makebox[5.25pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[5.25pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[3.67499pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[2.625pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}{\nu}}}}{\Lambda(-L)^{{{\mu}\mathchoice{\makebox[5.25pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[5.25pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[3.67499pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[2.625pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}_{{\mathchoice{\makebox[5.25pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[5.25pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[3.67499pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[2.625pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}{\nu}}}}{\Lambda(-L)^{{{\mu}\mathchoice{\makebox[5.25pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[5.25pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[3.67499pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[2.625pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}_{{\mathchoice{\makebox[5.25pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[5.25pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[3.67499pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[2.625pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}{\nu}}}}{\Lambda(-L)^{{{\mu}\mathchoice{\makebox[5.25pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[5.25pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[3.67499pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[2.625pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}_{{\mathchoice{\makebox[5.25pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[5.25pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[3.67499pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[2.625pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}{\nu}}}}

\displaystyle=\frac{1}{2}\Tr[(-L)\sigma_{\nu}(-L)^{\dagger}\bar{\sigma}^{\mu}],

(602a)

\displaystyle=\frac{1}{2}\Tr[L\sigma_{\nu}L^{\dagger}\bar{\sigma}^{\mu}],

(602b)

\displaystyle=\mathchoice{\Lambda(L)^{{{\mu}\mathchoice{\makebox[5.25pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[5.25pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[3.67499pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[2.625pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}_{{\mathchoice{\makebox[5.25pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[5.25pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[3.67499pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[2.625pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}{\nu}}}}{\Lambda(L)^{{{\mu}\mathchoice{\makebox[5.25pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[5.25pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[3.67499pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[2.625pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}_{{\mathchoice{\makebox[5.25pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[5.25pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[3.67499pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[2.625pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}{\nu}}}}{\Lambda(L)^{{{\mu}\mathchoice{\makebox[5.25pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[5.25pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[3.67499pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[2.625pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}_{{\mathchoice{\makebox[5.25pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[5.25pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[3.67499pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[2.625pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}{\nu}}}}{\Lambda(L)^{{{\mu}\mathchoice{\makebox[5.25pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[5.25pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[3.67499pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[2.625pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}_{{\mathchoice{\makebox[5.25pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[5.25pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[3.67499pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[2.625pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}{\nu}}}},

(602c)

and therefore
L
and
-L
are both mapped to
\Lambda(L)
. More rigorously, we find that the kernel of
\Lambda
, defined by

\Ker\Lambda=\quantity{L \in\SL(2,\Comp) \mid\Lambda(L) = \Eins},

(603)

is given by

\Ker\Lambda=\quantity{-\Eins, \Eins}.

(604)

Notice
\Ker\Lambda=\mathbb{Z}_{2}
. This also shows
\Lambda
maps exactly two elements of
\mathrm{SL}(2,\mathbb{C})
to each element of
\mathrm{SO}^{+}(3,1)
. Not more, not less.

Bringing everything together, we conclude that
\mathrm{SL}(2,\mathbb{C})
is a duplicated copy of
\mathrm{SO}^{+}(3,1)
. Hence,

\mathrm{SL}(2,\mathbb{C})/\mathbb{Z}_{2}\cong\mathrm{SO}^{+}(3,1).

(605)

This is in fact merely an application of the first isomorphism theorem for groups (see,
e.g.
, Theorem A-4.73 on Ref.
\citeonline
rotman2015AdvancedModernAlgebraI).

Appendix C
Brief Review of Linearized Gravity

This appendix briefly reviews linearized gravity on Minkowski spacetime with the goal of fixing notation for the many sections that build upon it. There are numerous references on linearized gravity. It is a standard topic in general relativity textbooks (I particularly notice those by
[
51
,
235
]
), but some more specialized references are the book by
[
169
]
and the review article by
[
103
]
.

This algebraic projection should be performed for each Fourier mode
\vec{\boldsymbol{k}}

\gls

TT gauge is a particular case of the de Donder gauge. The subsequent expressions can be derived in general de Donder gauge, but it may be useful to have them expressed in the more specific
\gls
TT gauge. This can be done by simply projecting both sides of the equation of interest accordingly.

C.2
Solving the Linearized Einstein Equations

It is convenient to work in global Cartesian coordinates. In this case, we write
